children.title: Operator Graphs
children.top_down_role: Graph-based representation of set-valued operators.

knowledge_statements.title: Operator Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph of a set-valued operator between arbitrary sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be sets and let \(A:X\rightrightarrows Y\) assign a subset \(Ax\subseteq Y\) to each \(x\in X\). The graph of \(A\) is
\[\operatorname{gra}A:=\{(x,y)\in X\times Y:y\in Ax\}.\]
Thus \(Ax=\{y\in Y:(x,y)\in\operatorname{gra}A\}\), so the operator and its graph determine one another uniquely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The graph records exactly the input-output pairs of a set-valued operator and uniquely determines every operator value.

notation.meaning: set-valued operator from X to Y

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard definition of the graph of a set-valued operator

children.title: Operator Domains
children.top_down_role: Input sets on which operator values are available.

knowledge_statements.title: Operator Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effective domain of a set-valued operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For sets \(X,Y\) and a set-valued operator \(A:X\rightrightarrows Y\), its domain is
\[\operatorname{dom}A:=\{x\in X:Ax\neq\varnothing\}=\{x\in X:\exists y\in Y,\ (x,y)\in\operatorname{gra}A\}.\]
Points outside \(\operatorname{dom}A\) have the empty operator value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The domain consists of inputs at which the operator has at least one output; it is the first-coordinate projection of the graph.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard effective-domain definition for a set-valued operator
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The effective-domain definition and graph-projection characterization are correct and appropriate for this leaf, but the record has no cited source with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Operator Ranges
children.top_down_role: Output sets attained by operator values.

knowledge_statements.title: Operator Ranges
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Range of a set-valued operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For sets \(X,Y\) and a set-valued operator \(A:X\rightrightarrows Y\), its range is
\[\operatorname{ran}A:=\bigcup_{x\in X}Ax=\{y\in Y:\exists x\in X,\ (x,y)\in\operatorname{gra}A\}.\]
Equivalently, \(y\in\operatorname{ran}A\) precisely when the inclusion \(y\in Ax\) is solvable for some \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The range contains all outputs attained by the operator and is the second-coordinate projection of its graph.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard range definition for a set-valued operator
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The range definition and second-coordinate graph characterization are correct and appropriate for this leaf, but no inspectable source is supplied.

children.title: Graph Projection Relations
children.top_down_role: Connections between graph projections, domains, and ranges.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph Projection Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain and range as coordinate projections of the graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:X\rightrightarrows Y\), and let \(\pi_X:X\times Y\to X\) and \(\pi_Y:X\times Y\to Y\) be the coordinate projections. Then
\[\operatorname{dom}A=\pi_X(\operatorname{gra}A),\qquad \operatorname{ran}A=\pi_Y(\operatorname{gra}A).\]
Moreover, for every \(x\in X\), the value \(Ax\) is the vertical section \(\{y\in Y:(x,y)\in\operatorname{gra}A\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projecting the graph onto its first or second coordinate gives the domain or range, while graph sections give individual operator values.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: immediate standard projection representation of graph, domain, and range
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projection identities and vertical-section representation are correct, and representation is the appropriate content kind, but the record lacks a cited source with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Adjoint of a Linear Operator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the algebraic adjoint through the dual pairings of the two spaces; it makes no computational-access or cost assertion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a linear operator \(A:\mathbb{E}\to\mathbb{H}^*\), its adjoint is the operator \(A^*:\mathbb{H}\to\mathbb{E}^*\) characterized by
\[
\langle Ax,y\rangle_{\mathbb H}=\langle A^*y,x\rangle_{\mathbb E},\qquad x\in\mathbb E,\ y\in\mathbb H.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The adjoint is the reverse-direction linear operator whose dual pairing with every original input equals the pairing of the original operator's output with every dual input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A^*:\mathbb{H}\to\mathbb{E}^*,\qquad \langle Ax,y\rangle_{\mathbb H}=\langle A^*y,x\rangle_{\mathbb E}\quad\forall x\in\mathbb E,\ \forall y\in\mathbb H.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Measurable Functional Calculus for a Selfadjoint Operator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and domain of a possibly unbounded function of a selfadjoint operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be selfadjoint on \(\mathcal X\) with spectral family \(\{E_\lambda\}_{\lambda\in\mathbb R}\), and let \(\mathcal M_0\) be the functions measurable with respect to \(d\|E_\lambda x\|^2\) for every \(x\in\mathcal X\). For \(f\in\mathcal M_0\), define \[f(A)x=\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}f(\lambda)\,dE_\lambda x\] on \[\mathcal D(f(A))=\left\{x\in\mathcal X:\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}f(\lambda)^2\,d\|E_\lambda x\|^2<\infty\right\}.\] In particular, every piecewise continuous function belongs to \(\mathcal M_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A measurable function of a selfadjoint operator is defined by spectral integration. Its domain is exactly the set of vectors for which the squared function has finite integral against the associated scalar spectral measure; piecewise continuous functions are admissible.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is selfadjoint on \(\mathcal X\) with spectral family \(\{E_\lambda\}_{\lambda\in\mathbb R}\).
\(f\in\mathcal M_0\), meaning that \(f\) is measurable with respect to \(d\|E_\lambda x\|^2\) for every \(x\in\mathcal X\).

children.title: Inverse Operators
children.top_down_role: Operator inversion as a representation transformation.

knowledge_statements.title: Inverse Operators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relational inverse of a set-valued operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(A:X\rightrightarrows Y\), the inverse operator \(A^{-1}:Y\rightrightarrows X\) is defined by
\[x\in A^{-1}y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y\in Ax.\]
Consequently,
\[\operatorname{gra}A^{-1}=\{(y,x):(x,y)\in\operatorname{gra}A\},\quad \operatorname{dom}A^{-1}=\operatorname{ran}A,\quad \operatorname{ran}A^{-1}=\operatorname{dom}A.\]
This definition does not require \(A\) to be single-valued or injective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inverse operator reverses every input-output pair; its domain and range are the original range and domain.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard relational inverse for set-valued operators
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The relational inverse definition and the stated graph, domain, and range identities are correct without injectivity or single-valuedness assumptions, but no inspectable source is cited.

children.title: Operator Sums
children.top_down_role: Additive combinations of set-valued or single-valued operators.

knowledge_statements.title: Operator Sums
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise Minkowski sum of compatible set-valued operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a set, let \(Y\) be a real vector space, and let \(A,B:X\rightrightarrows Y\). Their pointwise sum \(A+B:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is
\[(A+B)x:=Ax+Bx:=\{a+b:a\in Ax,\ b\in Bx\}.\]
Its domain satisfies
\[\operatorname{dom}(A+B)=\operatorname{dom}A\cap\operatorname{dom}B.\]
The equality uses the convention that a Minkowski sum involving the empty set is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compatible set-valued operators are added pointwise by taking all pairwise sums of their values; the sum is defined where both are nonempty.

notation.meaning: Minkowski sum of the two value sets

children.title: Operator Compositions
children.top_down_role: Composed operator structures relevant to transformed models.

knowledge_statements.title: Operator Compositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relational composition of set-valued operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:X\rightrightarrows Y\) and \(B:Y\rightrightarrows Z\). Their composition \(B\circ A:X\rightrightarrows Z\) is defined by
\[(B\circ A)x:=\bigcup_{y\in Ax}By=\{z\in Z:\exists y\in Y,\ y\in Ax\ \text{and}\ z\in By\}.\]
Hence
\[\operatorname{dom}(B\circ A)=\{x\in\operatorname{dom}A:Ax\cap\operatorname{dom}B\neq\varnothing\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Composition sends an input through every intermediate value of the first operator and collects all outputs of the second.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard relational composition of set-valued operators
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The relational composition definition and domain formula are mathematically correct and properly typed, but no source with a specific locator is cited.

assumptions_latex: \(A:\mathbb R\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^2\), \(B:\mathbb R\rightrightarrows\mathbb R\), and \(C:\mathbb R^3\rightrightarrows\mathbb R\).

children.title: Operator Zero Sets
children.top_down_role: Solution sets represented as zeros of operators.

knowledge_statements.title: Operator Zero Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zeros of a set-valued operator on a vector space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a real vector space and let \(A:X\rightrightarrows X\). The zero set of \(A\) is
\[\operatorname{zer}A:=\{x\in X:0\in Ax\}=A^{-1}(0).\]
Thus solving the inclusion \(0\in Ax\) is exactly the problem of finding a member of \(\operatorname{zer}A\). No single-valuedness or monotonicity assumption is part of this definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The zero set consists of points whose operator value contains the zero vector; equivalently, it is the inverse image of zero.

children.title: Mapping Fixed-Point Sets
children.top_down_role: Solution sets represented through fixed points of mappings.

knowledge_statements.title: Mapping Fixed-Point Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-point set of a self-map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a set and let \(T:X\to X\) be a single-valued self-map. Its fixed-point set is
\[\operatorname{Fix}T:=\{x\in X:Tx=x\}.\]
For a set-valued self-operator \(T:X\rightrightarrows X\), the corresponding relational convention is \(\operatorname{Fix}T:=\{x\in X:x\in Tx\}\); this convention must be stated when \(T\) is not a mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed point is unchanged by a self-map; for a set-valued operator, the relational version requires the point to belong to its image.

children.title: Zero-to-Fixed-Point Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural passage from operator-zero models to fixed-point models.

knowledge_statements.title: Zero-to-Fixed-Point Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resolvent correspondence for a nonzero scalar parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a real vector space, let \(A:X\rightrightarrows X\), and let \(\lambda\neq0\). Define the relational resolvent \(J_{\lambda A}:=(\operatorname{Id}+\lambda A)^{-1}\). Then
\[x\in\operatorname{zer}A\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in J_{\lambda A}x.\]
If \(J_{\lambda A}\) is single-valued on \(X\), this becomes
\[\operatorname{zer}A=\operatorname{Fix}J_{\lambda A}.\]
Indeed, both predicates are equivalent to \(x\in x+\lambda Ax\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zeros of an operator are precisely relational fixed points of its resolvent; when the resolvent is a self-map, the usual fixed-point sets coincide.
assumptions_latex: \(A:X\rightrightarrows X\) on a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{zer}A=\{x\in X:x\in J_{\lambda A}x\}\), and \(\operatorname{zer}A=\operatorname{Fix}J_{\lambda A}\) when the resolvent is single-valued.

children.title: Correspondence Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where the expected solution-set correspondence needs qualification.

knowledge_statements.title: Correspondence Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the mapping formulation when the resolvent is multivalued.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The usual equality with a mapping fixed-point set requires the resolvent to be a single-valued self-map. On \(X=\mathbb R\), define \(A0=\{0\}\), \(A1=\{-1\}\), and \(Ax=\varnothing\) otherwise. For \(\lambda=1\), both \(0\in0+A0\) and \(0\in1+A1\), so
\[J_A0=(\operatorname{Id}+A)^{-1}(0)=\{0,1\}.\]
Thus \(J_A\) is not a mapping and the conventional expression \(\operatorname{Fix}J_A=\{x:J_Ax=x\}\) is unavailable, although the relational equivalence \(0\in Ax\Longleftrightarrow x\in J_Ax\) remains valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without a single-valued resolvent, the conventional mapping fixed-point set is unavailable, though the relational zero-to-fixed-point equivalence still holds.
assumptions_latex: \(A:\mathbb R\rightrightarrows\mathbb R\) has the displayed values.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit counterexample follows directly from the relational resolvent definition

knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Operators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space definition for a possibly set-valued operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\). The operator \(A\) is monotone if
\[
(\forall (x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}A)\qquad \langle x-y,u-v\rangle\geq 0,
\]
where \(\operatorname{gra}A=\{(x,u)\in H\times H:u\in Ax\}\). Equivalently, every two graph points are monotonically related under the canonical product pairing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An operator is monotone when the displacement between any two inputs has nonnegative inner product with the corresponding displacement between selected outputs.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical Hilbert-space definition of a monotone set-valued operator
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically standard, well scoped to a real Hilbert space, and appropriate for a definition container, but no source with a specific inspectable locator is cited.

children.title: Maximally Monotone Operators
children.top_down_role: The graph-maximal monotonicity regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Maximally Monotone Operators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximality is taken with respect to graph inclusion among monotone operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be monotone. It is maximally monotone if no monotone operator \(B:H\rightrightarrows H\) properly extends its graph:
\[
\operatorname{gra}A\subseteq\operatorname{gra}B\ \text{and}\ B\ \text{monotone}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{gra}A=\operatorname{gra}B.
\]
Thus maximality concerns inclusion of graphs and does not mean that \(Ax\) is maximal pointwise or that \(\operatorname{dom}A=H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone operator is maximally monotone when its graph admits no proper monotone enlargement in the same ambient Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\text{ is maximally monotone}\iff A\text{ has no proper monotone graph extension}.\)
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard graph-inclusion definition of maximal monotonicity
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The graph-inclusion definition of maximal monotonicity is correct and fits the terminal container, but the record has no inspectable citation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Resolvent fixed-point rescaling identity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: No continuity or monotonicity assumption on the single-valued mapping \(B\) is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) be maximally monotone, let \(B:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\), and let \(\gamma>0\). Then \[\operatorname{Fix}\bigl(J_A\circ(\operatorname{Id}+\gamma(B-\operatorname{Id}))\bigr)=\operatorname{Fix}\bigl(J_{\gamma^{-1}A}\circ B\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Applying the resolvent of A after the affine map Id plus gamma times B minus Id has the same fixed points as applying B first and then the resolvent of the rescaled operator gamma inverse A.
assumptions_latex: A:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\text{ is maximally monotone}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak–strong primal–dual graph closure under linear coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Only the candidate primal and dual variables are assumed to converge weakly; both coupling residuals must converge strongly to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) and \(B:\mathcal K\rightrightarrows\mathcal K\) be maximally monotone, and let \(L\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H,\mathcal K)\). Suppose \((x_n,u_n)\in\operatorname{gra}A\), \((y_n,v_n)\in\operatorname{gra}B\), \(x_n\rightharpoonup x\), \(v_n\rightharpoonup v\), \(Lx_n-y_n\to0\), and \(u_n+L^*v_n\to0\). Then \((x,-L^*v)\in\operatorname{gra}A\), \((Lx,v)\in\operatorname{gra}B\), and \[x\in\operatorname{zer}(A+L^*\circ B\circ L),\qquad v\in\operatorname{zer}(-L\circ A^{-1}\circ(-L^*)+B^{-1}).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two maximally monotone operators coupled by a bounded linear map, weak limits of graph points satisfy the limiting primal and dual graph relations when both coupling residuals vanish strongly. The limits consequently solve the associated primal and dual inclusions.
assumptions_latex: A:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\text{ and }B:\mathcal K\rightrightarrows\mathcal K\text{ are maximally monotone}

children.title: Maximal Extension Relations
children.top_down_role: Relations between monotone graphs and their maximal extensions.

knowledge_statements.title: Maximal Extension Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes maximality through points monotonically related to an operator graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a monotone operator \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\), a pair \((x,u)\in H\times H\) is monotonically related to \(\operatorname{gra}A\) when
\[
(\forall (y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}A)\qquad \langle x-y,u-v\rangle\geq0.
\]
The graph \(\operatorname{gra}A\cup\{(x,u)\}\) is then monotone. Consequently, \(A\) is maximally monotone exactly when every pair monotonically related to its graph already belongs to its graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone graph is maximal exactly when every point compatible with all its monotonicity inequalities is already in the graph.

children.title: Nonmaximal Graph Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Consequences of working with monotone graphs lacking maximality.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonmaximal Graph Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete monotone graph whose restricted domain leaves proper monotone extensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On \(H=\mathbb R\), define \(A:\mathbb R\rightrightarrows\mathbb R\) by \(A0=\{0\}\) and \(Ax=\varnothing\) for \(x\neq0\). Its one-point graph is monotone, but it is not maximally monotone: the zero operator \(B:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\), given by \(Bx=0\) for every \(x\), is monotone and satisfies
\[
\operatorname{gra}A\subsetneq\operatorname{gra}B.
\]
Hence monotonicity alone does not ensure graph maximality, even in one dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The zero operator restricted to the singleton domain zero is monotone but not maximal, because the everywhere-defined zero operator properly extends it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\text{ is monotone but not maximally monotone}.\)

children.title: Strong Monotonicity

knowledge_statements.title: Strong Monotonicity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong monotonicity with a fixed positive quadratic modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\), and let \(\alpha>0\). The operator \(A\) is \(\alpha\)-strongly monotone if
\[
(\forall (x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}A)\qquad
\langle x-y,u-v\rangle\geq\alpha\lVert x-y\rVert^2.
\]
Dropping the nonnegative term on the right shows that every strongly monotone operator is monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An operator is strongly monotone when its monotonicity pairing dominates a fixed positive multiple of the squared input distance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle x-y,u-v\rangle\geq\alpha\lVert x-y\rVert^2\) for all graph pairs.

children.title: Uniform Monotonicity
children.top_down_role: Modulus-based strengthened monotonicity across nonlinear growth regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Monotonicity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform monotonicity expressed by a positive distance-dependent modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\). The operator \(A\) is uniformly monotone with modulus \(\phi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty]\) if \(\phi\) is increasing, \(\phi(0)=0\), \(\phi(t)>0\) for \(t>0\), and
\[
(\forall (x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}A)\qquad
\langle x-y,u-v\rangle\geq\phi(\lVert x-y\rVert).
\]
The modulus may be nonquadratic and need not yield a positive strong-monotonicity constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform monotonicity lower-bounds the monotonicity pairing by a positive function of every nonzero input distance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle x-y,u-v\rangle\geq\phi(\lVert x-y\rVert)\) for all graph pairs.

children.title: Strengthening Hierarchy

knowledge_statements.title: Strengthening Hierarchy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-way implications among quadratic, uniform, strict, and ordinary monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is \(\alpha\)-strongly monotone for some \(\alpha>0\), then it is uniformly monotone with modulus \(\phi(t)=\alpha t^2\). Every uniformly monotone operator is strictly monotone in the sense that
\[
x\neq y\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\langle x-y,u-v\rangle>0
\]
for \((x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}A\), and every strictly monotone operator is monotone. Thus
\[
\text{strong}\Longrightarrow\text{uniform}\Longrightarrow\text{strict}\Longrightarrow\text{monotone}.
\]
The reverse implications do not hold without additional hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong monotonicity implies uniform monotonicity, which implies strict monotonicity, which implies monotonicity; the converses generally fail.

notation.meaning: Quadratic modulus induced by strong monotonicity.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: implications follow directly from the displayed definitions

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: strict monotonicity gives uniqueness of a zero, while strong monotonicity gives inverse single-valuedness and the reciprocal-modulus Lipschitz bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniqueness of zeros under strict monotonicity and inverse stability under strong monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\). Suppose first that \(A\) is strictly monotone, meaning that for all \((x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}A\),
\[
x\neq y\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\langle x-y,u-v\rangle>0.
\]
If \(0\in Ax\) and \(0\in Ay\), strict monotonicity excludes \(x\neq y\), so \(x=y\). Separately, if \(A\) is \(\alpha\)-strongly monotone for some \(\alpha>0\), then for every \((x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}A\),
\[
\alpha\lVert x-y\rVert\leq\lVert u-v\rVert.
\]
Consequently, any zero of a strictly monotone operator is unique, and under \(\alpha\)-strong monotonicity the inverse \(A^{-1}\) is single-valued and \(1/\alpha\)-Lipschitz on \(\operatorname{ran}A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict monotonicity makes any zero unique. Strong monotonicity additionally makes the inverse single-valued and Lipschitz on the operator range.

children.title: Cocoercive Operators

knowledge_statements.title: Cocoercive Operators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-valued Hilbert-space cocoercivity convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(B:H\to H\), and let \(\beta>0\). The operator \(B\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive if
\[
(\forall x,y\in H)\qquad
\langle x-y,Bx-By\rangle\geq\beta\lVert Bx-By\rVert^2.
\]
Cocoercivity is also called inverse strong monotonicity. The displayed inequality immediately implies monotonicity of \(B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single-valued operator is cocoercive when its monotonicity pairing controls the squared distance between its output values.

children.title: Monotone-Lipschitz Operators

knowledge_statements.title: Monotone-Lipschitz Operators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intersection of monotonicity and global Lipschitz continuity for single-valued maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(B:H\to H\). For \(L\geq0\), the operator \(B\) is monotone and \(L\)-Lipschitz if, for every \(x,y\in H\),
\[
\langle x-y,Bx-By\rangle\geq0
\quad\text{and}\quad
\lVert Bx-By\rVert\leq L\lVert x-y\rVert.
\]
Neither inequality strengthens the other in general; this class can contain nonsymmetric and skew components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone-Lipschitz map simultaneously satisfies the monotonicity inequality and a global Lipschitz bound on output differences.

children.title: Cocoercivity–Lipschitz Relations
children.top_down_role: Implications and separations between the two regularity classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Cocoercivity–Lipschitz Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General implication and convex-gradient converse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(B:H\to H\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive, then Cauchy–Schwarz yields
\[
\lVert Bx-By\rVert\leq\beta^{-1}\lVert x-y\rVert,
\]
so \(B\) is monotone and \(1/\beta\)-Lipschitz. The converse fails for general monotone Lipschitz operators. In the structured case \(B=\nabla f\), where \(f:H\to\mathbb R\) is convex, Fréchet differentiable, and has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient with \(L>0\), the Baillon–Haddad relation gives that \(B\) is \(1/L\)-cocoercive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cocoercivity implies monotonicity and Lipschitz continuity. The converse is false generally but holds with reciprocal constants for gradients of convex smooth functions.
assumptions_latex: For the converse, \(B=\nabla f\) with \(f\) convex and \(\nabla f\) \(L\)-Lipschitz.

children.title: Forward-Treatment Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on direct forward handling across the two classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Forward-Treatment Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cocoercivity permits a forward step; monotone Lipschitz continuity alone does not.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(B:H\to H\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive, then \(I-\gamma B\) is nonexpansive for \(0\leq\gamma\leq2\beta\). This conclusion fails for a merely monotone Lipschitz map. On \(H=\mathbb R^2\), let \(B(x_1,x_2)=(-x_2,x_1)\). Then \(B\) is monotone and \(1\)-Lipschitz, but for every \(\gamma>0\),
\[
\lVert (I-\gamma B)x\rVert=\sqrt{1+\gamma^2}\,\lVert x\rVert.
\]
Thus the explicit forward map is expansive for every positive step size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cocoercivity makes suitably small forward steps nonexpansive, whereas a skew monotone Lipschitz operator produces an expansive forward step at every positive step size.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space for the cocoercive assertion.
For the boundary example, \(H=\mathbb R^2\) and \(B(x_1,x_2)=(-x_2,x_1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\text{ cocoercive}\Rightarrow I-\gamma B\text{ nonexpansive for }0\leq\gamma\leq2\beta;\) monotone Lipschitz continuity alone is insufficient.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: nonexpansiveness follows by expanding the squared norm; the skew example is directly checkable

children.title: Cyclic Monotonicity
children.top_down_role: The monotonicity regime tied to convex-potential representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Cyclic Monotonicity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-cycle definition for a set-valued operator on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\). The operator \(A\) is cyclically monotone if, for every integer \(m\geq 2\), every \((x_i,u_i)\in\operatorname{gra}A\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and the convention \(x_{m+1}=x_1\), one has
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{m}\langle x_i-x_{i+1},u_i\rangle\geq 0.
\]
Taking \(m=2\) shows that every cyclically monotone operator is monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An operator is cyclically monotone when its graph satisfies the monotonicity inequality around every finite closed cycle; ordinary monotonicity follows from two-point cycles.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is cyclically monotone exactly when the displayed cycle inequality holds for every finite graph cycle.

children.title: Nonexpansive Mappings

knowledge_statements.title: Nonexpansive Mappings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric definition on a subset of a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty subset of a real Hilbert space \(H\). A mapping \(T:C\to H\) is nonexpansive if
\[
\|Tx-Ty\|\leq \|x-y\|\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in C.
\]
Thus \(T\) has Lipschitz constant at most \(1\) on \(C\). If additionally \(T(C)\subseteq C\), it is a nonexpansive self-map of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mapping is nonexpansive when it never increases the distance between two points in its domain.
assumptions_latex: \(C\neq\varnothing\) is contained in a real Hilbert space \(H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is nonexpansive if and only if \(\|Tx-Ty\|\leq\|x-y\|\) for all \(x,y\in C\).

notation.meaning: Norm induced by the Hilbert-space inner product.

children.title: Firmly Nonexpansive Mappings

knowledge_statements.title: Firmly Nonexpansive Mappings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space definition characteristic of resolvents of monotone operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty subset of a real Hilbert space \(H\). A mapping \(T:C\to H\) is firmly nonexpansive if
\[
\|Tx-Ty\|^2\leq \langle Tx-Ty,x-y\rangle
\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in C.
\]
Equivalently, \(T\) is firmly nonexpansive precisely when \(2T-\operatorname{Id}\) is nonexpansive on \(C\). Every firmly nonexpansive mapping is nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mapping is firmly nonexpansive when its squared output distance is bounded by the output-input displacement inner product; equivalently, its reflection is nonexpansive.
assumptions_latex: \(C\neq\varnothing\) is contained in a real Hilbert space \(H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is firmly nonexpansive exactly when the displayed inequality holds, equivalently when \(2T-\operatorname{Id}\) is nonexpansive.

children.title: Averaged Mappings

knowledge_statements.title: Averaged Mappings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard averaged-operator definition with averaging parameter in the open unit interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of a real Hilbert space \(H\), and let \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). A self-map \(T:C\to C\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged if there exists a nonexpansive self-map \(R:C\to C\) such that
\[
T=(1-\alpha)\operatorname{Id}+\alpha R.
\]
A mapping is averaged if it is \(\alpha\)-averaged for at least one \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). Firm nonexpansiveness is equivalent to \(1/2\)-averagedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An averaged mapping is a strict convex combination of the identity and a nonexpansive self-map. Firmly nonexpansive mappings are exactly one-half averaged mappings.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty convex subset of a real Hilbert space \(H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged exactly when \(T=(1-\alpha)\operatorname{Id}+\alpha R\) for some nonexpansive \(R:C\to C\).

notation.meaning: Nonexpansive component of the averaged representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Contractive Mappings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform strict Lipschitz contraction on a metric subset of a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty subset of a real Hilbert space \(H\). A mapping \(T:C\to C\) is contractive, or a contraction, if there exists \(q\in[0,1)\) such that
\[
\|Tx-Ty\|\leq q\|x-y\|
\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in C.
\]
The least admissible \(q\), when considered as an infimum, is the Lipschitz modulus of \(T\). Every contraction is nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A contraction uniformly reduces pairwise distances by a fixed factor strictly below one, and therefore is nonexpansive.
assumptions_latex: \(C\neq\varnothing\) is contained in a real Hilbert space \(H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is contractive exactly when it satisfies the displayed estimate for some \(q<1\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Contraction Mapping, Contraction Modulus, and Fixed Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Norm-dependent contractions on self-mapped subsets of finite-dimensional space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(g:X\to X\), and fix a norm \(\|\cdot\|\). The map \(g\) is a contraction with contraction modulus \(\gamma\) if \(0\le\gamma<1\) and \[\|g(x)-g(y)\|\le\gamma\|x-y\|\qquad\forall x,y\in X.\] A point \(x^*\in X\) is a fixed point of \(g\) if \(g(x^*)=x^*\). The associated fixed-point iteration is \(x^{k+1}=g(x^k)\). Contractivity is norm-dependent: a map can be contractive under one norm and fail to be contractive under another.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A self-map is a contraction in a chosen norm if it reduces every pairwise distance by a common factor strictly below one. A fixed point is left unchanged by the map, and repeated application gives the standard fixed-point iteration. Contractivity may depend on the chosen norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g\text{ is a contraction of modulus }\gamma\iff \|g(x)-g(y)\|\le\gamma\|x-y\|\ \forall x,y\in X;\quad g(x^*)=x^*\text{ defines a fixed point}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Contraction Mapping Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence, uniqueness, global convergence, and a geometric error bound for contractions on closed subsets of finite-dimensional normed space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be closed, and let \(g:X\to X\) be a contraction with modulus \(\gamma\in[0,1)\) in a fixed norm. Then \(g\) has a unique fixed point \(x^*\in X\). For every \(x^0\in X\), the sequence defined by \(x^{k+1}=g(x^k)\) converges to \(x^*\), and \[\|x^k-x^*\|\le\gamma^k\|x^0-x^*\|\qquad\forall k\ge0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A contraction from a closed subset of finite-dimensional space into itself has exactly one fixed point. Starting from any point in the set, fixed-point iteration converges to that point, with the kth error bounded by gamma to the kth power times the initial error.

children.title: Quasi-Nonexpansive Mappings
children.top_down_role: Mappings controlled relative to their fixed-point sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Quasi-Nonexpansive Mappings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance decrease measured only relative to fixed points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty subset of a real Hilbert space \(H\), and let \(T:C\to C\) have at least one fixed point. The mapping \(T\) is quasi-nonexpansive if
\[
\|Tx-p\|\leq\|x-p\|
\qquad\text{for every }x\in C\text{ and }p\in\operatorname{Fix}T.
\]
Unlike nonexpansiveness, this condition does not directly compare \(Tx\) and \(Ty\) for two arbitrary points \(x,y\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quasi-nonexpansive map does not increase the distance from any point to any fixed point, but need not control distances between arbitrary images.
assumptions_latex: \(C\neq\varnothing\) is contained in a real Hilbert space \(H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is quasi-nonexpansive exactly when \(\|Tx-p\|\leq\|x-p\|\) for all \(x\in C\) and \(p\in\operatorname{Fix}T\).

notation.meaning: Fixed-point set of T, consisting of p with Tp=p.

children.title: Fixed-Point-Relative Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometric behavior measured against fixed points.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Point-Relative Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent displacement geometry for quasi-nonexpansiveness in Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty subset of a real Hilbert space \(H\), let \(T:C\to C\), and fix \(p\in\operatorname{Fix}T\). For every \(x\in C\), expansion of the squared norm gives
\[
\|Tx-p\|^2\leq\|x-p\|^2
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
2\langle x-p,x-Tx\rangle\geq\|x-Tx\|^2.
\]
Consequently, \(T\) is quasi-nonexpansive exactly when the right-hand displacement inequality holds for every \(x\in C\) and every \(p\in\operatorname{Fix}T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance decrease toward a fixed point is equivalent to a positive alignment inequality between the fixed-point displacement and the residual.
assumptions_latex: \(C\neq\varnothing\) lies in a real Hilbert space \(H\).

children.title: Strictness Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Containment and separation among contractive, nonexpansive, and quasi-nonexpansive regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Strictness Hierarchy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict inclusion hierarchy among fixed-point mapping regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On any nonempty subset \(C\) of a real Hilbert space, every contraction is nonexpansive. Every nonexpansive self-map with a nonempty fixed-point set is quasi-nonexpansive. Among self-maps with nonempty fixed-point sets, the inclusions
\[
\{\text{contractions}\}\subsetneq
\{\text{nonexpansive maps}\}\subsetneq
\{\text{quasi-nonexpansive maps}\}
\]
are strict in general. The identity map witnesses the first strictness. On \(\mathbb R\), the map \(T(x)=((2+\sin(x^2))/4)x\) is quasi-nonexpansive with unique fixed point \(0\), but is not nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Contractions form a strict subclass of nonexpansive maps, which, when fixed points exist, form a strict subclass of quasi-nonexpansive maps.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty subset of a real Hilbert space.
Mappings in the second inclusion have \(\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\).

children.title: Minty Surjectivity Family

knowledge_statements.title: Minty Surjectivity Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minty characterization of maximal monotonicity on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be monotone on a real Hilbert space \(H\), and let \(\lambda>0\). Then \(A\) is maximally monotone if and only if
\[
\operatorname{ran}(\operatorname{Id}+\lambda A)=H.
\]
If this condition holds for one \(\lambda>0\), it holds for every \(\lambda>0\). In that case the resolvent \(J_{\lambda A}=(\operatorname{Id}+\lambda A)^{-1}\) is an everywhere-defined, single-valued, firmly nonexpansive mapping from \(H\) to \(H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone operator is maximal exactly when every shifted inclusion is solvable; its resolvent is then everywhere defined, single-valued, and firmly nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is maximally monotone if and only if \(\operatorname{ran}(\operatorname{Id}+\lambda A)=H\); then \(J_{\lambda A}\) is firmly nonexpansive on \(H\).

notation.meaning: Resolvent of the scaled operator λA.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Minty characterization and resolvent consequences are stated with appropriate Hilbert-space hypotheses and theorem content kind, but no exact theorem citation is supplied.

children.title: Subdifferential Maximality
children.top_down_role: Maximal monotonicity of convex subdifferentials.

knowledge_statements.title: Subdifferential Maximality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximal monotonicity of a proper lower-semicontinuous convex subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Define
\[
\partial f(x)=\{u\in H: f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle u,y-x\rangle\text{ for every }y\in H\}.
\]
Then the convex subdifferential \(\partial f:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone. Equivalently, its graph admits no proper monotone extension in \(H\times H\), and \(\operatorname{ran}(\operatorname{Id}+\lambda\partial f)=H\) for every \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdifferential of every proper lower-semicontinuous convex function on a Hilbert space is maximally monotone and has an everywhere-defined resolvent.
assumptions_latex: \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f\) is maximally monotone, and \(\operatorname{ran}(\operatorname{Id}+\lambda\partial f)=H\) for every \(\lambda>0\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The maximal-monotonicity theorem and Minty consequence are correctly scoped, but the record provides no inspectable theorem citation.

children.title: Cyclic-Monotonicity Representation
children.top_down_role: Representation of convex-potential-generated operators.

knowledge_statements.title: Cyclic-Monotonicity Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rockafellar representation of cyclically monotone operators by convex potentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) have nonempty graph. The operator \(A\) is cyclically monotone if and only if there exists a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) such that
\[
\operatorname{gra}A\subseteq\operatorname{gra}\partial f.
\]
Moreover, \(A\) is maximally cyclically monotone if and only if there exists a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) such that
\[
A=\partial f.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cyclically monotone operators are precisely graph restrictions of convex subdifferentials; maximal cyclic monotonicity corresponds to equality with a convex subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is cyclically monotone if and only if \(A\subseteq\partial f\) for some proper lower-semicontinuous convex \(f\); maximal cyclic monotonicity is equivalent to \(A=\partial f\) for such an \(f\).

notation.meaning: Graph inclusion between the two set-valued operators.

children.title: Sum Maximality Principles
children.top_down_role: Qualification-dependent maximality of operator sums.

knowledge_statements.title: Sum Maximality Principles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rockafellar sum theorem under an interior-domain qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, and let \(A,B:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximally monotone. Suppose the Rockafellar qualification
\[
\operatorname{dom}A\cap\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}B)\neq\varnothing
\]
holds, with the roles of \(A\) and \(B\) interchangeable. Define the pointwise sum by
\[
(A+B)x=\{a+b:a\in Ax,\ b\in Bx\}.
\]
Then \(A+B\) is maximally monotone. Consequently, for every \(\lambda>0\), one has \(\operatorname{ran}(\operatorname{Id}+\lambda(A+B))=H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sum of two maximally monotone operators remains maximally monotone when one domain meets the interior of the other domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A+B\) is maximally monotone and \(\operatorname{ran}(\operatorname{Id}+\lambda(A+B))=H\) for every \(\lambda>0\).

notation.meaning: Pointwise Minkowski sum of the operator values.
Norm-topological interior of the domain of B.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Resolvent Transformation Geometry

children.title: Resolvent Mapping Family
children.top_down_role: Parameter-dependent resolvent mappings of monotone operators.

knowledge_statements.title: Resolvent Mapping Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines parameter-dependent resolvents on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be an operator, and let \(\gamma>0\). The resolvent of \(A\) with parameter \(\gamma\) is the set-valued mapping
\[J_{\gamma A}:=(\operatorname{Id}+\gamma A)^{-1}.\]
Thus \(p\in J_{\gamma A}(x)\) exactly when \(x-p\in\gamma A p\). If \(A\) is maximally monotone, then every \(J_{\gamma A}\) is single-valued, defined on all of \(H\), and firmly nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The resolvent transforms an inclusion into a fixed-point map; maximal monotonicity makes every positive-parameter resolvent everywhere defined, single-valued, and firmly nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J_{\gamma A}=(\operatorname{Id}+\gamma A)^{-1}\), with \(p\in J_{\gamma A}(x)\iff x-p\in\gamma Ap\).

notation.meaning: Resolvent of the scaled operator gamma A.
Identity mapping on the Hilbert space.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and maximal-monotonicity properties are mathematically standard, internally consistent, and appropriate for the resolvent-family container, but no inspectable source citation is supplied for the nontrivial full-domain, single-valuedness, and firm-nonexpansiveness claims.

children.title: Reflected Resolvent Family
children.top_down_role: Cayley and reflection constructions used by splitting methods.

knowledge_statements.title: Reflected Resolvent Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the Cayley-type reflection associated with each resolvent parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) and \(\gamma>0\). The reflected resolvent, or Cayley transform, associated with \(A\) is
\[R_{\gamma A}:=2J_{\gamma A}-\operatorname{Id}.\]
Equivalently, if \(p=J_{\gamma A}(x)\), then \(R_{\gamma A}(x)=2p-x\). When \(A\) is maximally monotone, firm nonexpansiveness of \(J_{\gamma A}\) is equivalent to nonexpansiveness of \(R_{\gamma A}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The reflected resolvent reflects an input across its resolvent image; for maximal monotone operators it is nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_{\gamma A}=2J_{\gamma A}-\operatorname{Id}\); if \(A\) is maximally monotone, then \(R_{\gamma A}\) is nonexpansive.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reflected-resolvent definition and nonexpansiveness statement fit the container and are mathematically standard, but the record supplies no source with a specific locator supporting the definition and equivalence claim.

children.title: Minty Parametrization
children.top_down_role: Graph representation through resolvent coordinates.

knowledge_statements.title: Minty Parametrization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parametrizes a monotone graph using resolvent coordinates at fixed positive scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximally monotone and let \(\gamma>0\). Its graph admits the resolvent parametrization
\[\operatorname{gra}A=\left\{\left(J_{\gamma A}x,\,\gamma^{-1}(x-J_{\gamma A}x)\right):x\in H\right\}.\]
Indeed, every \(x\in H\) determines one graph pair, and every \((p,u)\in\operatorname{gra}A\) is obtained uniquely from the coordinate \(x=p+\gamma u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every graph point of a maximally monotone operator is represented uniquely by a resolvent input and its scaled residual.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is the correct Minty resolvent parametrization, with explicit scale and compatible plain and LaTeX statements. No inspectable citation is provided for the graph representation or uniqueness assertion.

children.title: Inverse-Dual Resolvent Correspondence

children.title: Resolvents of Inverse Operators
children.top_down_role: Resolvent structures induced by operator inversion.

knowledge_statements.title: Resolvents of Inverse Operators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the unit-scale inverse-resolvent identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximally monotone. Then \(A^{-1}\) is maximally monotone and its unit-scale resolvent satisfies
\[J_{A^{-1}}=\operatorname{Id}-J_A.\]
Consequently, for each \(x\in H\), the pair \(p=J_Ax\) and \(u=J_{A^{-1}}x\) obeys \(x=p+u\), \(u\in Ap\), and \(p\in A^{-1}u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At unit scale, the resolvents of a maximal monotone operator and its inverse are complementary mappings.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The unit-scale inverse-resolvent identity and graph-coordinate consequences are correct and fit this property container, but the record has no citation with a section, theorem, definition, or page locator.

children.title: Dual Resolvent Families
children.top_down_role: Resolvents associated with dual operator representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Resolvent Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairs primal resolvents with reciprocally scaled inverse-operator resolvents.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a maximally monotone operator \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) and \(\gamma>0\), define the primal-dual resolvent pair at scale \(\gamma\) by
\[P_\gamma:=J_{\gamma A},\qquad D_\gamma:=J_{\gamma^{-1}A^{-1}}.\]
For each \(x\in H\), \(P_\gamma x\) resolves the inclusion in \(A\), while \(D_\gamma(x/\gamma)\) resolves the corresponding inverse inclusion in \(A^{-1}\). Both mappings are everywhere defined and firmly nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal resolvent at scale gamma pairs naturally with the inverse-operator resolvent at reciprocal scale.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two displayed families are well-defined and firmly nonexpansive under maximal monotonicity, but the named primal-dual pairing and its intended correspondence are not sourced. A specific authoritative locator is required, particularly because this terminology is not fully standardized.

children.title: Resolvent Complementarity
children.top_down_role: Complementary relations linking primal and inverse-side resolvents.

knowledge_statements.title: Resolvent Complementarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the scaled decomposition linking primal and inverse resolvents.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximally monotone and let \(\gamma>0\). For every \(x\in H\), the scaled resolvent decomposition is
\[J_{\gamma A}(x)+\gamma J_{\gamma^{-1}A^{-1}}(x/\gamma)=x.\]
If \(p=J_{\gamma A}(x)\) and \(u=J_{\gamma^{-1}A^{-1}}(x/\gamma)\), then \(x=p+\gamma u\), \(u\in Ap\), and \(p\in A^{-1}u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal and reciprocally scaled inverse resolvents split every input into compatible primal and dual graph coordinates.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scaled resolvent complementarity formula, reciprocal scale, argument rescaling, and graph inclusions are correct and match the duality container. The nontrivial identity nevertheless lacks an inspectable source locator.

children.title: Duality Compatibility Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions limiting transfer between primal, inverse, and dual resolvent views.

knowledge_statements.title: Duality Compatibility Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows why reciprocal scaling and argument rescaling cannot be omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The unit-scale identity \(J_A+J_{A^{-1}}=\operatorname{Id}\) does not extend as \(J_{\gamma A}+J_{\gamma A^{-1}}=\operatorname{Id}\) for arbitrary \(\gamma\). On \(H=\mathbb{R}\), take \(A=\operatorname{Id}\). Then \(A^{-1}=\operatorname{Id}\) and
\[J_{\gamma A}(x)+J_{\gamma A^{-1}}(x)=\frac{2}{1+\gamma}x,\]
which equals \(x\) for every \(x\) only when \(\gamma=1\). Thus reciprocal operator scaling and argument rescaling are essential in the general complementarity formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Using the same nonunit scale for an operator and its inverse destroys resolvent complementarity, even for the identity operator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The identity-operator counterexample is correct, and failure_boundary is the exact mathematical role for this container. Because the record advances a general boundary claim without any citation, it requires an authoritative locator or a citable source presenting the scaled complementarity boundary.

children.title: Proximal Existence

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Existence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence of a quadratic-regularized minimizer in a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and let \(\lambda>0\). For every \(x\in H\), the function
\[y\mapsto f(y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\lVert y-x\rVert^2\]
is proper, lower semicontinuous, coercive, and strongly convex. In particular, it attains its infimum at some point of \(H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every proper lower-semicontinuous convex function has a proximal minimizer at every point and every positive scale.
assumptions_latex: \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Hilbert-space existence theorem is mathematically standard and appropriate for this theorem container. However, the cited Beck locator is ordinarily framed in finite-dimensional Euclidean space, while the candidate asserts an infinite-dimensional Hilbert-space result and additionally claims coercivity. Source uncertainty therefore affects the exact mathematical version, so a Hilbert-space authoritative locator is required.

children.title: Proximal Uniqueness
children.top_down_role: Single-valuedness regimes for standard convex proximal evaluations.

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Uniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniqueness supplied by the quadratic term in the convex proximal problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and let \(\lambda>0\). For every \(x\in H\), the objective
\[y\mapsto f(y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\lVert y-x\rVert^2\]
is \(1/\lambda\)-strongly convex and therefore has at most one minimizer. Combined with proximal existence, its minimizer is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The positive quadratic regularizer makes each convex proximal subproblem strongly convex, so its minimizer is unique.
assumptions_latex: \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in H}\{f(y)+(2\lambda)^{-1}\lVert y-x\rVert^2\}\) is a singleton for every \(x\in H\).

notation.meaning: Unique minimizer of the proximal objective.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The strong-convexity and uniqueness claim is correct and belongs in the proximal-uniqueness theorem container. The supplied Beck locator does not clearly support the stated general Hilbert-space scope; an authoritative Hilbert-space source locator is required for this exact version.

children.title: Full-Domain Proximal Mappings
children.top_down_role: Global availability of the proximal mapping across its ambient space.

knowledge_statements.title: Full-Domain Proximal Mappings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Everywhere-defined proximal mapping under standard closed-convex assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and let \(\lambda>0\). The proximal mapping
\[\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in H}\left\{f(y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\lVert y-x\rVert^2\right\}\]
is single-valued for every \(x\in H\). Hence \(\operatorname{dom}(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f})=H\), and \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}=J_{\lambda\partial f}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper closed convex function has an everywhere-defined, single-valued proximal mapping, equal to the resolvent of its subdifferential.
assumptions_latex: \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The full-domain, single-valued proximal mapping statement and subdifferential-resolvent identity are mathematically correct under the stated Hilbert-space assumptions. The cited locator does not clearly support both the Hilbert-space scope and the resolvent equivalence, so the exact theorem remains insufficiently sourced.

children.title: Well-Posedness Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Departures from the convex setting that can compromise attainment or uniqueness.

knowledge_statements.title: Well-Posedness Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonattainment when lower semicontinuity is removed from the proximal assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Lower semicontinuity cannot be omitted from the standard existence theorem. On \(H=\mathbb{R}\), define \(f(t)=0\) for \(t>0\) and \(f(t)=+\infty\) for \(t\leq0\). Then \(f\) is proper and convex but not lower semicontinuous. For \(x=0\) and any \(\lambda>0\),
\[\inf_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\left(f(t)+\frac{t^2}{2\lambda}\right)=0,\]
yet no feasible \(t>0\) attains this value. Thus the proximal mapping is empty at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper convex function that is not lower semicontinuous can have a proximal subproblem whose infimum is not attained.

notation.meaning: Extended-real value excluding a point from the effective domain.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is correct: the function is proper and convex but not lower semicontinuous, and the proximal infimum at zero is not attained. The failure_boundary kind fits exactly, but no inspectable source citation supports the claimed necessity boundary.

children.title: Proximal Parameter Family

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Parameter Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the positive-scale family and its subdifferential-resolvent form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Its proximal parameter family is
\[\left(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}\right)_{\lambda>0},\qquad \operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in H}\left\{f(y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\lVert y-x\rVert^2\right\}.\]
For every \(\lambda>0\), this mapping is single-valued on \(H\) and satisfies \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}=(\operatorname{Id}+\lambda\partial f)^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal family consists of quadratic-regularized minimizers indexed by positive scale and equals the resolvent family of the convex subdifferential.
assumptions_latex: \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.

notation.meaning: Proximal mapping of f at scale lambda.

children.title: Strongly Convex Proximal Regime
children.top_down_role: Enhanced contraction and conditioning under stronger curvature.

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Convex Proximal Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space contraction induced by strong convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x,y\in H\), the strongly convex proximal problems have unique minimizers, and
\[
\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)=\underset{u\in H}{\operatorname{argmin}}\left\{f(u)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|u-x\|^2\right\}.
\]
Moreover,
\[
\|\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)-\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(y)\|\leq\frac{1}{1+\lambda\mu}\|x-y\|.
\]
Thus the proximal mapping is a strict contraction with contraction factor at most \((1+\lambda\mu)^{-1}\), improving as either curvature \(\mu\) or scale \(\lambda\) increases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal map of a strongly convex function has Lipschitz factor at most 1/(1 + scale times curvature).
assumptions_latex: H\text{ is a real Hilbert space}
f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper, lower semicontinuous, and }\mu\text{-strongly convex with }\mu>0

notation.meaning: proximal mapping of the scaled function

children.title: Proximal Fixed Sets
children.top_down_role: Fixed-point sets of proximal mappings and their optimization interpretation.

assumptions_latex: H\text{ is a real Hilbert space}
f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed points are characterized through global convex minimizers.

source_refs.locator: 10.4 Analysis of the Proximal Gradient Method-The Convex Case p. 281

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For any \(x\in H\), proximal optimality gives
\[
x=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0\in\partial f(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in\underset{u\in H}{\operatorname{argmin}}\,f(u).
\]
Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{Fix}(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f})=\underset{u\in H}{\operatorname{argmin}}\,f(u),
\]
including the case in which both sets are empty. The fixed-point set is independent of the positive scale \(\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every positive scale, the fixed points of a convex proximal map are exactly the global minimizers of the function.
knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Fixed Sets

children.title: Projection as Proximity
children.top_down_role: Projection theory as the indicator-function specialization of proximal theory.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Euclidean Projection and Projected Iterations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines Euclidean projection, including box projection and its use in projected algorithms; projection existence, uniqueness, and computational tractability are not assumed for arbitrary sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), the Euclidean projection of \(x\) onto \(\Omega\), when the minimizer exists uniquely, is \(\Pi_\Omega(x)=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{z\in\Omega}\|z-x\|\). A sufficient condition for single-valued well-definedness is that \(\Omega\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. If \(\Omega=\{z:l_i\le z_i\le u_i,\ i=1,\ldots,n\}\), then \((\Pi_\Omega(x))_i=\min\{u_i,\max\{l_i,x_i\}\}\). Whenever \(\Pi_\Omega\) is well defined, the projected update \(x^{k+1}=\Pi_\Omega(x^k+\alpha_k d^k)\) lies in \(\Omega\); in particular, projected gradient uses \(d^k=-\nabla f(x^k)\). Projection need not be easy to compute: minimizing \(\|x\|^2\) over \(\Omega\) amounts to computing \(\Pi_\Omega(0)\), and when \(0\notin\Omega\) this projection solves the stated constrained problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Euclidean projection is the closest feasible point, provided that closest point exists uniquely; nonempty closed convex sets guarantee this. Projection onto a box is coordinatewise clipping. Applying projection after an unconstrained step keeps the next iterate feasible, yielding projected-gradient methods when the direction is the negative gradient. Projection may itself require solving an optimization problem and can be as difficult as the original norm-minimization problem.
assumptions_latex: \Pi_\Omega(x)\text{ exists uniquely whenever it is used}
\Omega\ne\varnothing\text{ is closed and convex as a sufficient condition for single-valued projection}
l_i\le u_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,n)\text{ in the box case}

children.title: Indicator-Function Projections
children.top_down_role: Closed convex constraints represented through proximal indicator models.

assumptions_latex: H\text{ is a real Hilbert space}
C\subseteq H\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}

notation.meaning: indicator function of the constraint set
metric projection onto the constraint set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed convex constraints represented by extended-valued indicators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the indicator by \(\delta_C(u)=0\) for \(u\in C\) and \(\delta_C(u)=+\infty\) otherwise. Then, for every \(x\in H\),
\[
\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda\delta_C}(x)=\underset{u\in H}{\operatorname{argmin}}\left\{\delta_C(u)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|u-x\|^2\right\}=\underset{u\in C}{\operatorname{argmin}}\,\|u-x\|^2=P_Cx.
\]
Hence the proximal mapping of a closed convex indicator is the metric projection and is independent of \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal mapping of a closed convex set's indicator is exactly the metric projection onto that set, independently of scale.
knowledge_statements.title: Indicator-Function Projections

children.title: Projection–Normal-Cone Correspondence
children.top_down_role: The operator relationship connecting projections and constrained inclusions.

assumptions_latex: H\text{ is a real Hilbert space}
C\subseteq H\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}

notation.meaning: convex normal-cone operator of the set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resolvent characterization of Hilbert-space metric projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x,p\in H\), the projection variational inequality and the normal-cone inclusion are equivalent:
\[
p=P_Cx\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p\in C\ \text{ and }\ \langle x-p,u-p\rangle\leq 0\ \text{ for every }u\in C
\]
\[
\Longleftrightarrow\quad x-p\in N_C(p)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in p+\lambda N_C(p).
\]
Because a normal cone is a cone, multiplication by \(\lambda>0\) does not change its values. Therefore \(P_C=(I+\lambda N_C)^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto a closed convex set is the resolvent of its normal cone, equivalently the solution of its projection variational inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection–Normal-Cone Correspondence

children.title: Direct Projection Regimes
children.top_down_role: Affine, subspace, ball, cone, and other directly projectable families.

knowledge_statements.title: Direct Projection Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representative closed-form projection families in Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the polar cone by \(K^\circ=\{y\in H:\langle y,k\rangle\leq0\text{ for every }k\in K\}\). Several projection families admit direct formulas. For every \(x\in H\),
\[
P_{a+V}x=a+P_V(x-a).
\]
For a closed ball,
\[
P_{\overline B(a,r)}x=
\begin{cases}
a, & r=0,\\
a, & r>0\text{ and }x=a,\\
a+\min\left\{1,\dfrac{r}{\|x-a\|}\right\}(x-a), & r>0\text{ and }x\neq a.
\end{cases}
\]
For the cone and its polar,
\[
x=P_Kx+P_{K^\circ}x,\qquad \langle P_Kx,P_{K^\circ}x\rangle=0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine subspaces, closed balls, and closed convex cones have direct projection formulas based respectively on orthogonal projection, radial clipping, and polar decomposition.
assumptions_latex: H\text{ is a real Hilbert space}
V\subseteq H\text{ is a closed vector subspace},\ a\in H,\ r\geq0
K\subseteq H\text{ is a nonempty closed convex cone}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_{a+V}x=a+P_V(x-a),\quad P_{\overline B(a,r)}x\text{ is given by the stated piecewise radial formula},\quad x=P_Kx+P_{K^\circ}x

notation.meaning: metric projection onto a closed convex set
closed ball with center a and radius r
polar cone \(\{y\in H:\langle y,k\rangle\leq0\text{ for every }k\in K\}\)

children.title: Projection onto Intersections
children.top_down_role: The boundary between direct projection and multi-set projection algorithms.

assumptions_latex: H=\mathbb R^2\text{ with its Euclidean inner product}

notation.meaning: metric projection onto a set S

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of replacing intersection projection by one projection cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Although \(C\) and \(D\) are closed convex subspaces, projection onto their intersection is not generally one cycle of individual projections. Here \(C\cap D=\{(0,0)\}\). For \(x=(1,0)\),
\[
P_Dx=(1/2,1/2),\qquad P_CP_Dx=(1/2,0),\qquad P_{C\cap D}x=(0,0).
\]
Thus \(P_{C\cap D}\neq P_CP_D\). Computing an intersection projection generally requires additional structure or an iterative multi-set projection method.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even for two lines, one cycle of successive projections need not equal projection onto their intersection; intersection projection is generally algorithmic.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection onto Intersections

children.title: Proximal–Resolvent Correspondence
children.top_down_role: The specialization of monotone resolvents to convex subdifferentials.

children.title: Subdifferential Resolvents
children.top_down_role: Convex proximal mappings represented as subdifferential resolvents.

assumptions_latex: H\text{ is a real Hilbert space}
f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex proximal mappings as single-valued subdifferential resolvents.

source_refs.locator: 10.4 Analysis of the Proximal Gradient Method-The Convex Case p. 281

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x,p\in H\), first-order optimality for the proximal problem yields
\[
p=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
0\in\partial f(p)+\lambda^{-1}(p-x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x\in p+\lambda\partial f(p).
\]
Therefore
\[
\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}=(I+\lambda\partial f)^{-1}.
\]
Since \(\partial f\) is maximally monotone, this resolvent is everywhere defined, single-valued, and firmly nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex proximal mapping is exactly the resolvent of the function's scaled subdifferential, as follows from proximal optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Subdifferential Resolvents

source_witnesses.locator: 10.4 Analysis of the Proximal Gradient Method-The Convex Case p. 281

children.title: General Monotone Resolvent Boundary
children.top_down_role: Resolvents that do not arise from convex subdifferentials.

assumptions_latex: H=\mathbb R^2\text{ with its Euclidean inner product}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: J_{\lambda A}=(I+\lambda A)^{-1}\text{ is a firmly nonexpansive resolvent but }A\neq\partial f\text{ for every proper lower-semicontinuous convex }f
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit monotone resolvent lying outside the convex-proximal subclass.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The linear operator \(A\) is monotone because \(\langle Az,z\rangle=0\) for every \(z\in H\), and its full domain and continuity make it maximally monotone. Hence \(J_{\lambda A}=(I+\lambda A)^{-1}\) is everywhere defined and firmly nonexpansive. However, \(A\) is nonzero and skew-adjoint, so it is not cyclically monotone. Convex subdifferentials are cyclically monotone; therefore no proper lower-semicontinuous convex function \(f\) satisfies \(A=\partial f\). Thus not every maximally monotone resolvent is a convex proximal mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The resolvent of a quarter-turn operator is firmly nonexpansive, yet it is not a convex proximal map because the operator is not cyclically monotone.
knowledge_statements.title: General Monotone Resolvent Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quarter-turn example is mathematically plausible and fits the failure-boundary leaf, but no source is supplied for the maximal-monotonicity, firm-resolvent, and non-subdifferential conclusions. An inspectable authoritative locator is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Moreau Envelope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition by quadratic infimal convolution on a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(\gamma>0\). The Moreau envelope of \(f\) with parameter \(\gamma\) is \[{}^{\gamma}f=f\square\left(\frac{1}{2\gamma}\|\cdot\|^2\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an extended-real-valued function on a Hilbert space and a positive parameter gamma, its Moreau envelope is its infimal convolution with the squared norm scaled by 1/(2 gamma).
