children.title: Envelope Regularization
children.top_down_role: The regularized function family generated by proximal minimization.

assumptions_latex: H\text{ is a real Hilbert space}
f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-valued quadratic infimal regularization in Hilbert space.

source_refs.locator: 10.4 Analysis of the Proximal Gradient Method-The Convex Case p. 281

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Moreau envelope of \(f\) at scale \(\lambda\) is the function \(e_\lambda f:H\to\mathbb R\) defined by
\[
e_\lambda f(x)=\inf_{u\in H}\left\{f(u)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|u-x\|^2\right\}.
\]
The infimum has the unique minimizer \(p=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\), so
\[
e_\lambda f(x)=f(p)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|p-x\|^2.
\]
In particular, \(e_\lambda f\) is finite and convex on \(H\), and \(e_\lambda f(x)\leq f(x)\) whenever \(f(x)<+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Moreau envelope infimizes a convex function plus a scaled squared distance, producing a finite convex lower approximation attained at the proximal point.
knowledge_statements.title: Envelope Regularization

source_witnesses.locator: 10.4 Analysis of the Proximal Gradient Method-The Convex Case p. 281

children.title: Envelope Differentiability
children.top_down_role: Smoothness and derivative-recovery results associated with proximal mappings.

assumptions_latex: H\text{ is a real Hilbert space}
f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fréchet differentiability and gradient recovery for convex envelopes.

source_refs.locator: 10.4 Analysis of the Proximal Gradient Method-The Convex Case p. 281

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Moreau envelope \(e_\lambda f\) is Fréchet differentiable throughout \(H\), and for every \(x\in H\),
\[
\nabla e_\lambda f(x)=\frac{1}{\lambda}\left(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\right).
\]
Its gradient is \(1/\lambda\)-Lipschitz:
\[
\|\nabla e_\lambda f(x)-\nabla e_\lambda f(y)\|\leq\frac{1}{\lambda}\|x-y\|\qquad(x,y\in H).
\]
Moreover, \(\nabla e_\lambda f(x)\in\partial f(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x))\), so the envelope gradient recovers a subgradient at the associated proximal point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex Moreau envelope is everywhere differentiable; its gradient is the scaled displacement from a point to its proximal point and is 1/scale-Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.title: Envelope Differentiability

source_witnesses.locator: 10.4 Analysis of the Proximal Gradient Method-The Convex Case p. 281

children.title: Envelope Scale-Regime Family
children.top_down_role: Minimizer preservation and parameter-dependent regularization behavior.

children.title: Envelope Minimizer Preservation
children.top_down_role: Correspondence between minimizers of an objective and its envelope.

assumptions_latex: H\text{ is a real Hilbert space}
f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in H}e_\lambda f(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in H}f(x),\qquad \inf_H e_\lambda f=\inf_H f
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact preservation of minimizers and optimal value at every positive scale.

source_refs.locator: 10.4 Analysis of the Proximal Gradient Method-The Convex Case p. 281

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in H\), infimal convolution with the nonnegative quadratic gives \(e_\lambda f(x)\geq\inf_H f\), while choosing any minimizing point of \(f\) in the envelope formula gives equality there. Consequently,
\[
\inf_{x\in H}e_\lambda f(x)=\inf_{x\in H}f(x)
\]
and
\[
\underset{x\in H}{\operatorname{argmin}}\,e_\lambda f(x)=\underset{x\in H}{\operatorname{argmin}}\,f(x).
\]
These equalities remain valid when the common minimizer set is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every positive-scale Moreau envelope has the same infimum and exactly the same minimizers as the original proper closed convex function.
knowledge_statements.title: Envelope Minimizer Preservation

source_witnesses.locator: 10.4 Analysis of the Proximal Gradient Method-The Convex Case p. 281

children.title: Small-Scale Envelope Regime
children.top_down_role: Regularization behavior at small envelope parameters.

assumptions_latex: H\text{ is a real Hilbert space}
f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise recovery as the quadratic regularization scale vanishes.

source_refs.locator: 10.4 Analysis of the Proximal Gradient Method-The Convex Case p. 281

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in H\), increasing the quadratic penalty by decreasing its scale gives
\[
e_{\lambda_2}f(x)\leq e_{\lambda_1}f(x)\leq f(x).
\]
As \(\lambda\downarrow0\), lower semicontinuity and convexity imply the pointwise recovery
\[
e_\lambda f(x)\uparrow f(x),
\]
where the limit is understood in \(( -\infty,+\infty]\). In addition,
\[
\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\to x
\]
for every \(x\in\overline{\operatorname{dom}f}\). Thus small scales retain increasingly fine pointwise features while reducing smoothing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: As the envelope scale decreases to zero, envelope values increase pointwise to the original function, and proximal points approach points in the closed domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Small-Scale Envelope Regime

source_witnesses.locator: 10.4 Analysis of the Proximal Gradient Method-The Convex Case p. 281

children.title: Large-Scale Envelope Regime
children.top_down_role: Regularization behavior at large envelope parameters.

knowledge_statements.title: Large-Scale Envelope Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise degeneration of the Moreau envelope as its scale diverges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and define \(e_\lambda f(x)=\inf_{y\in H}\{f(y)+\|x-y\|^2/(2\lambda)\}\) for \(\lambda>0\). For every \(x\in H\), the map \(\lambda\mapsto e_\lambda f(x)\) is nonincreasing and
\[
\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}e_\lambda f(x)=\inf_{y\in H}f(y),
\]
where the limit may equal \(-\infty\). Thus the large-scale envelope loses dependence on \(x\) and retains only the optimal value of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: As the envelope scale tends to infinity, its value decreases pointwise to the infimum of the original function and therefore loses dependence on the evaluation point.
assumptions_latex: \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.

children.title: Scale-Sensitivity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Parameter ranges where smoothing or approximation behavior changes qualitatively.

knowledge_statements.title: Scale-Sensitivity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Endpoint limitations of positive-scale envelope and proximal formulas.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the Moreau envelope of a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function, the scale formulas are intrinsically restricted to \(\lambda>0\). Although \(e_\lambda f(x)\uparrow f(x)\) as \(\lambda\downarrow0\), the proximal points need not converge to \(x\) when \(x\notin\overline{\operatorname{dom}f}\). At the other boundary, \(e_\lambda f(x)\downarrow\inf f\) as \(\lambda\to\infty\), but proximal points need not converge if the infimum is unattained; for example, for \(f(t)=e^t\) on \(\mathbb R\), \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\to-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Envelope values have meaningful endpoint limits, but proximal points may fail to approach the input at zero scale or converge at infinite scale.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Endpoint convergence of envelope values does not imply endpoint convergence of proximal points.

children.title: Second Prox Theorem
children.top_down_role: The named conjugate-side proximal representation preceding Moreau decomposition.

knowledge_statements.title: Second Prox Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space conjugate-side proximal identity with explicit scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and let \(f^*\) be its Fenchel conjugate. For every \(x\in H\) and \(\lambda>0\),
\[
\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f^*}(x)=x-\lambda\operatorname{prox}_{f/\lambda}(x/\lambda).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)+\lambda\operatorname{prox}_{f^*/\lambda}(x/\lambda)=x.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proximal mapping of a Fenchel conjugate is obtained by subtracting a scaled primal proximal evaluation from the original point.
assumptions_latex: \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.

notation.meaning: minimizer of g plus one-half squared distance

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Fermat and proximal characterizations of convex minimizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function on a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\). Then \[\operatorname{Argmin}f=\operatorname{zer}\partial f=\partial f^*(0)=\operatorname{Fix}\operatorname{Prox}_f=\operatorname{zer}\operatorname{Prox}_{f^*}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every proper lower-semicontinuous convex function on a Hilbert space, its minimizers are exactly the zeros of its subdifferential, the subgradients of its conjugate at zero, the fixed points of its proximal mapping, and the zeros of the conjugate-side proximal mapping.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotonicity and Descent Along the Proximal Parameter
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-value monotonicity and a displacement estimate as the proximal parameter varies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), let \(x\in\mathcal H\), and define \(\phi:\mathbb R_{++}\to\mathbb R\) by \(\phi(\gamma)=f(\operatorname{Prox}_{\gamma f}x)\). Then \(\phi\) is decreasing, \[\sup\phi(\mathbb R_{++})\le f(x),\] and, for every \(\gamma>0\), \[\|x-\operatorname{Prox}_{\gamma f}x\|^2+\gamma f(\operatorname{Prox}_{\gamma f}x)\le\gamma f(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function and a fixed x, the value of f at the gamma-scaled proximal point decreases with positive gamma and never has supremum above f(x). For every positive gamma, the squared proximal displacement plus gamma times the attained function value is at most gamma times f(x).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \phi\ \text{is decreasing},\quad \sup\phi(\mathbb R_{++})\le f(x),\quad (\forall\gamma\in\mathbb R_{++})\ \|x-\operatorname{Prox}_{\gamma f}x\|^2+\gamma f(\operatorname{Prox}_{\gamma f}x)\le\gamma f(x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Transformation identities for proximity operators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nine identities for transformed proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H), x,z\in\mathcal H, and \gamma>0. Then: (i) if g=f+(\alpha/2)\|\cdot-z\|^2+\langle\cdot,u\rangle+\beta, where u\in\mathcal H, \alpha\ge0, and \beta\in\mathbb R, then \operatorname{Prox}_{\gamma g}x=\operatorname{Prox}_{\gamma(\gamma\alpha+1)^{-1}f}((\gamma\alpha+1)^{-1}(x+\gamma(\alpha z-u))); (ii) if g=\tau_zf, then \operatorname{Prox}_{\gamma g}x=z+\operatorname{Prox}_{\gamma f}(x-z); (iii) if g=\tau_zf-\langle\cdot,z\rangle, then \operatorname{Prox}_g x=z+\operatorname{Prox}_f x; (iv) if g=f\circ L and L^{-1}=L^*, then \operatorname{Prox}_{\gamma g}x=L^*(\operatorname{Prox}_{\gamma f}(Lx)); (v) if g=f(\mu\cdot-z), \mu\ne0, then \operatorname{Prox}_{\gamma g}x=\mu^{-1}(z+\operatorname{Prox}_{\gamma\mu^2f}(\mu x-z)); (vi) if g=f^\vee, then \operatorname{Prox}_g x=-\operatorname{Prox}_f(-x); (vii) if g={}^\mu f, \mu>0, then \operatorname{Prox}_{\gamma g}x=x+\frac{\gamma}{\gamma+\mu}(\operatorname{Prox}_{(\gamma+\mu)f}x-x); (viii) if g=(2\mu)^{-1}\|\cdot\|^2-{}^\mu f, \mu>0, then \operatorname{Prox}_{\gamma g}x=x-\frac{\gamma}{\mu}\operatorname{Prox}_{\mu^2/(\mu+\gamma)f}(\frac{\mu}{\mu+\gamma}x); (ix) if g=f^*, then \operatorname{Prox}_{\gamma g}x=x-\gamma\operatorname{Prox}_{\gamma^{-1}f}(\gamma^{-1}x).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proximity operators admit explicit formulas under quadratic or linear perturbation, translation, unitary change of variables, affine scaling, reflection, Moreau-envelope transformation, and Fenchel conjugation, with the stated parameter rescalings.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Resolvent and dual representations of a variable-metric proximity operator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Self-adjoint strongly monotone metric operators on a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), and let \(U\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H)\) be self-adjoint and strongly monotone. Define
\[
\operatorname{Prox}_f^U x=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\mathcal H}\left(f(y)+\tfrac12\langle U(x-y)\mid x-y\rangle\right).
\]
Then
\[
\operatorname{Prox}_f^U=J_{U^{-1}\partial f}
=U^{-1/2}\operatorname{Prox}_{f\circ U^{-1/2}}U^{1/2}
=\operatorname{Id}-U^{-1}\operatorname{Prox}_{f^*}^{U^{-1}}U.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proximity operator in a strongly positive self-adjoint metric is the resolvent of the preconditioned subdifferential; it is also reducible to an ordinary proximal mapping by a square-root change of variables and satisfies a variable-metric conjugate decomposition.
assumptions_latex: U\text{ is self-adjoint and strongly monotone}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proximal mapping and conjugate proximal decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of the unit-parameter Euclidean proximal mapping together with the conjugate-side Moreau identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be closed, proper, and convex. For each \(z\in\mathbb{R}^n\), there is a unique decomposition
\[
z=x+x^*,\qquad x^*\in\partial f(x).
\]
The component \(x\), equivalently the unique minimizer of
\[
\inf_{u\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{f(u)+\tfrac12\lVert z-u\rVert^2\right\},
\]
is denoted \(\operatorname{prox}(z\mid f)\), and \(z\mapsto\operatorname{prox}(z\mid f)\) is the proximation corresponding to \(f\). Moreover,
\[
\operatorname{prox}(z\mid f^*)=z-\operatorname{prox}(z\mid f)\qquad(\forall z\in\mathbb{R}^n).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal mapping of a closed proper convex function sends each vector to the unique minimizer of the function plus one half the squared Euclidean distance. It is the primal component of the unique subgradient decomposition, and the proximal mappings of the function and its conjugate sum to the identity.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is closed, proper, and convex}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proximity Operator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unique quadratic-regularized minimizer for a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\) and \(x\in\mathcal H\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function on a Hilbert space, the proximal point at x is the unique minimizer of the function plus one half of the squared distance to x; this minimizer realizes the unit-parameter Moreau-envelope value.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointwise proximity operator for an integral functional
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-valued L² integral functional under finite-measure or normalized-nonnegative integrand assumptions.

For every x\in\mathcal H, if p(\omega)=\operatorname{Prox}_\varphi(x(\omega)) for \mu\text{-a.e. }\omega, then p=\operatorname{Prox}_f x.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Moreau Envelope and Proximal Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded Moreau decomposition for a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function on a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), let \(\gamma>0\), and set \(q=\tfrac12\|\cdot\|^2\). Then
\[
\gamma^{-1}q
=f\boxdot(\gamma^{-1}q)+\bigl(f^*\boxdot(\gamma q)\bigr)\circ\gamma^{-1}\operatorname{Id}
={}^\gamma f+{}^{1/\gamma}(f^*)\circ\gamma^{-1}\operatorname{Id}.
\]
Moreover, for every \(x\in\mathcal H\),
\[
x=\operatorname{Prox}_{\gamma f}x+\gamma\operatorname{Prox}_{f^*/\gamma}(x/\gamma),
\]
and
\[
f\bigl(\operatorname{Prox}_{\gamma f}x\bigr)+f^*\bigl(\operatorname{Prox}_{f^*/\gamma}(x/\gamma)\bigr)
=\left\langle\operatorname{Prox}_{\gamma f}x,\operatorname{Prox}_{f^*/\gamma}(x/\gamma)\right\rangle.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every proper lower-semicontinuous convex function f and positive gamma, the reciprocal-scaled half-squared norm decomposes into complementary Moreau envelopes of f and its conjugate. Pointwise, every x decomposes into the proximal point of gamma f plus gamma times the conjugate-side proximal point at x divided by gamma; this primal-dual proximal pair also satisfies Fenchel equality.
assumptions_latex: x\in\mathcal H\text{ for the pointwise identities}

knowledge_statements.title: Conjugate Proximal Pairing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Moreau pairing of primal and Fenchel-conjugate proximal points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the hypotheses of the Second Prox Theorem, define \(p=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\) and \(q=\operatorname{prox}_{f^*/\lambda}(x/\lambda)\). Then
\[
x=p+\lambda q,
\qquad q\in\partial f(p),
\qquad p\in\partial f^*(q).
\]
Conversely, any pair \((p,q)\) satisfying \(x=p+\lambda q\) and \(q\in\partial f(p)\) is exactly this conjugate proximal pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal and conjugate proximal points split the input and satisfy mutually inverse Fenchel subgradient relations.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on a real Hilbert space.

children.title: Polar-Cone Decomposition

knowledge_statements.title: Polar-Cone Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Moreau decomposition specialized to a closed convex cone and its polar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\) be a nonempty closed convex cone in a real Hilbert space \(H\), and let \(K^\circ=\{u\in H:\langle u,k\rangle\le0\text{ for every }k\in K\}\). For every \(x\in H\),
\[
x=P_Kx+P_{K^\circ}x,
\qquad \langle P_Kx,P_{K^\circ}x\rangle=0.
\]
The two displayed vectors are the unique orthogonal components of \(x\) belonging respectively to \(K\) and \(K^\circ\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point splits uniquely into orthogonal projections onto a closed convex cone and its polar cone.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq H\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Proximal Evaluation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Evaluation of a proximal map through an available conjugate-side oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function \(f\), a point \(x\) in its real Hilbert space, a scale \(\lambda>0\), and an oracle evaluating \(\operatorname{prox}_{f^*/\lambda}\). Compute
\[
q\leftarrow\operatorname{prox}_{f^*/\lambda}(x/\lambda),
\qquad p\leftarrow x-\lambda q.
\]
Return \(p\). The Second Prox Theorem guarantees that \(p=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\). No iteration is required beyond the single conjugate-side proximal evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluate the conjugate-side proximal map once, scale its result, and subtract it from the input to obtain the primal proximal point.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on a real Hilbert space.
\(x\in H\), \(\lambda>0\), and the conjugate-side proximal oracle is available.

knowledge_statements.title: Argument Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar dilation rule for proximal mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on a real Hilbert space, let \(a\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\), and set \(g(x)=f(ax)\). Then, for every \(x\in H\) and \(\lambda>0\),
\[
\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda g}(x)=a^{-1}\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda a^2 f}(ax).
\]
The factor \(a^2\) arises from transporting the squared-distance term under the change of variables \(z=ay\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling a function's argument scales the proximal input by the same factor, the function weight by its square, and the output inversely.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on a real Hilbert space.

knowledge_statements.title: Function-Value Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive objective-scaling rule for proximal mappings and envelopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, let \(c>0\), and define \(g=cf\). For every \(x\in H\) and \(\lambda>0\),
\[
\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda g}(x)=\operatorname{prox}_{(\lambda c)f}(x),
\qquad e_\lambda g(x)=c\,e_{\lambda c}f(x).
\]
Thus multiplying objective values by \(c\) is equivalent to multiplying the proximal scale by \(c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive scaling of function values is absorbed by multiplying the proximal or envelope scale by the same constant.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on a real Hilbert space.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: identities follow directly from the standard scaled proximal and envelope definitions
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

knowledge_statements.title: Argument Translation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translation-equivariance rule for proximal mappings and envelopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, fix \(a\in H\), and define \(g(x)=f(x-a)\). Then for every \(x\in H\) and \(\lambda>0\),
\[
\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda g}(x)=a+\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x-a),
\qquad e_\lambda g(x)=e_\lambda f(x-a).
\]
Hence translating the argument transports the proximal point by the same vector and translates the envelope's argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Translating a function's argument translates its proximal output by the same vector and shifts its envelope accordingly.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on a real Hilbert space.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Objective Offsets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proximal transport under addition of an affine functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, let \(b\in H\), \(c\in\mathbb R\), and define \(g(y)=f(y)+\langle b,y\rangle+c\). For every \(x\in H\) and \(\lambda>0\),
\[
\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda g}(x)=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x-\lambda b),
\]
and
\[
e_\lambda g(x)=e_\lambda f(x-\lambda b)+\langle b,x\rangle+c-\frac{\lambda}{2}\|b\|^2.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding an affine objective term shifts the proximal input and modifies the envelope by an explicit affine-quadratic correction.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on a real Hilbert space.

knowledge_statements.title: Orthogonal Transformations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivariance of proximal mappings under surjective linear isometries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(U:H\to H\) be orthogonal, so \(U^*U=UU^*=I\), and let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. With \(g=f\circ U\), for every \(x\in H\) and \(\lambda>0\),
\[
\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda g}(x)=U^*\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(Ux),
\qquad e_\lambda g(x)=e_\lambda f(Ux).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An orthogonal change of coordinates conjugates the proximal mapping and transports the Moreau envelope without changing scale.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.

knowledge_statements.title: Isometric Embeddings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proximal transport through a possibly nonsurjective linear isometric embedding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:H\to G\) be a linear isometric embedding between real Hilbert spaces, so \(A^*A=I_H\), and let \(R=\operatorname{ran}A\) be closed. If \(f:G\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex with \(R\cap\operatorname{dom}f\ne\varnothing\), then for every \(x\in H\) and \(\lambda>0\),
\[
\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda(f\circ A)}(x)
=A^*\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda(f+\iota_R)}(Ax).
\]
The range constraint is essential when \(A\) is not surjective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonsurjective isometric embedding, proximal transport requires restricting the ambient function to the embedding's range before mapping back by the adjoint.
assumptions_latex: \(f:G\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex with \(R\cap\operatorname{dom}f\ne\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: closed range of the isometric embedding A

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard isometric change of variables with an explicit range constraint
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The range-restricted transport formula is correct for a linear isometric embedding and properly distinguishes the nonsurjective case, but no specific source is provided.

children.title: Isometric Restrictions
children.top_down_role: Proximal transport through norm-preserving restrictions or adjoint structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Isometric Restrictions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restriction of a convex function to the range of an isometric embedding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H,G\) be real Hilbert spaces, let \(U:H\to G\) be a linear isometry, and set \(M=\operatorname{ran}U\). Let \(f\in\Gamma_0(G)\) satisfy \(M\cap\operatorname{dom}f\neq\varnothing\), and define \(g=f\circ U\). Then \(g\in\Gamma_0(H)\) and
\[\operatorname{prox}_{g}(x)=U^*\operatorname{prox}_{f+\iota_M}(Ux),\qquad x\in H.\]
Thus the ambient proximal problem must be constrained to \(M\). Replacing \(\operatorname{prox}_{f+\iota_M}\) by \(\operatorname{prox}_f\) requires an additional condition, such as \(\operatorname{prox}_f(M)\subseteq M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the restriction is proper, its proximal point is obtained by constraining the ambient problem to the isometry's range and transporting the solution back with the adjoint.

notation.meaning: Proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions on G.
The closed range of the isometry U.

children.title: Dimension-Mismatch Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limitations arising when orthogonality is replaced by rectangular isometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Mismatch Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of unconstrained proximal transport for a non-surjective isometric embedding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^2\) satisfy \(Ut=(t,0)\), and let \(f(a,b)=\tfrac12(a-b)^2\). Although \(U^*U=I\), direct calculation yields
\[\operatorname{prox}_{f\circ U}(x)=\frac{x}{2},\qquad U^*\operatorname{prox}_f(Ux)=\frac{2x}{3}.\]
Hence \(\operatorname{prox}_{f\circ U}\neq U^*\operatorname{prox}_fU\) for \(x\neq0\). The mismatch occurs because \(UU^*\) is only the projector onto \(\operatorname{ran}U\), while the unconstrained ambient proximal point can leave that range.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper isometric embedding, projecting an unconstrained ambient proximal point back need not equal the proximal map of the restricted function.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample and both proximal values are mathematically correct and fit the boundary container, but no source or inspectable locator is supplied.

children.title: Frame-Isometry Composition Family
children.top_down_role: Special linear compositions retaining explicit proximal structure.

children.title: Tight-Frame Compositions
children.top_down_role: Proximal structure preserved through tight-frame operators.

knowledge_statements.title: Tight-Frame Compositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed proximal formula for composition with a surjective scaled coisometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H,G\) be real Hilbert spaces, let \(L:H\to G\) be bounded linear with \(LL^*=\kappa I_G\) for some \(\kappa>0\), and let \(f\in\Gamma_0(G)\). Then
\[\operatorname{prox}_{f\circ L}(x)=x+\kappa^{-1}L^*\bigl(\operatorname{prox}_{\kappa f}(Lx)-Lx\bigr),\qquad x\in H.\]
The identity uses the tight-frame condition on the synthesis-side operator \(L\); no injectivity of \(L\) is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tight-frame composition has a closed proximal formula using one evaluation of the scaled proximal map and one application each of the frame operator and its adjoint.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The tight-frame proximal representation is correct under the stated scaled-coisometry hypothesis and fits the container, but it has no supporting citation.

children.title: Partial-Isometry Compositions
children.top_down_role: Proximal structure preserved on initial or final subspaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Isometry Compositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition formula when a partial isometry is viewed onto its final space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L:H\to G\) be a partial isometry with initial space \(E=(\ker L)^\perp\) and final space \(R=\operatorname{ran}L\). Regard \(L\) as mapping into \(R\), so \(LL^*=I_R\), and let \(f\in\Gamma_0(R)\). Then
\[\operatorname{prox}_{f\circ L}(x)=x+L^*\bigl(\operatorname{prox}_f(Lx)-Lx\bigr),\qquad x\in H.\]
The component of \(x\) in \(\ker L\) is unchanged, while the component in \(E\) is transported through the isometry \(L|_E:E\to R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a partial isometry, the kernel component remains fixed and the initial-space component is updated through the proximal map on the final space.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) is a partial isometry with closed final space \(R\).

notation.meaning: Initial space of the partial isometry.
Final space of the partial isometry.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The partial-isometry formula is correct when the codomain is the closed final space, as stated, but no supporting source or locator is provided.

children.title: Frame–Isometry Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural overlap between normalized tight frames and partial isometries.

knowledge_statements.title: Frame–Isometry Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between a tight-frame operator and its normalized adjoint isometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L:H\to G\) be bounded linear and let \(\kappa>0\). Define \(U=\kappa^{-1/2}L^*:G\to H\). Then
\[LL^*=\kappa I_G\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad U^*U=I_G.\]
Consequently, \(L\) is a surjective scaled coisometry with tight-frame constant \(\kappa\) exactly when its normalized adjoint is an isometric embedding. Under this correspondence, \(\operatorname{ran}U=(\ker L)^\perp\), and \(L=\sqrt\kappa\,U^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tight-frame operator is precisely a scaled adjoint of an isometric embedding; normalization converts one structure into the other.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The normalized-adjoint equivalence and range identity are correct and match the correspondence container, but the record lacks a frame-theory citation.

children.title: Non-Tight Composition Boundary
children.top_down_role: Loss of direct proximal transport beyond tight or partially isometric regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Non-Tight Composition Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the scalar tight-frame proximal formula for unequal singular values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On \(\mathbb R^2\), let \(L=\operatorname{diag}(1,2)\) and \(f(z)=\tfrac12\lVert z\rVert^2\). Then
\[\operatorname{prox}_{f\circ L}(x)=(I+L^*L)^{-1}x=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,1/5)x.\]
Because \(LL^*=\operatorname{diag}(1,4)\), no scalar \(\kappa>0\) satisfies the tight-frame identity. Moreover, no choice of \(\kappa\) makes
\[x+\kappa^{-1}L^*\bigl(\operatorname{prox}_{\kappa f}(Lx)-Lx\bigr)\]
equal to the true proximal map for every \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unequal singular values destroy the scalar tight-frame formula; even a quadratic function gives different corrections in different directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{prox}_{f\circ L}\) cannot be represented by the scalar tight-frame formula for any \(\kappa>0\).

notation.meaning: Identity operator on the relevant Euclidean space.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quadratic counterexample is correct and appropriately demonstrates failure of every scalar tight-frame formula, but it is uncited.

children.title: General Linear Composition Boundary
children.top_down_role: The transition from direct calculus to auxiliary or primal-dual solution models.

knowledge_statements.title: General Linear Composition Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between closed proximal transport and an auxiliary monotone inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H,G\) be real Hilbert spaces, let \(L:H\to G\) be bounded linear, and let \(f\in\Gamma_0(G)\). Assume that \(f\) is continuous at some point of \(\operatorname{ran}L\). For \(x\in H\), a point \(p\) equals \(\operatorname{prox}_{f\circ L}(x)\) if and only if there exists \(v\in G\) such that
\[v\in\partial f(Lp),\qquad p=x-L^*v.\]
Equivalently, \(v\) solves
\[0\in\partial f^*(v)+LL^*v-Lx,\qquad p=x-L^*v.\]
Unless \(LL^*\) has a simplifying structure, such as being a positive scalar multiple of the identity, proximal evaluation therefore requires an auxiliary inclusion rather than one ordinary evaluation of \(\operatorname{prox}_f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a standard subdifferential chain-rule qualification, evaluating a general linear composition reduces to an auxiliary dual inclusion involving the operator LL*, and a one-call proximal transport formula requires additional operator structure.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is continuous at some point of \(\operatorname{ran}L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p=\operatorname{prox}_{f\circ L}(x)\iff\exists v\in G:\ 0\in\partial f^*(v)+LL^*v-Lx\ \text{ and }\ p=x-L^*v\).

children.title: Proximal Decomposition-Aggregation Calculus
children.top_down_role: Decomposition and aggregation across independent factors and coupled terms.

children.title: Coordinate-Block Separability Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Independent scalar and block proximal evaluations.

children.title: Coordinatewise Separability
children.top_down_role: Independent proximal evaluation across scalar coordinates.

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinatewise Separability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise decomposition of a proximal map under additive separability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H=H_1\oplus\cdots\oplus H_m\) be an orthogonal Hilbert direct sum, and let
\[f(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x_i),\qquad f_i\in\Gamma_0(H_i).\]
Then for every \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in H\),
\[\operatorname{prox}_f(x)=\bigl(\operatorname{prox}_{f_1}(x_1),\ldots,\operatorname{prox}_{f_m}(x_m)\bigr).\]
In particular, when every \(H_i=\mathbb R\), proximal evaluation reduces to independent scalar problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal map of a sum of independent coordinate functions is obtained by applying each scalar or coordinate proximal map separately.
assumptions_latex: \(H=\bigoplus_{i=1}^m H_i\) is an orthogonal direct sum.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite orthogonal-sum separability property is correct and appropriately scoped, but no proximal-calculus source is cited.

children.title: Blockwise Separability
children.top_down_role: Independent proximal evaluation across vector or grouped blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Blockwise Separability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent proximal evaluation over mutually orthogonal variable blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H=\bigoplus_{j=1}^r B_j\) be an orthogonal decomposition into closed subspaces, with orthogonal projectors \(P_j\). Suppose
\[f(x)=\sum_{j=1}^r f_j(P_jx),\qquad f_j\in\Gamma_0(B_j).\]
Then
\[\operatorname{prox}_f(x)=\sum_{j=1}^r \operatorname{prox}_{f_j}(P_jx),\qquad x\in H,\]
where each block proximal point is embedded canonically in \(H\). Thus blocks may be multidimensional, but no objective term or metric term may couple distinct blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An additively separable function on orthogonal blocks has a proximal map assembled from independent block proximal evaluations.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The blockwise proximal decomposition is mathematically correct for the stated orthogonal decomposition and fits the container, but it is unsupported by a citation.

children.title: Partition Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Alignment between objective decomposition and the chosen coordinate or block partition.

knowledge_statements.title: Partition Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient structural predicate for proximal decomposition over a prescribed partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a prescribed decomposition \(H=\bigoplus_{j=1}^r B_j\), call \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\) compatible with the partition when the sum is orthogonal for the proximal metric and there exist \(f_j\in\Gamma_0(B_j)\) and \(c\in\mathbb R\) satisfying
\[f(x)=c+\sum_{j=1}^r f_j(P_jx),\qquad x\in H.\]
Under this condition, minimizing \(f(y)+\tfrac12\lVert y-x\rVert^2\) separates into \(r\) independent block problems, and \(P_j\operatorname{prox}_f(x)=\operatorname{prox}_{f_j}(P_jx)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partition is compatible when both the objective and proximal metric decompose across its blocks, ensuring independent block minimizations.

notation.meaning: Orthogonal projector associated with the partition.
Additive constant, irrelevant to the proximal map.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated additive decomposition is a valid sufficient partition-compatibility condition, and its proximal consequence is correct, but no source is supplied.

children.title: Cross-Block Coupling Boundary
children.top_down_role: Loss of termwise evaluation when dependencies cross the selected blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Block Coupling Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A quadratic interaction showing failure of coordinatewise proximal evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On \(\mathbb R^2\) with its coordinate partition, let \(f(x_1,x_2)=\tfrac12(x_1-x_2)^2\). Then
\[\operatorname{prox}_f(x_1,x_2)=\left(\frac{2x_1+x_2}{3},\frac{x_1+2x_2}{3}\right).\]
Each output coordinate depends on both input coordinates, so no maps \(T_1,T_2:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) can satisfy \(\operatorname{prox}_f(x_1,x_2)=(T_1x_1,T_2x_2)\) for all inputs. The cross-block quadratic term therefore destroys coordinatewise separability despite convexity and smoothness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex cross-block interaction makes each proximal output depend on multiple input blocks, preventing independent block evaluation.
assumptions_latex: The prescribed blocks are the two coordinate axes.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proximal formula and nonseparability conclusion are correct and fit the cross-block boundary container, but the example has no supporting citation.

children.title: Product-Space Separability
children.top_down_role: Componentwise structure exposed by product-space models.

knowledge_statements.title: Product-Space Separability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proximal representation for a separable function on a finite Hilbert product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H=H_1\times\cdots\times H_m\) carry the product inner product, and let \(f_i\in\Gamma_0(H_i)\). Define \(F:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by
\[F(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x_i).\]
Then \(F\in\Gamma_0(H)\), its subdifferential and resolvent decompose as
\[\partial F=\partial f_1\times\cdots\times\partial f_m,\qquad \operatorname{prox}_F=\operatorname{prox}_{f_1}\times\cdots\times\operatorname{prox}_{f_m}.\]
Thus a product-space model exposes independent component inclusions and proximal evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a Hilbert product, the subdifferential and proximal map of a componentwise sum are Cartesian products of the component operators.
assumptions_latex: \(H=\prod_{i=1}^m H_i\) has the product inner product.

notation.meaning: Separable function on the product space.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite product-space subdifferential and resolvent decompositions are correct and match the topic, but the record lacks an authoritative source and locator.

children.title: Metric-Compatible Separability
children.top_down_role: Dependence of decomposition on the selected proximal metric.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Compatible Separability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block separability under a strongly positive proximal metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H=H_1\oplus\cdots\oplus H_m\), let \(M:H\to H\) be self-adjoint and strongly positive, and define \(\|z\|_M^2=\langle Mz,z\rangle\). Suppose every \(H_j\) is invariant under \(M\), so that \(M=\bigoplus_{j=1}^m M_j\), and let \(f(x)=\sum_{j=1}^m f_j(x_j)\), where \(f_j\in\Gamma_0(H_j)\). Then, for every \(\gamma>0\),
\[\operatorname{prox}^{M}_{\gamma f}(v)=\bigl(\operatorname{prox}^{M_j}_{\gamma f_j}(v_j)\bigr)_{j=1}^m.\]
Thus a metric preserving the functional block decomposition is sufficient for componentwise proximal evaluation; metric cross-terms generally couple the block variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separable function has a blockwise proximal map when the proximal metric is block diagonal for the same decomposition; metric cross-terms generally reintroduce coupling.
assumptions_latex: \(H=\bigoplus_{j=1}^m H_j\) is a finite orthogonal product of real Hilbert spaces.
\(M\) is self-adjoint, strongly positive, and block diagonal.

notation.meaning: Proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions on H.
Proximal mapping defined using the squared M-norm.
Restriction of M to the invariant block H_j.

children.title: Proximal-Infimal Aggregation Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Aggregation mechanisms distinct from termwise proximal decomposition.

children.title: Proximal Averages
children.top_down_role: Function aggregation through proximal-average constructions.

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Averages
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite weighted proximal average with common parameter \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space, let \(f_i\in\Gamma_0(H)\), and let \(\lambda_i>0\) satisfy \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\). For \(q(x)=\tfrac12\|x\|^2\) and \(\mu>0\), the proximal average is
\[\operatorname{pav}_{\mu}(f_1,\ldots,f_m;\lambda)=\left(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\bigl(f_i+\mu^{-1}q\bigr)^*\right)^*-\mu^{-1}q.\]
The conjugates and weighted sum are taken in the common ambient space, and the resulting function belongs to \(\Gamma_0(H)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal average conjugates quadratically regularized functions, averages those conjugates, conjugates back, and removes the same quadratic regularizer.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space and \(f_i\in\Gamma_0(H)\).

notation.meaning: The quadratic q(x)=one half the squared norm of x.
Weighted proximal average with parameter μ.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the leaf and use a standard parameter convention, but no source or inspectable locator supports the formula or closure claim.

children.title: Infimal Aggregation
children.top_down_role: Aggregation through infimal convolution or related value constructions.

knowledge_statements.title: Infimal Aggregation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted infimal aggregation of quadratically regularized convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the proximal-average assumptions, define the infimal aggregation at \(x\in H\) by
\[\mathcal I_{\mu,\lambda}(x)=\inf_{\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i=x}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f_i(x_i)+\frac{1}{2\mu}\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\|x_i\|^2-\frac{1}{2\mu}\|x\|^2\right\}.\]
Using the weighted-variance identity, the same quantity equals
\[\inf_{\sum_i\lambda_i x_i=x}\left\{\sum_i\lambda_i f_i(x_i)+\frac{1}{2\mu}\sum_i\lambda_i\|x_i-x\|^2\right\}.\]
The linear barycenter constraint couples the component variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Infimal aggregation minimizes the weighted function values plus dispersion around a prescribed barycenter.
assumptions_latex: \(f_i\in\Gamma_0(H)\) on a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal I_{\mu,\lambda}\) is given equivalently by either displayed constrained infimum.

notation.meaning: Component variables whose weighted barycenter is x.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two constrained-infimum formulas agree by the weighted-variance identity and fit the leaf, but the specialized aggregation definition has no cited source.

children.title: Average–Infimum Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural links between proximal averaging and infimal aggregation.

knowledge_statements.title: Average–Infimum Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infimal and resolvent representations of the proximal average.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p=\operatorname{pav}_{\mu}(f_1,\ldots,f_m;\lambda)\) under the finite-dimensional proximal-average assumptions. Then
\[p(x)=\inf_{\sum_i\lambda_i x_i=x}\left\{\sum_i\lambda_i f_i(x_i)+\frac{1}{2\mu}\sum_i\lambda_i\|x_i-x\|^2\right\}=\mathcal I_{\mu,\lambda}(x).\]
Moreover its proximal mapping is the weighted average of the component proximal mappings:
\[\operatorname{prox}_{\mu p}(v)=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\operatorname{prox}_{\mu f_i}(v).\]
Thus conjugate averaging, constrained infimal aggregation, and resolvent averaging describe the same convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal average equals a barycentrically constrained infimum, and its proximal map is the weighted average of the component proximal maps.
assumptions_latex: \(f_i\in\Gamma_0(H)\) on a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space.

notation.meaning: The proximal average of the functions f_i.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind is appropriate and the formulas are consistent with the stated proximal-average convention, but the infimal and proximal-map identities require an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: Aggregation Degeneracy Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where aggregation loses regularity, properness, or informative structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Aggregation Degeneracy Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameter boundaries preserving the convex proximal-average construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The standard proximal-average construction requires \(\mu>0\) and nonnegative normalized weights. If \(\lambda_i=0\), the corresponding function is inoperative and may be deleted without changing the aggregate. If some \(\lambda_i<0\), the expression \(\sum_i\lambda_i(f_i+\mu^{-1}q)^*\) need not be convex, so its conjugate no longer represents convex averaging. At \(\mu=0\), the terms \(\mu^{-1}q\) are undefined; for \(\mu<0\), quadratic regularization becomes concave and proper convexity can fail. Improper component functions likewise fall outside the stated \(\Gamma_0\) calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero weights delete components, while negative weights, nonpositive proximal parameters, or improper components can destroy or invalidate proximal aggregation.
assumptions_latex: The aggregate is interpreted by the standard conjugate formula for proximal averages.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mu>0\), \(\lambda_i\ge 0\), \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\), and proper convex components are the admissible boundary conditions.

notation.meaning: One half of the squared norm.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits, but the admissibility summary mentions only proper convex components rather than the full lower-semicontinuous \(\Gamma_0\) condition, and none of the parameter-boundary claims has a source.

children.title: Coupled-Sum Boundary
children.top_down_role: Nonseparable sums requiring an inclusion or splitting reformulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Coupled-Sum Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of naive proximal composition for nonseparable sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For general \(f,g\in\Gamma_0(H)\), neither \(\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma(f+g)}=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f}\circ\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}\) nor the reversed composition is valid. For example, in \(H=\mathbb R^2\), let \(C=\mathbb R(1,0)\), \(D=\mathbb R(1,1)\), \(f=\iota_C\), and \(g=\iota_D\). Since \(C\cap D=\{0\}\),
\[\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma(f+g)}=P_{C\cap D}=0,\]
whereas \(P_C P_D(1,0)=(1/2,0)\neq0\). Such sums require a coupled optimality inclusion or a splitting formulation unless additional separability or commutation structure is present.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal map of a coupled sum is generally not a composition of the individual proximal maps, as two nonorthogonal subspace indicators demonstrate.

children.title: Generic Proximal Evaluation Mechanisms
children.top_down_role: Reusable reductions for proximal mappings without immediate closed forms.

children.title: Dual Reduction Mechanisms
children.top_down_role: Lower-dimensional or structurally simpler conjugate-side evaluations.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Reduction Mechanisms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel-dual evaluation of a proximal composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) and \(G\) be finite-dimensional real Hilbert spaces, let \(L:H\to G\) be linear, and let \(f\in\Gamma_0(G)\). If \(f\) is continuous at \(Lx_0\) for some \(x_0\in H\), then the proximal problem
\[\min_x\left\{f(Lx)+\frac{1}{2\gamma}\|x-v\|^2\right\}\]
has the dual reduction
\[\min_u\left\{f^*(u)+\frac{\gamma}{2}\|L^*u\|^2-\langle u,Lv\rangle\right\}.\]
For any dual minimizer \(u^*\), the unique primal solution is \(x^*=v-\gamma L^*u^*\). The dual variable may inhabit a lower-dimensional or more structured space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proximal problem involving a linear composition can be solved through a conjugate-side dual problem, then recovered by one adjoint operation.
assumptions_latex: \(H,G\) are finite-dimensional real Hilbert spaces, \(L:H\to G\) is linear, and \(\gamma>0\).
There exists \(x_0\) such that \(f\) is continuous at \(Lx_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma(f\circ L)}(v)=v-\gamma L^*u^*\) for every dual minimizer \(u^*\).

notation.meaning: A minimizer of the reduced dual problem.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dual objective and recovery formula are mathematically consistent, and duality is the correct kind, but the qualification and dual-attainment claims require an authoritative locator.

children.title: Scalar-Equation Reductions
children.top_down_role: Monotone root-finding interfaces for parameterized proximal families.

knowledge_statements.title: Scalar-Equation Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bisection interface for one-parameter proximal characterizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\), fix \(v\in H\), and suppose the desired proximal solution has the parameterization \(x(\tau)=\operatorname{prox}_{\tau f}(v)\). Assume its defining constraint is equivalent to \(F(\tau)=0\), where \(F(\tau)=\phi(x(\tau))-b\) is continuous and strictly decreasing on \([\ell,r]\), with \(F(\ell)\ge0\ge F(r)\). Initialize this bracket and repeatedly set \(m=(\ell+r)/2\); replace \(\ell\) by \(m\) when \(F(m)>0\), and otherwise replace \(r\) by \(m\). Stop when \(r-\ell\le\varepsilon\) and output \(x((\ell+r)/2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When a parameterized proximal formula leaves one continuous monotone scalar equation, bracketed bisection computes the parameter and hence the proximal point.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuous and strictly decreasing on \([\ell,r]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned parameter has bracket error at most \(\varepsilon/2\), after at most \(\lceil\log_2((r-\ell)/\varepsilon)\rceil\) bisections.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Structured Linear-System Reductions
children.top_down_role: Quadratic and affine proximal evaluations governed by linear algebra.

knowledge_statements.title: Structured Linear-System Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variable-metric proximal evaluation of convex quadratics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H=\mathbb R^n\), let \(Q\succeq0\) and \(M\succ0\) be symmetric, and define \(f(x)=\tfrac12\langle Qx,x\rangle+\langle c,x\rangle+d\). For \(\gamma>0\), the variable-metric proximal point
\[y=\operatorname{prox}^{M}_{\gamma f}(v)=\mathop{\arg\min}_{x}\left\{\gamma f(x)+\tfrac12\|x-v\|_M^2\right\}\]
is the unique solution of
\[(M+\gamma Q)y=Mv-\gamma c.\]
Because \(M+\gamma Q\succ0\), factorization or a structured linear solver determines the proximal point; repeated evaluations may reuse a factorization when the matrices and parameter remain fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex quadratic proximal map is represented by one positive-definite linear system, whose structure can support reusable factorizations.

notation.meaning: The quadratic form given by the positive-definite matrix M.

children.title: Level-Epigraph Reduction Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Projection and lifting representations for level and epigraph constraints.

children.title: Sublevel-Set Reductions
children.top_down_role: Proximal evaluations represented through projection onto sublevel sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Sublevel-Set Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection onto a convex sublevel set through a proximal multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\) on a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space, let \(C_\alpha=\{x:f(x)\le\alpha\}\), and assume \(\inf f<\alpha<f(v)<+\infty\). Then there exists \(\lambda>0\) such that
\[y=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(v),\qquad f(y)=\alpha,\]
and every such multiplier produces
\[P_{C_\alpha}(v)=y.\]
If \(v\in C_\alpha\), the projection is simply \(v\) and the multiplier may be taken as zero. Hence sublevel projection reduces to finding a scalar multiplier for a proximal family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto a nontrivial convex sublevel set equals a proximal point whose positive multiplier makes the level constraint active.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{C_\alpha}(v)=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(v)\) for a multiplier satisfying \(f(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(v))=\alpha\).

notation.meaning: Closed convex α-sublevel set of f.
Metric projection onto the sublevel set.

source_refs.locator: 6.2 First Set of Examples of Proximal Mappings p. 131

source_witnesses.locator: 6.2 First Set of Examples of Proximal Mappings p. 131

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the leaf and the multiplier characterization is plausible under the stated finite-dimensional hypotheses, but the generic proximal-examples locator does not specifically support multiplier existence and active-level attainment.

children.title: Epigraph Reductions
children.top_down_role: Proximal evaluations represented through projection onto epigraphs.

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraph projection through a scalar proximal parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\) on a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space and let \((v,\eta)\in H\times\mathbb R\). If \(f(v)\le\eta\), then \(P_{\operatorname{epi}f}(v,\eta)=(v,\eta)\). Otherwise there is a unique \(\lambda>0\) satisfying
\[f\bigl(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(v)\bigr)=\eta+\lambda,\]
and
\[P_{\operatorname{epi}f}(v,\eta)=\bigl(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(v),\eta+\lambda\bigr).\]
Thus epigraph projection reduces to evaluations of the proximal family and a one-dimensional root search for the vertical displacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outside an epigraph, its projection is a proximal point paired with a lifted height; one scalar equation determines the lift.
assumptions_latex: The product space uses the norm \(\|(x,t)\|^2=\|x\|^2+t^2\).

notation.meaning: The set of pairs (x,t) satisfying f(x)≤t.
Positive vertical displacement and proximal parameter.

source_refs.locator: 6.2 First Set of Examples of Proximal Mappings p. 131

source_witnesses.locator: 6.2 First Set of Examples of Proximal Mappings p. 131

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exterior epigraph formula and scalar equation are standard and internally consistent, but the cited locator does not specifically establish existence and uniqueness of the scalar displacement.

children.title: Level–Epigraph Lifting Relations
children.top_down_role: Connections between level-set projections and lifted epigraph representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Level–Epigraph Lifting Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraph projection represented as optimization over horizontal levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space, let \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\), define \(C_t=\{x\in H:f(x)\le t\}\), and fix \((v,\eta)\in H\times\mathbb R\). Epigraph projection admits the level lifting
\[t^*\in\mathop{\arg\min}_{t:C_t\ne\varnothing}\left\{\frac12 d_{C_t}(v)^2+\frac12(t-\eta)^2\right\},\qquad y^*=P_{C_{t^*}}(v),\]
with
\[P_{\operatorname{epi}f}(v,\eta)=(y^*,t^*).\]
The unique epigraph projection determines the resulting pair, although the minimizing level need not be presented as a separate proximal multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Epigraph projection can be lifted from sublevel projections by minimizing the sum of horizontal sublevel distance and vertical displacement over the level.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space and \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\).
The epigraph carries the standard product-space norm.

children.title: Projection-Reduction Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where projection reformulation does not yield a simpler evaluation interface.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection-Reduction Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of recovering prescribed proximal parameters from sublevel or epigraph projections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Suppose \(\inf f<\eta<f(x)\), and let \(y=P_{\{f\leq\eta\}}x\). Then there exists \(\lambda>0\) such that \(y=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\) and \(f(y)=\eta\). Likewise, if \((y,t)=P_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,\alpha)\) and \(t>\alpha\), then \(y=\operatorname{prox}_{(t-\alpha)f}(x)\) and \(t=f(y)\). In both reductions the projection determines the proximal multiplier; it need not equal a prescribed parameter \(\bar\lambda>0\), and an inactive projection constraint has multiplier zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the strict-level qualification, sublevel and epigraph projections produce proximal points with multipliers determined by projection optimality, not generally with a prescribed proximal parameter.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H\) is a real Hilbert space.
\(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The projection multiplier is endogenous and need not equal a prescribed \(\bar\lambda>0\).

notation.meaning: metric projection onto a nonempty closed convex set C

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: qualified convex projection optimality and proximal optimality give the endogenous-multiplier correspondence

children.title: Cataloged Function Proximal Families
children.top_down_role: Canonical function families organized by the structure used in evaluation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent characterizations of a proximal thresholder
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space equivalences involving the subdifferential at zero, the conjugate proximity operator, and conjugate minimizers, followed by a sufficient support-function representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\), and let \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\). The following are equivalent: \(\operatorname{Prox}_f\) is a proximal thresholder on \(\Omega\); \(\partial f(0)=\Omega\); \(\operatorname{Fix}(\operatorname{Prox}_{f^*})=\Omega\); and \(\operatorname{Argmin}f^*=\Omega\). Moreover, these conditions hold if \(f=g+\sigma_\Omega\), where \(g\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\) is Gâteaux differentiable at \(0\) and \(\nabla g(0)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximity operator of f thresholds exactly on Ω if and only if Ω is the subdifferential of f at zero, the fixed-point set of the conjugate proximity operator, and the minimizer set of the conjugate. These conditions hold when f is the support function of Ω plus a convex function with zero derivative at the origin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Prox}_f\text{ is a proximal thresholder on }\Omega\iff \partial f(0)=\Omega\iff \operatorname{Fix}(\operatorname{Prox}_{f^*})=\Omega\iff \operatorname{Argmin}f^*=\Omega;\quad [f=g+\sigma_\Omega,\ g\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H),\ g\text{ Gâteaux differentiable at }0,\ \nabla g(0)=0]\Rightarrow\text{ these conditions hold}.

source_evidence.locator: Proximity Operators / 24.5. Proximal Thresholding / Proposition 24.49

knowledge_statements.title: Equivalent characterizations of a proximal thresholder

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scalar proximal-thresholder factorization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proximity-operator factorization for a support-function perturbation associated with a closed interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R\) be a nonempty closed interval, let \(\psi\in\Gamma_0(\mathbb R)\) be differentiable at \(0\) with \(\psi'(0)=0\), and set \(\phi=\psi+\sigma_\Omega\). Then \(\operatorname{Prox}_\phi=\operatorname{Prox}_\psi\circ\operatorname{soft}_\Omega\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If φ is the sum of the support function of a nonempty closed interval Ω and a convex function whose derivative vanishes at zero, then its proximity operator is soft thresholding with respect to Ω followed by the proximity operator of that convex function.

source_evidence.locator: Proximity Operators / 24.5. Proximal Thresholding / Proposition 24.54

knowledge_statements.title: Scalar proximal-thresholder factorization

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scalar characterization of proximal thresholders
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary-and-sufficient characterization for a nonempty closed interval in the real line.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R\) be a nonempty closed interval and let \(\phi\in\Gamma_0(\mathbb R)\). Then \(\operatorname{Prox}_\phi\) is a proximal thresholder on \(\Omega\) if and only if \(\phi=\psi+\sigma_\Omega\) for some \(\psi\in\Gamma_0(\mathbb R)\) that is differentiable at \(0\) and satisfies \(\psi'(0)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On the real line, a convex proximity operator thresholds on Ω exactly when its defining function is the support function of Ω plus a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function differentiable at zero with derivative zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Prox}_\phi\text{ is a proximal thresholder on }\Omega\iff \exists\psi\in\Gamma_0(\mathbb R):\ \phi=\psi+\sigma_\Omega,\ \psi\text{ differentiable at }0,\ \psi'(0)=0.

source_evidence.locator: Proximity Operators / 24.5. Proximal Thresholding / Theorem 24.52

knowledge_statements.title: Scalar characterization of proximal thresholders

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proximal thresholder
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition relative to a prescribed nonempty closed convex zero set in a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\), and let \(T:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\). Then \(T\) is a proximal thresholder on \(\Omega\) if there exists \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\) such that \(T=\operatorname{Prox}_f\) and \(\operatorname{zer}T=\Omega\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mapping is a proximal thresholder on Ω when it is the proximity operator of a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function and its zero set is exactly Ω.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\text{ is a proximal thresholder on }\Omega\iff \exists f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H):\ T=\operatorname{Prox}_f\ \text{and}\ \operatorname{zer}T=\Omega.

source_evidence.locator: Proximity Operators / 24.5. Proximal Thresholding / Definition 24.48

children.title: Smooth Scalar Forms

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Scalar Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional smooth convex proximal mappings as monotone root problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and convex, and let \(\lambda>0\). For every \(x\in\mathbb R\), the proximal point \(y=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\) is the unique solution of \[y+\lambda f'(y)=x.\] The function \(F_x(y)=y+\lambda f'(y)-x\) is strictly increasing because \(f'\) is nondecreasing. Consequently, proximal evaluation reduces to finding the unique zero of \(F_x\); any root-finding method used must preserve or otherwise exploit this monotonicity and terminate according to a specified residual or interval tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal point of a differentiable convex scalar function is the unique root of a strictly increasing first-order equation.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable and convex.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: differentiable convex first-order optimality and strong convexity of the proximal objective

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scalar optimality equation, uniqueness, and monotonicity are mathematically standard, and representation is appropriate for this leaf. No citation or inspectable locator is supplied.

children.title: Nonsmooth Scalar Forms
children.top_down_role: One-dimensional nonsmooth functions underlying coordinatewise proximal mappings.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Scalar Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subdifferential characterization of one-dimensional nonsmooth proximal mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and let \(\lambda>0\). For \(x,y\in\mathbb R\), \[y=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0\in\partial f(y)+\lambda^{-1}(y-x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in y+\lambda\partial f(y).\] Thus nonsmooth scalar proximal evaluation is inversion of the strictly monotone relation \(I+\lambda\partial f\). At a kink, the entire interval \(y+\lambda\partial f(y)\) maps to the same proximal output \(y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsmooth scalar proximal point is characterized by a subgradient inclusion; kink subgradient intervals become constant-output input intervals.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\) if and only if \(x\in y+\lambda\partial f(y)\).

notation.meaning: convex subdifferential of f at y
identity mapping on the real line

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Fermat subdifferential rule for the strongly convex proximal objective
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The subdifferential characterization and kink interval interpretation are precise and fit a representation record, but no supporting citation with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Piecewise-Affine Forms
children.top_down_role: Scalar proximal families built from affine pieces.

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Affine Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite active-region evaluation of convex scalar piecewise-affine proximal mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be convex and piecewise affine with finitely many maximal open affine regions, and let \(\lambda>0\). On each such region \(R_k\), write \(f(t)=a_kt+b_k\) and form \(y_k=x-\lambda a_k\); accept \(y_k\) when \(y_k\in R_k\). For every breakpoint \(c\), accept \(c\) exactly when \[x-c\in\lambda\partial f(c).\] Exactly one region or breakpoint candidate is accepted, and the accepted value is \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Test the shifted candidate from every maximal affine region and the subgradient condition at every breakpoint; the unique accepted value is the proximal point.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is convex and has finitely many maximal affine regions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unique accepted candidate equals \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\).

notation.meaning: maximal open affine region of f
slope and intercept on affine region k

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: scalar proximal optimality applied on maximal affine regions and at their breakpoints

children.title: Piecewise-Quadratic Forms
children.top_down_role: Scalar proximal families built from quadratic pieces.

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Quadratic Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite interval evaluation of convex scalar piecewise-quadratic proximal mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and quadratic on the interiors \(R_j\) of finitely many interval pieces of \(\operatorname{dom}f\), with \(f(t)=\tfrac12q_jt^2+a_jt+b_j\) on \(R_j\) and \(q_j\geq0\). Let \(\lambda>0\) and \(x\in\mathbb R\). For every nonempty \(R_j\), form \[y_j=\frac{x-\lambda a_j}{1+\lambda q_j}\] and accept it when \(y_j\in R_j\). At every finite boundary point \(c\) of the interval partition, including finite endpoints of \(\operatorname{dom}f\), accept \(c\) when \(x-c\in\lambda\partial f(c)\). Exactly one candidate is accepted, and it equals \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve the affine optimality equation on each quadratic-region interior and test the full subgradient condition at every finite region or domain boundary; the unique accepted candidate is the proximal point.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and quadratic on the interiors of finitely many interval pieces of its effective domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unique accepted candidate equals \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\).

notation.meaning: interior of quadratic interval piece j
finite boundary point of the interval partition or effective domain

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: scalar proximal inclusion solved on quadratic interiors and tested at all finite boundaries

children.title: Breakpoint Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Breakpoint Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact input regime for which a scalar breakpoint is the proximal output.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, let \(\lambda>0\), and let \(c\in\operatorname{dom}f\). Then \[\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)=c\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in c+\lambda\partial f(c).\] If the finite one-sided derivatives exist and \(\partial f(c)=[f'_-(c),f'_+(c)]\), this input regime is \[[c+\lambda f'_-(c),\;c+\lambda f'_+(c)].\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A breakpoint is the proximal output exactly for inputs in the breakpoint plus its scaled subgradient interval.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on \(\mathbb R\).

notation.meaning: left and right derivatives at the breakpoint

children.title: Coordinate-Sparsity Forms

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate-Sparsity Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted coordinatewise soft-thresholding for separable convex sparsity penalties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(w_i\geq0\), let \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n w_i|x_i|\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), and let \(\lambda>0\). Separability gives \[\bigl(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\bigr)_i=\operatorname{sign}(x_i)\max\{|x_i|-\lambda w_i,0\},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n,\] with \(\operatorname{sign}(0)=0\). Hence coordinate \(i\) is zero exactly when \(|x_i|\leq\lambda w_i\); otherwise its magnitude is reduced by \(\lambda w_i\) without changing its sign.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The weighted ℓ1 proximal mapping independently soft-thresholds each coordinate, setting it to zero within its threshold interval.

notation.meaning: nonnegative sparsity weight for coordinate i
sign function with value zero at zero

children.title: Group-Norm Forms
children.top_down_role: Block-structured norm penalties with groupwise shrinkage behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Group-Norm Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block soft-thresholding for a weighted sum of Euclidean group norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_1,\ldots,G_m\) partition the coordinates of \(\mathbb R^n\), let \(w_g\geq0\), and define \(f(x)=\sum_{g=1}^m w_g\|x_{G_g}\|_2\). For \(\lambda>0\), proximal separability across groups yields \[\bigl(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\bigr)_{G_g}=\begin{cases}\left(1-\dfrac{\lambda w_g}{\|x_{G_g}\|_2}\right)x_{G_g},&\|x_{G_g}\|_2>\lambda w_g,\\0,&\|x_{G_g}\|_2\leq\lambda w_g.\end{cases}\] Thus each group is preserved in direction and either radially shrunk or annihilated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The weighted group-norm proximal mapping shrinks each block radially and zeros blocks whose norm does not exceed the threshold.
assumptions_latex: The groups \(G_g\) form a coordinate partition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each block undergoes Euclidean block soft-thresholding at level \(\lambda w_g\).

notation.meaning: coordinate block indexed by group g

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: separability and radial optimality for the Euclidean norm
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The block soft-thresholding formula is correct for a coordinate partition and fits the group-norm leaf. No supporting source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Radial Function Forms
children.top_down_role: Rotationally symmetric functions reduced through radial geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Radial Function Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of a Hilbert-space radial proximal mapping to one scalar radius problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(f(x)=\phi(\|x\|)\), where \(\phi:[0,+\infty)\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and nondecreasing. For \(\lambda>0\), set \(\rho=\|x\|\) and \[r=\operatorname*{argmin}_{s\geq0}\left\{\phi(s)+\frac{(s-\rho)^2}{2\lambda}\right\}.\] If \(x\neq0\), then \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)=(r/\rho)x\); if \(x=0\), then \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(0)=0\). Thus proximal evaluation changes only the radius, not a nonzero input's direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex nondecreasing radial penalty preserves direction and computes the output radius through a one-dimensional constrained proximal problem.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H\) is a real Hilbert space.
\(\phi\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and nondecreasing on \([0,+\infty)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: rotational symmetry and scalar minimization of the radial proximal objective
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Block-Radial Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Connections between groupwise norms and radial reductions within blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Block-Radial Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block-separable radial proximal mappings correspond to independent scalar radius problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the Hilbert space decompose orthogonally as \(\mathcal H=\mathcal H_1\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathcal H_m\), and define \(f(x)=\sum_{g=1}^m\phi_g(\|x_g\|)\), where every \(\phi_g\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and nondecreasing on \([0,+\infty)\). For \(\lambda>0\), define \[r_g=\operatorname*{argmin}_{s\geq0}\left\{\phi_g(s)+\frac{(s-\|x_g\|)^2}{2\lambda}\right\}.\] Then each output block is \(y_g=(r_g/\|x_g\|)x_g\) when \(x_g\neq0\), and \(y_g=0\) otherwise. The vector \(y=(y_g)_g\) equals \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An orthogonally block-separable radial penalty reduces to one independent scalar radius proximal problem per block.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H\) is an orthogonal direct sum of finitely many Hilbert spaces.
Each \(\phi_g\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}\) is obtained by independent radial scaling of its blocks.

notation.meaning: component of x in block g

children.title: Zero-Radius Regimes
