knowledge_statements.title: Operator-Count Scaling Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Per-sweep resource scaling for an explicitly specified finite-sum product-space oracle model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a full-sweep method for \(0\in\sum_{i=1}^{m}A_i x+B x\), where \(m\geq1\), each positive stepsize \(\gamma_i>0\) is fixed, and every component resolvent \(J_{\gamma_iA_i}=(I+\gamma_iA_i)^{-1}\) is queried exactly once per sweep. Assume that the method stores one auxiliary vector in \(H\) for each component. Then one full sweep uses exactly \(m\) component-resolvent evaluations, optionally one evaluation of \(B\), and \(\Theta(m)\) auxiliary vectors. The lifted state lies in \(H^m\). This count applies to full sweeps; randomized or block-iterative methods need not have the same per-iteration cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated full-sweep oracle model, m components require exactly m component-resolvent calls and linear auxiliary-vector storage per sweep; block or randomized iterations can have different costs.
assumptions_latex: \(m\geq1\) is the number of component operators.
\(\gamma_i>0\) and \(J_{\gamma_iA_i}\) is an exposed component oracle for every \(i\).
Each full sweep queries every component resolvent exactly once.
The method stores one auxiliary vector in \(H\) per component.

notation.meaning: resolvent of the ith scaled component operator

children.title: Primal–Dual Optimality Systems
children.top_down_role: Coupled primal and dual variables represented as structured monotone inclusions.

children.title: KKT Operator Systems
children.top_down_role: Convex KKT systems assembled as block inclusions.

knowledge_statements.title: KKT Operator Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel KKT conditions assembled as a maximally monotone block plus skew coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) and \(G\) be real Hilbert spaces, let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(g:G\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and let \(L:H\to G\) be bounded and linear. Assume
\[0\in\operatorname{sri}\bigl(L(\operatorname{dom}f)-\operatorname{dom}g\bigr).\]
For the primal problem \(\inf_{x\in H}f(x)+g(Lx)\) and its Fenchel dual \(\sup_{v\in G}-f^*(-L^*v)-g^*(v)\), the KKT system is
\[0\in\partial f(x)+L^*v,\qquad 0\in\partial g^*(v)-Lx.\]
With \(z=(x,v)\), this is equivalently
\[0\in\begin{pmatrix}\partial f&0\\0&\partial g^*\end{pmatrix}z+\begin{pmatrix}0&L^*\\-L&0\end{pmatrix}z.\]
Its zeros are precisely the primal–dual optimal pairs whenever the corresponding optima are attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated Fenchel qualification, attained primal–dual optimal pairs are exactly the zeros of a block subdifferential operator plus the bounded skew primal–dual coupling.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
The primal and dual optima are attained when asserting the optimal-pair correspondence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in(\partial f\times\partial g^*)z+(L^*v,-Lx)\), and its zeros are the attained primal–dual optimal pairs.

notation.meaning: Fenchel conjugate of the composite term
Hilbert-space adjoint of the linear map

children.title: Saddle-Operator Systems
children.top_down_role: Convex-concave saddle structures represented by coupled operators.

assumptions_latex: For every \(y\in Y\), the function \(x\mapsto\mathcal L(x,y)\) is finite-valued and convex.
For every \(x\in X\), the function \(y\mapsto\mathcal L(x,y)\) is finite-valued and concave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{zer}T\) equals the saddle-point set of \(\mathcal L\).

notation.meaning: Convex subdifferential with respect to the first variable.
Convex subdifferential of the negative saddle function with respect to the second variable.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order operator representation of a finite-valued convex-concave saddle point.

source_refs.locator: 3.4. Saddle Point and Minimax Theory p. 127

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be real Hilbert spaces, and let \(\mathcal L:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\) be convex in its first argument and concave in its second argument. Define \(T:X\times Y\rightrightarrows X\times Y\) by \[T(x,y)=\partial_x\mathcal L(x,y)\times\partial_y(-\mathcal L)(x,y).\] Then \(0\in T(\bar x,\bar y)\) if and only if \[(\forall x\in X)(\forall y\in Y)\qquad \mathcal L(\bar x,y)\leq \mathcal L(\bar x,\bar y)\leq \mathcal L(x,\bar y).\] Thus the zeros of \(T\) are precisely the saddle points of \(\mathcal L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite-valued convex-concave function, the coupled partial-subdifferential operator vanishes exactly at points that minimize the function in the primal variable and maximize it in the dual variable.

children.title: Linear-Composite Primal–Dual Systems

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Composite Primal–Dual Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel primal–dual inclusion for a two-function linear composite objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be real Hilbert spaces, let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(g:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions, and let \(L:X\to Y\) be bounded linear. The saddle function \(\mathcal L(x,y)=f(x)+\langle Lx,y\rangle-g^*(y)\) yields the system \[0\in\partial f(x)+L^*y,\qquad 0\in\partial g^*(y)-Lx.\] Its solutions are exactly the zeros of \[T(x,y)=\bigl(\partial f(x)+L^*y,\,\partial g^*(y)-Lx\bigr),\] and are saddle points of \(\mathcal L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear-composite primal problem and its Fenchel dual form a coupled zero inclusion involving two subdifferentials and the adjoint linear map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in T(x,y)\) is equivalent to the displayed primal–dual optimality system.

notation.meaning: Proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions on X.

children.title: Skew Coupling Operators

knowledge_statements.title: Skew Coupling Operators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical skew block operator generated by a bounded linear primal–dual coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be real Hilbert spaces and let \(L:X\to Y\) be bounded linear. Define \(S:X\times Y\to X\times Y\) by \[S(x,y)=(L^*y,-Lx).\] With the product-space inner product, \(S^*=-S\), and hence \[\langle (x,y),S(x,y)\rangle=0\qquad(\forall(x,y)\in X\times Y).\] Consequently \(S\) is monotone. Since it is bounded, linear, and has full domain, it is maximally monotone. Adding \(S\) to block-diagonal monotone operators represents the linear coupling in primal–dual inclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard primal–dual block coupling is skew-adjoint, contributes zero quadratic form, and is a full-domain maximally monotone linear operator.

notation.meaning: Skew block coupling induced by L.

children.title: Operator-Zero Representation
children.top_down_role: The base set-valued or single-valued zero model.

knowledge_statements.title: Operator-Zero Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Base feasibility model for a possibly set-valued operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(A:X\rightrightarrows X\) be an operator. The operator-zero problem is \[\text{find }\bar x\in X\text{ such that }0\in A\bar x.\] Its solution set is denoted by \[\operatorname{zer}A=\{x\in X:0\in Ax\}=A^{-1}(0).\] If \(A\) is single-valued, the inclusion reduces to the equation \(A\bar x=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An operator-zero problem asks for a point whose operator value contains zero; its solution set is the inverse image of zero.
assumptions_latex: \(A:X\rightrightarrows X\) is a possibly set-valued operator on a real Hilbert space.

children.title: Resolvent Fixed-Point Representation
children.top_down_role: A monotone zero problem transported to a resolvent fixed-point problem.

knowledge_statements.title: Resolvent Fixed-Point Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between an operator zero and a resolvent fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(A:X\rightrightarrows X\), and fix \(\gamma>0\). Define the resolvent relation \(J_{\gamma A}=(\operatorname{Id}+\gamma A)^{-1}\). For every \(x\in X\), \[0\in Ax\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in J_{\gamma A}x.\] If \(A\) is maximally monotone, \(J_{\gamma A}\) is everywhere-defined and single-valued, so the relation becomes the fixed-point equation \[x=J_{\gamma A}x,\qquad \operatorname{zer}A=\operatorname{Fix}J_{\gamma A}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zeros of an operator are precisely fixed points of its resolvent; maximal monotonicity makes the resolvent an everywhere-defined mapping.
assumptions_latex: \(A:X\rightrightarrows X\) is an operator on a real Hilbert space.
Single-valued full-domain form additionally assumes that \(A\) is maximally monotone.

notation.meaning: Resolvent of the scaled operator gamma A.

children.title: Normal-Map Representation
children.top_down_role: Constraint geometry encoded through projection-based normal maps.

knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Map Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection-based normal map for a variational inequality over a convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(C\subset X\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(F:C\to X\). Define \[F_C(z)=F(P_Cz)+z-P_Cz\qquad(z\in X).\] Then \[F_C(z)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=P_Cz,\ z=x-F(x),\text{ and }0\in F(x)+N_C(x).\] Conversely, every solution \(x\) of the normal-cone inclusion produces the zero \(z=x-F(x)\) of \(F_C\). Hence projection transports the constrained inclusion to an unconstrained normal-map equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constrained normal-cone inclusion is equivalent to a zero of a projection-based normal map on the ambient Hilbert space.

notation.meaning: Normal map associated with F and C.

children.title: Product-Space Lifting

knowledge_statements.title: Product-Space Lifting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted product-space reformulation of a finite sum of operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_i:X\rightrightarrows X\) for \(1\leq i\leq m\), and choose \(\omega_i>0\) with \(\sum_i\omega_i=1\). On \(\mathcal X=X^m\), use \(\langle\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol u\rangle_{\omega}=\sum_i\omega_i\langle x_i,u_i\rangle\), define \(\boldsymbol A=\mathop{\times}_{i=1}^m A_i\), and set \(D=\{(x,\ldots,x):x\in X\}\). Then \[0\in\boldsymbol A\boldsymbol x+N_D\boldsymbol x\] holds exactly when \(\boldsymbol x=(x,\ldots,x)\) and there exist \(u_i\in A_i x\) satisfying \(\sum_i\omega_i u_i=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replicating a variable in a weighted product space turns a sum inclusion into a block-separable operator plus a consensus normal cone.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real Hilbert space and \(m<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lifted zero inclusion is equivalent to \(0\in\sum_i\omega_iA_i x\).

notation.meaning: Diagonal consensus subspace of the product space.
Cartesian product of the component operators.
Normal-cone operator of the diagonal subspace.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial Inverse Operators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spingarn partial inverse of an operator relative to a closed subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(V\subset X\) be a closed vector subspace, and let \(A:X\rightrightarrows X\). The partial inverse of \(A\) with respect to \(V\) is the operator \(A_V:X\rightrightarrows X\) defined by \[y\in A_Vx\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad P_Vy+P_{V^\perp}x\in A\bigl(P_Vx+P_{V^\perp}y\bigr).\] Thus the graph transformation retains the \(V\)-components of the input and output while interchanging their \(V^\perp\)-components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The partial inverse swaps the input and output components orthogonal to a chosen subspace while retaining their components in that subspace.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a closed vector subspace of the real Hilbert space \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Membership in \(A_V\) is given by the displayed projection identity.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Sum Operators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parallel sum of two set-valued operators through inverse relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A,B:X\rightrightarrows X\) be operators on a real Hilbert space. Their parallel sum is \[A\mathbin{\square}B=(A^{-1}+B^{-1})^{-1}.\] Equivalently, for \(x,y\in X\), \[y\in(A\mathbin{\square}B)x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in A^{-1}y+B^{-1}y.\] Hence membership holds exactly when there exist \(u,v\in X\) such that \(x=u+v\), \(y\in Au\), and \(y\in Bv\). The definition extends to finitely many operators by inverting the pointwise sum of their inverse relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The parallel sum inverts the pointwise sum of inverse operators and aggregates decomposed primal components sharing one dual value.

notation.meaning: Parallel sum of A and B.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Involution and inverse identities for the partial-inverse construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be a closed vector subspace of a real Hilbert space \(X\), and let \(A:X\rightrightarrows X\). Orthogonal decomposition gives \(x=P_Vx+P_{V^\perp}x\) and \(y=P_Vy+P_{V^\perp}y\). The partial-inverse graph transformation is involutive, and ordinary inversion commutes with partial inversion relative to the same subspace. Consequently, \[(A_V)_V=A\qquad\text{and}\qquad(A_V)^{-1}=(A^{-1})_V.\] These are equalities of set-valued operators and require no monotonicity assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial inversion relative to a subspace is involutive, and taking the ordinary inverse commutes with partial inversion relative to that same subspace.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Aggregation Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common-dual-variable representation of a finite parallel sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_i:X\rightrightarrows X\) for \(1\leq i\leq m<\infty\), and define \[\mathop{\square}_{i=1}^m A_i=\left(\sum_{i=1}^m A_i^{-1}\right)^{-1}.\] For \(x,y\in X\), \[y\in\left(\mathop{\square}_{i=1}^m A_i\right)x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists(x_i)_{i=1}^m:\ x=\sum_{i=1}^m x_i\ \text{ and }\ y\in\bigcap_{i=1}^m A_i x_i.\] Thus primal components aggregate additively, while the same dual value belongs to every component image.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite parallel sum decomposes the primal argument across operators while enforcing one common dual value for all components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y\in(\mathop{\square}_iA_i)x\) exactly when \(x=\sum_i x_i\) and \(y\in A_i x_i\) for every \(i\).

children.title: Construction Compatibility Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Restrictions affecting maximality or representational equivalence under these constructions.

knowledge_statements.title: Construction Compatibility Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Qualification boundary for preserving maximal monotonicity under partial and parallel constructions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space. If \(A:X\rightrightarrows X\) is maximally monotone and \(V\subset X\) is a closed vector subspace, then \(A_V\) is maximally monotone. For maximally monotone \(A,B:X\rightrightarrows X\), however, maximal monotonicity of \(A\mathbin{\square}B\) is not automatic: it follows from maximal monotonicity of \(A^{-1}+B^{-1}\), for example under \[\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}A^{-1})\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}B^{-1})\neq\varnothing.\] Without an applicable sum qualification, the algebraic parallel sum remains defined, but maximal monotonicity cannot generally be inferred from that of its factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial inversion preserves maximal monotonicity over closed subspaces, whereas a parallel sum needs a qualification ensuring maximality of the sum of inverse operators.
assumptions_latex: \(V\subset X\) is a closed vector subspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The partial inverse preserves maximal monotonicity, while the parallel sum requires a sum qualification such as the displayed relative-interior condition.

notation.meaning: Proximal mapping of the scaled function.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained convex minimization on a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in H\), the proximal optimality condition gives \[x=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f}(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0\in\partial f(x).\] Consequently, the fixed-point set of the proximal mapping is exactly the minimizer set: \[\operatorname{Fix}(\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f})=\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in H}f(u).\] This equivalence holds for every \(\gamma>0\), including when the minimizer set is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point minimizes a proper closed convex function exactly when it is a fixed point of any positive-parameter proximal mapping.

For \(x\in C\), constrained optimality is equivalent to \[0\in
abla f(x)+N_C(x).\] By the projection characterization, this is equivalent, for every \(\gamma>0\), to \[x=P_C igl(x-\gamma
abla f(x) igr).\] Hence \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in C}f(u)=\operatorname{Fix} igl(P_C\circ(I-\gamma
abla f) igr).\] No stepsize restriction is required for this fixed-point identity; stepsize restrictions arise when convergence of an iteration is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constrained convex optimality is equivalent to being a fixed point of a gradient step followed by projection onto the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.title: Projected Optimality Fixed Points

source_witnesses.locator: 8 Primal and Dual Projected Subgradient Methods p. 195

children.title: Forward–Backward Fixed Points
children.top_down_role: Composite convex optimality encoded by a gradient-proximal map.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(f:H\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex and Fréchet differentiable, and \(g:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.

notation.meaning: Convex subdifferential of the nonsmooth term.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composite convex minimization with a differentiable smooth term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in H\), \[x=T_\gamma x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0\in\nabla f(x)+\partial g(x).\] Therefore \[\operatorname{Fix}(T_\gamma)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in H}\{f(u)+g(u)\}.\] The identity is valid for every \(\gamma>0\). Bounds such as \(0<\gamma<2/L\), when \(\nabla f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, concern averagedness and iterative convergence rather than the fixed-point characterization itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A composite convex minimizer is exactly a fixed point of the gradient step followed by the proximal mapping of the nonsmooth term.
knowledge_statements.title: Forward–Backward Fixed Points

children.title: Primal–Dual Fixed Points
children.top_down_role: Coupled optimality encoded through block resolvents or primal-dual maps.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) and \(G\) are real Hilbert spaces, \(K:H\to G\) is bounded linear, and \(f\) and \(g\) are proper, lower semicontinuous, convex functions on \(H\) and \(G\), respectively.

notation.meaning: Adjoint of the bounded linear operator.
Fenchel conjugate of the dualized function.
Block primal-dual proximal map defined in the statement.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel-type primal-dual inclusion without an iterative convergence claim.

source_refs.locator: 3.1.9 Basic Elements of Primal-Dual Methods p. 191

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[T_{\tau,\sigma}(x,y)=\bigl(\operatorname{prox}_{\tau f}(x-\tau K^*y),\operatorname{prox}_{\sigma g^*}(y+\sigma Kx)\bigr).\] Then \((x,y)\in H\times G\) is a fixed point of \(T_{\tau,\sigma}\) if and only if \[0\in\partial f(x)+K^*y,\qquad 0\in\partial g^*(y)-Kx.\] Thus fixed points are precisely primal-dual saddle pairs for \(f(x)+g(Kx)\), whenever such pairs exist. Restrictions coupling \(\tau\), \(\sigma\), and \(\|K\|\) are needed for particular iterations, not for this equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal-dual saddle pair is exactly a fixed point of the coupled primal and dual proximal equations.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Fixed Points

source_witnesses.locator: 3.1.9 Basic Elements of Primal-Dual Methods p. 191

children.title: Reflected-Shadow Fixed-Point Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Fixed-point variables whose associated shadows recover inclusion solutions.

children.title: Reflected-Resolvent Fixed Variables
children.top_down_role: Fixed variables associated with reflected-resolvent operators.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(A,B:H\rightrightarrows H\) are maximally monotone.

notation.meaning: Resolvent of a scaled monotone operator.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Douglas-Rachford fixed variables for two maximally monotone operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A reflected-resolvent fixed variable is a point \(z\in H\) satisfying \[z=Tz=\tfrac12\bigl(z+R_{\gamma B}R_{\gamma A}z\bigr).\] Equivalently, \[R_{\gamma B}R_{\gamma A}z=z.\] This variable generally need not itself solve \(0\in A x+B x\); the associated solution candidate is obtained through the resolvent shadow \(J_{\gamma A}z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reflected-resolvent fixed variable is fixed by the Douglas-Rachford operator, or equivalently by the composition of the two reflected resolvents.
knowledge_statements.title: Reflected-Resolvent Fixed Variables

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and reflected-resolvent equivalence are mathematically standard and fit the leaf, but the record provides no inspectable citation for its nontrivial Douglas–Rachford claims.

children.title: Shadow Fixed Variables
children.top_down_role: Shadow variables used to represent inclusion solutions.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(A,B:H\rightrightarrows H\) are maximally monotone, and \(\gamma>0\).

notation.meaning: Resolvent shadow associated with the first operator.
Set of zeros of an operator.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Douglas-Rachford shadows associated with a reflected fixed variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The shadow fixed variable associated with \(z\) is \(x=J_{\gamma A}z\). Fixedness of \(z\) implies equality of the two resolvent shadows: \[J_{\gamma A}z=J_{\gamma B}(R_{\gamma A}z).\] Their common value satisfies \[x\in\operatorname{zer}(A+B).\] Thus the solution-bearing quantity is the resolvent image of the reflected variable, rather than necessarily the reflected variable itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a Douglas-Rachford fixed point, the two resolvent shadows coincide, and their common value solves the original monotone inclusion.
knowledge_statements.title: Shadow Fixed Variables

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The shadow equality and zero-of-the-sum conclusion are correct under the stated ordering of the Douglas–Rachford operator, but no source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Shadow Recovery Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Links between reflected fixed variables and recovered solution shadows.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(A,B:H\rightrightarrows H\) are maximally monotone, and \(\gamma>0\).

notation.meaning: Zero set of the sum inclusion.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued correspondence between Douglas-Rachford fixed points and inclusion solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(z\in\operatorname{Fix}T\), the shadow \(J_{\gamma A}z\) belongs to \(\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\). Conversely, if \(x\in\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\), choose \(a\in Ax\) and \(b\in Bx\) with \(a+b=0\), and set \(z=x+\gamma a\). Then \(z\in\operatorname{Fix}T\) and \(J_{\gamma A}z=x\). Consequently, \[J_{\gamma A}(\operatorname{Fix}T)=\operatorname{zer}(A+B).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Resolvent shadows of all Douglas-Rachford fixed points are exactly the solutions of the original sum inclusion.
knowledge_statements.title: Shadow Recovery Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The recovery identity is correct, but it lacks any citation and the statement includes a converse construction constituting proof text. After sourcing, that construction should be removed from the knowledge statement.

children.title: Inclusion Solution Method Interfaces
children.top_down_role: A compact taxonomy by operator access pattern; iterations and detailed convergence theory remain in algorithm chapters.

children.title: Single-Operator Resolvent Methods
children.top_down_role: Proximal-point families for one maximally monotone operator.

children.title: Proximal-Point Accuracy Regime Family
children.top_down_role: Resolvent iterations distinguished by evaluation accuracy.

children.title: Exact Proximal-Point Families
children.top_down_role: Proximal-point families using exact resolvent evaluations.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone with \(\operatorname{zer}A\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact resolvent evaluation for a single maximally monotone operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(x_0\in H\). For \(k=0,1,\ldots\), choose \(\gamma_k>0\) and evaluate the resolvent exactly: \[x_{k+1}=J_{\gamma_k A}x_k.\] Equivalently, find \(x_{k+1}\) satisfying \[0\in A x_{k+1}+\gamma_k^{-1}(x_{k+1}-x_k).\] Stop when a prescribed residual, displacement, or iteration criterion is met, and output the latest iterate. Exactness means that the displayed resolvent inclusion has zero evaluation error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact proximal-point method repeatedly evaluates the resolvent of a maximally monotone operator with no subproblem error.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Proximal-Point Families

children.title: Inexact Proximal-Point Families
children.top_down_role: Proximal-point families using approximate resolvent evaluations.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone with \(\operatorname{zer}A\neq\varnothing\).
\(x_0\in H\), \(\gamma_k>0\), and error vectors \(e_k\in H\) satisfy \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\|e_k\|<\infty\).

notation.meaning: Absolute error in the resolvent evaluation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute summable-error form of the inexact proximal-point method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(x_0\in H\). At iteration \(k\), choose \(\gamma_k>0\), compute an approximate resolvent value, and set \[x_{k+1}=J_{\gamma_k A}x_k+e_k.\] The absolute-error regime requires \[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\|e_k\|<\infty.\] Stop under a prescribed residual, displacement, or iteration criterion and output the latest iterate. This record specifies the evaluation model; convergence additionally requires appropriate control of the parameters, commonly \(\inf_k\gamma_k>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inexact proximal-point family permits resolvent errors, with a standard convergence regime requiring their norms to be summable.
knowledge_statements.title: Inexact Proximal-Point Families

children.title: Evaluation-Accuracy Transitions
children.top_down_role: Structural transitions between exact and inexact evaluation models.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone, and \(\gamma_k>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transition from approximate to exact resolvent evaluation under absolute error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The evaluation \(y_k=J_{\gamma_k A}x_k+e_k\) is exact precisely when \(e_k=0\), equivalently when \[0\in A y_k+\gamma_k^{-1}(y_k-x_k).\] A sequence of evaluations is asymptotically exact in the absolute-error sense when \(\|e_k\|\to0\); the stronger summable-error regime requires \[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\|e_k\|<\infty.\] Thus exact, asymptotically exact, and summably inexact evaluations differ by explicit conditions on the same resolvent error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Resolvent evaluation changes from inexact to exact when its error vanishes; asymptotic and summable accuracy impose progressively stronger sequence conditions.
knowledge_statements.title: Evaluation-Accuracy Transitions

children.title: Relaxation-Metric Proximal-Point Family
children.top_down_role: Relaxation and metric variants of the proximal-point framework.

children.title: Relaxed Proximal-Point Families
children.top_down_role: Proximal-point variants organized by relaxation behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone with \(\operatorname{zer}A\neq\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Exact proximal point at iteration k.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar relaxation of exact proximal-point resolvent steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(x_0\in H\). For each \(k\geq0\), choose \(\gamma_k>0\) and \(\lambda_k\in(0,2)\), compute \(p_k=J_{\gamma_k A}x_k\), and update \[x_{k+1}=x_k+\lambda_k(p_k-x_k).\] The choices \(\lambda_k=1\), \(0<\lambda_k<1\), and \(1<\lambda_k<2\) give the ordinary, under-relaxed, and over-relaxed proximal-point steps, respectively. Stop under a prescribed residual, displacement, or iteration criterion and output the latest iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relaxed proximal-point method moves a scalar fraction of the way from the current iterate toward its exact resolvent image.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxed Proximal-Point Families

children.title: Variable-Metric Proximal-Point Families
children.top_down_role: Proximal-point variants using changing metric geometry.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone with \(\operatorname{zer}A\neq\varnothing\).
\(x_0\in H\), \(\gamma_k>0\), and each \(M_k:H\to H\) is bounded, self-adjoint, and strongly positive.

notation.meaning: Norm induced by the metric operator.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact proximal-point iteration in iteration-dependent strongly positive metrics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(x_0\in H\). At iteration \(k\), choose \(\gamma_k>0\) and a bounded, self-adjoint, strongly positive operator \(M_k\), then compute \[x_{k+1}=J_{\gamma_k M_k^{-1}A}x_k.\] Equivalently, \[0\in A x_{k+1}+\gamma_k^{-1}M_k(x_{k+1}-x_k).\] Stop under a prescribed residual, displacement, or iteration criterion and output the latest iterate. Convergence claims require additional uniform metric bounds and controlled variation of \((M_k)_{k\geq0}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variable-metric proximal-point method evaluates each resolvent in a strongly positive metric that may change between iterations.
knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Metric Proximal-Point Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The variable-metric resolvent update and equivalent inclusion are mathematically consistent and appropriately classified as an algorithm, but no source or locator supports this specialized variant.

children.title: Relaxation–Metric Interaction
children.top_down_role: Combined use of relaxation parameters with variable metrics.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation–Metric Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fejér decrease for a relaxed resolvent in a fixed positive-definite metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximally monotone, and let \(U:H\to H\) be bounded, self-adjoint, and strongly positive. Put \(p=J_{\gamma UA}x\), where \(\gamma>0\), and set \(x^+=x+\lambda(p-x)\). For every \(z\in\operatorname{zer}A\) and \(0\leq\lambda\leq2\), firm nonexpansiveness of \(J_{\gamma UA}\) in the \(U^{-1}\)-metric gives
\[\|x^+-z\|_{U^{-1}}^2\leq\|x-z\|_{U^{-1}}^2-\lambda(2-\lambda)\|p-x\|_{U^{-1}}^2.\]
Thus the admissible relaxation interval is unchanged by the metric when distances and firm nonexpansiveness use the compatible metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compatible positive-definite metric preserves the resolvent’s relaxation range, while the Fejér decrease is measured in the inverse metric.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The metric-resolvent inequality and property classification fit the leaf, but no inspectable source supports the compatible-metric firm-nonexpansiveness claim or relaxation range.

children.title: Two-Operator Splitting Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Method families distinguished by forward, backward, and reflected access.

children.title: Forward–Backward Interface
children.top_down_role: One forward and one resolvent evaluation.

knowledge_statements.title: Forward–Backward Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical forward–backward splitting for a cocoercive forward component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x^0\in H\), generate
\[x^{k+1}=J_{\gamma A}\bigl(x^k-\gamma Bx^k\bigr).\]
Here \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is accessed once through its resolvent and \(B:H\to H\) once by direct evaluation per iteration. If \(A\) is maximally monotone, \(B\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive, \(0<\gamma<2\beta\), and \(\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\neq\varnothing\), then every fixed point of the update is a zero of \(A+B\); in finite dimensions, the iterates converge to such a zero. A standard stopping residual is \(r^k=\gamma^{-1}(x^k-x^{k+1})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forward–backward splitting uses one evaluation of the cocoercive operator and one resolvent evaluation of the maximally monotone operator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^{k+1}=J_{\gamma A}(x^k-\gamma Bx^k)\), with fixed points equal to \(\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\).

notation.meaning: cocoercivity constant of the forward operator

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the interface, but the cited proximal-operator section does not clearly support the stated general maximally-monotone Hilbert-space convergence result. The record also does not explicitly define H as a real Hilbert space.

children.title: Backward–Backward Interface
children.top_down_role: Two-resolvent access without a forward evaluation.

knowledge_statements.title: Backward–Backward Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle interface for splitting two maximally monotone operators using resolvents only.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the inclusion \(0\in Ax+Bx\), a backward–backward interface permits evaluations of \(J_{\gamma A}\) and \(J_{\gamma B}\), together with affine combinations of stored vectors, but requires no direct single-valued evaluation of \(A\) or \(B\). A canonical interface map is
\[T=\tfrac12\bigl(I+R_{\gamma A}R_{\gamma B}\bigr),\qquad R_{\gamma A}=2J_{\gamma A}-I.\]
When \(A\) and \(B\) are maximally monotone, each resolvent is everywhere defined and single-valued. If \(z\in\operatorname{Fix}T\), then the shadow \(x=J_{\gamma B}z\) belongs to \(\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The backward–backward interface accesses both operators only through resolvents; fixed-point shadows solve the original two-operator inclusion.

notation.meaning: fixed-point set of the interface map

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The resolvent-only definition and fixed-point shadow relation fit the backward–backward interface, but they lack an inspectable source and H is not explicitly introduced as a real Hilbert space.

children.title: Douglas-Rachford-Peaceman-Rachford Averaging Family
children.top_down_role: Averaged and unaveraged reflected-resolvent families.

children.title: Douglas–Rachford Families
children.top_down_role: Averaged reflected-resolvent splitting families.

knowledge_statements.title: Douglas–Rachford Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relaxed Douglas–Rachford iteration and its primal shadow for two monotone operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose \(z^0\in H\), \(\gamma>0\), and relaxation parameters \(0<\lambda_k<2\). For \(k\geq0\), compute
\[x^k=J_{\gamma B}z^k,\qquad y^k=J_{\gamma A}(2x^k-z^k),\qquad z^{k+1}=z^k+\lambda_k(y^k-x^k).\]
Each iteration uses one resolvent of each operator. If \(A\) and \(B\) are maximally monotone, \(\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\neq\varnothing\), and the relaxations remain bounded away from \(0\) and \(2\), then in finite dimensions \((z^k)\) converges to a fixed point and the shadow sequence \((x^k)\) converges to a point of \(\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxed Douglas–Rachford alternates two resolvents and updates an auxiliary point; the resolvent shadow converges to an inclusion solution.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed relaxed Douglas–Rachford algorithm and finite-dimensional convergence claim fit the leaf, but no source supports the precise relaxation hypotheses and shadow convergence statement; H is also not defined.

children.title: Peaceman–Rachford Families
children.top_down_role: Unaveraged reflected-resolvent splitting families.

knowledge_statements.title: Peaceman–Rachford Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unaveraged composition of two reflected resolvents.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(z^0\in H\) and \(\gamma>0\), the Peaceman–Rachford iteration is
\[z^{k+1}=R_{\gamma A}R_{\gamma B}z^k,\qquad x^k=J_{\gamma B}z^k.\]
Equivalently, compute \(x^k=J_{\gamma B}z^k\), \(y^k=J_{\gamma A}(2x^k-z^k)\), and \(z^{k+1}=z^k+2(y^k-x^k)\). If \(z^\star\) is a fixed point, then \(J_{\gamma B}z^\star\in\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\). Maximal monotonicity alone makes the reflected composition nonexpansive but does not generally ensure convergence of its unaveraged iterates; additional regularity or an averaging relaxation is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Peaceman–Rachford applies the full composition of two reflected resolvents; its fixed-point shadow solves the inclusion, but unaveraged convergence needs extra conditions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm correctly targets the unaveraged reflected-resolvent family and appropriately warns that maximal monotonicity alone does not ensure iterative convergence, but the claims require a source and H is undefined.

children.title: Averaging-Regime Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural relation between averaged and unaveraged reflector compositions.

knowledge_statements.title: Averaging-Regime Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameter correspondence between reflected-resolvent, Douglas–Rachford, and Peaceman–Rachford maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S=R_{\gamma A}R_{\gamma B}\) and define the relaxed map
\[T_\theta=(1-\theta)I+\theta S.\]
For maximally monotone \(A\) and \(B\), the map \(S\) is nonexpansive. Hence \(T_\theta\) is \(\theta\)-averaged when \(0<\theta<1\). The choice \(\theta=\tfrac12\) gives the classical Douglas–Rachford map \(\tfrac12(I+S)\), whereas \(\theta=1\) gives the unaveraged Peaceman–Rachford map \(S\). Whenever \(\operatorname{Fix}S\neq\varnothing\), all choices \(0<\theta\leq1\) have the same fixed-point set and therefore the same primal shadows under \(J_{\gamma B}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Douglas–Rachford is the half-averaged reflected composition, while Peaceman–Rachford is its unaveraged endpoint; both share fixed points.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property accurately expresses the Douglas–Rachford/Peaceman–Rachford averaging correspondence, but no source supports the averagedness and common-fixed-point claims, and the ambient Hilbert space is not introduced.

children.title: Forward–Backward–Forward Interface
children.top_down_role: Splitting for monotone-Lipschitz forward components.

knowledge_statements.title: Forward–Backward–Forward Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tseng splitting for a maximally monotone operator plus a monotone Lipschitz operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x^0\in H\) and choose \(0<\gamma<1/L\). For \(k\geq0\), compute
\[y^k=J_{\gamma A}(x^k-\gamma Bx^k),\qquad x^{k+1}=y^k-\gamma(By^k-Bx^k).\]
Thus each iteration uses one resolvent evaluation of \(A\) and two forward evaluations of \(B\). If \(A\) is maximally monotone, \(B\) is monotone and \(L\)-Lipschitz, and \(\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\neq\varnothing\), then in finite dimensions the iterates converge to a zero of \(A+B\). The correction \(-\gamma(By^k-Bx^k)\) replaces the cocoercivity requirement of ordinary forward–backward splitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forward–backward–forward adds a second forward evaluation, allowing a monotone Lipschitz component that need not be cocoercive.

notation.meaning: Lipschitz constant of the forward operator

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Tseng forward–backward–forward algorithm and oracle counts fit the interface, but the step-size and convergence theorem have no cited source and H is not defined as a real Hilbert space.

children.title: Multi-Operator Primal-Dual Method Interface
children.top_down_role: Methods for multiple separately accessible operators and coupled primal-dual systems.

children.title: Dedicated-Lifted Multi-Operator Splitting
children.top_down_role: Dedicated or lifted treatment of multiple operators.

children.title: Three-Operator Splitting
children.top_down_role: Dedicated splitting interfaces for three separately accessible operators.

knowledge_statements.title: Three-Operator Splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Davis–Yin splitting with two resolvents and one cocoercive forward evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(z^0\in H\) and \(0<\gamma<2\beta\), compute
\[x^k=J_{\gamma A}z^k,\qquad y^k=J_{\gamma B}(2x^k-z^k-\gamma Cx^k),\qquad z^{k+1}=z^k+y^k-x^k.\]
The method uses one resolvent of each maximally monotone operator and one evaluation of the cocoercive operator per iteration. If \(A\) and \(B\) are maximally monotone, \(C\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive, and \(\operatorname{zer}(A+B+C)\neq\varnothing\), then in finite dimensions the shadow sequence \((x^k)\) converges to a point in \(\operatorname{zer}(A+B+C)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Three-operator splitting combines two resolvent calls with one cocoercive forward call, and its shadow solves the summed inclusion.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Davis–Yin iteration has the appropriate algorithm role and matches the three-operator leaf, but its convergence and step-size claims lack a source and H is not explicitly defined.

children.title: Product-Space Splitting
children.top_down_role: Lifted formulations for splitting multiple operators in a product space.

knowledge_statements.title: Product-Space Splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagonal product-space reformulation of a finite sum of monotone operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A_i:H\rightrightarrows H\) for \(1\leq i\leq m\), and choose weights \(\omega_i>0\) with \(\sum_i\omega_i=1\). Equip \(\mathcal H=H^m\) with \(\langle\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\rangle_\omega=\sum_i\omega_i\langle x_i,y_i\rangle\), define \(D=\{(x,\ldots,x):x\in H\}\), and set \(\boldsymbol A=\mathop{\times}_{i=1}^m(A_i/\omega_i)\). Then
\[0\in\sum_{i=1}^m A_i x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0\in\boldsymbol A\boldsymbol{x}+N_D\boldsymbol{x}\ \text{ for }\ \boldsymbol{x}=(x,\ldots,x).\]
Moreover, \(J_{\gamma\boldsymbol A}\) acts coordinatewise and \(J_{N_D}=P_D\) is weighted averaging.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite operator sum becomes a two-operator inclusion between a coordinatewise product operator and the normal cone to the diagonal.
assumptions_latex: \(A_i:H\rightrightarrows H\) are maximally monotone for \(1\leq i\leq m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{zer}(\sum_iA_i)\) is the diagonal shadow of \(\operatorname{zer}(\boldsymbol A+N_D)\).

notation.meaning: diagonal subspace of the product space

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation correctly uses weighted product geometry, diagonal consensus, and scaled component operators, but no source supports the equivalence and coordinatewise resolvent assertions, and H is undefined.

children.title: Dedicated-to-Lifted Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Connections between native multi-operator schemes and product-space representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Dedicated-to-Lifted Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correspondence between shared-primal multi-operator variables and a diagonal product-space inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For maximally monotone \(A_1,\ldots,A_m:H\rightrightarrows H\), a primal point \(x\) solves \(0\in\sum_iA_i x\) exactly when there exist certificates \(a_i\in A_i x\) satisfying \(\sum_i a_i=0\). Given positive weights \(\omega_i\) summing to one, define \(u_i=a_i/\omega_i\) and \(\boldsymbol{x}=(x,\ldots,x)\). Then
\[u_i\in(A_i/\omega_i)x,\qquad \boldsymbol{u}\in D^\perp=N_D\boldsymbol{x},\qquad 0\in\boldsymbol A\boldsymbol{x}+N_D\boldsymbol{x}.\]
Conversely, every zero of the lifted inclusion is diagonal and yields \(a_i=\omega_i u_i\in A_i x\) with zero sum. Thus dedicated shared-primal and lifted coordinates encode identical solutions and certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dedicated shared-primal variables and diagonal product-space variables represent the same solutions, with operator certificates related by weight scaling.

notation.meaning: orthogonal complement in the weighted product metric

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the correspondence leaf, but an authoritative source is needed to fix the normal-cone sign convention connecting the operator certificates to the lifted inclusion. The ambient Hilbert space is also not introduced.

children.title: Parallel-Projective Splitting Family
children.top_down_role: Parallel component access and graph-separation frameworks.

children.title: Parallel Splitting
children.top_down_role: Splitting families based on concurrent component evaluations.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parallel Douglas–Rachford splitting of a finite operator sum in product space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(z_i^0\in H\), choose \(\gamma>0\), weights \(\omega_i>0\) summing to one, and \(0<\lambda_k<2\). Compute all coordinates in parallel:
\[p_i^k=J_{\gamma A_i/\omega_i}z_i^k,\qquad \bar p^k=\sum_i\omega_i p_i^k,\qquad \bar z^k=\sum_i\omega_i z_i^k,\]
\[z_i^{k+1}=z_i^k+\lambda_k(2\bar p^k-\bar z^k-p_i^k).\]
This is relaxed Douglas–Rachford splitting for \(\boldsymbol A+N_D\). If every \(A_i\) is maximally monotone, the summed inclusion has a zero, and the relaxations stay away from \(0\) and \(2\), then in finite dimensions \(\bar p^k\) converges to a zero of \(\sum_iA_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Product-space Douglas–Rachford evaluates every operator resolvent in parallel and couples the coordinates only through weighted averages.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The parallel product-space Douglas–Rachford algorithm fits the leaf, but the coordinate update, relaxation conditions, and convergence of the weighted shadow lack supporting evidence; H is also undefined.

children.title: Projective Splitting
children.top_down_role: Splitting families based on graph-separating projections.

knowledge_statements.title: Projective Splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separator-projection step for a finite sum of maximally monotone operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Represent a candidate by \(q=(z,w_1,\ldots,w_{m-1})\) and set \(w_m=-\sum_{i<m}w_i\). Obtain graph points \((x_i,y_i)\in\operatorname{gra}A_i\), and define the affine separator
\[\phi(q)=\sum_{i=1}^m\langle z-x_i,y_i-w_i\rangle.\]
The Kuhn–Tucker set \(S=\{q:w_i\in A_i z,\ \sum_iw_i=0\}\) is contained in \(\{q:\phi(q)\leq0\}\). If \(\phi(q)>0\), perform
\[q^+=q-\lambda\frac{\phi(q)}{\|\nabla\phi\|^2}\nabla\phi,\qquad 0<\lambda<2,\]
where \(\nabla_z\phi=\sum_i y_i\) and \(\nabla_{w_i}\phi=x_i-x_m\). If \(\phi(q)\leq0\), retain \(q^+=q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projective splitting constructs a separator from individual operator graph points and projects the primal-dual iterate toward the Kuhn–Tucker set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\subseteq\{q:\phi(q)\leq0\}\), and the displayed step is a relaxed projection onto the separator halfspace.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The separator and relaxed halfspace-projection step are plausible projective-splitting components, but the graph-point generation rule and convergence-enabling conditions are absent. A source is needed to validate the precise separator convention, and H is not defined.

children.title: Parallel Projective Architectures
children.top_down_role: Projective frameworks supporting concurrent operator access.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(A_i:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), are maximally monotone.
The target inclusion \(0\in\sum_{i=1}^m A_i x\) has a solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p^k\in H_k\) for every solution-related Kuhn–Tucker point \(p^k\), and the relaxed projection step processes all graph evaluations in parallel.

notation.meaning: Kuhn–Tucker solution set in a primal–dual product space
separator halfspace containing the solution set
metric projection onto a closed convex set

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard parallel-projective splitting architecture for sums of maximally monotone operators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract separator-projection architecture; convergence conditions for particular block schedules are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At iteration \(k\), independently select graph points \((a_i^k,a_i^{*k})\in\operatorname{gra}A_i\) for the activated operators and use them to construct a closed affine halfspace \(H_k\) in a primal–dual product space such that \(Z\subseteq H_k\). Given the current product-space iterate \(p^k\), choose \(\lambda_k\in(0,2)\) and update
\[
p^{k+1}=p^k+\lambda_k\bigl(P_{H_k}p^k-p^k\bigr).
\]
Thus the operator graph evaluations are parallel, while their information is coupled only through the separating halfspace and one relaxed projective step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel graph evaluations build a separator containing every Kuhn–Tucker solution; a relaxed projection onto that separator produces the next product-space iterate.
knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Projective Architectures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No cited source supports the separator construction. Arbitrary selected graph points do not by themselves ensure Z is contained in H_k, and conclusion_latex incorrectly uses p^k both as the current iterate and as a solution-related point instead of stating Z\subseteq H_k.

children.title: Primal–Dual Hybrid Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Coupled proximal methods for linearly composed convex terms.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are real Hilbert spaces, \(K:X\to Y\) is bounded linear, and \(f\) and \(g\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions.
A saddle point exists and \(\tau\sigma\lVert K\rVert^2<1\), with \(\tau,\sigma>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The updates use one proximal evaluation of each convex term and couple the primal and dual variables only through \(K\) and \(K^*\).

notation.meaning: proximal mapping of a convex function
Hilbert adjoint of the linear operator

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Chambolle–Pock-type interface for minimizing a convex term plus a linearly composed convex term.

source_refs.locator: 3.1.9 Basic Elements of Primal-Dual Methods p. 191

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the problem \(\min_{x\in X} f(x)+g(Kx)\), choose \(x^0\in X\), \(y^0\in Y\), set \(\bar x^0=x^0\), and fix \(\theta\in[0,1]\). For \(k=0,1,\ldots\), compute
\[
y^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\sigma g^*}\bigl(y^k+\sigma K\bar x^k\bigr),\qquad
x^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\tau f}\bigl(x^k-\tau K^*y^{k+1}\bigr),
\]
\[
\bar x^{k+1}=x^{k+1}+\theta\bigl(x^{k+1}-x^k\bigr).
\]
Stop when a prescribed primal–dual residual tolerance is met and return \((x^{k+1},y^{k+1})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alternating proximal steps for the dual and primal terms are coupled by a linear map and its adjoint, with optional primal extrapolation.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Hybrid Interfaces

source_witnesses.locator: 3.1.9 Basic Elements of Primal-Dual Methods p. 191

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited Nesterov section does not specifically identify this Chambolle–Pock update or support convergence for every theta in [0,1] under only the stated product condition. A source for this precise algorithm and parameter regime is required.

children.title: ADMM–Resolvent Interface
children.top_down_role: The dual and reflected-resolvent relationship underlying ADMM.

assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions on a real Hilbert space.
The consensus problem \(\min f(x)+g(z)\) subject to \(x=z\) has a primal–dual solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Scaled ADMM on the consensus formulation is a Douglas–Rachford resolvent iteration for the dual inclusion.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical equivalence of consensus ADMM and Douglas–Rachford splitting on the Fenchel dual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consensus-form ADMM and Douglas–Rachford splitting on its Fenchel dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Fenchel dual of \(\min_{x=z} f(x)+g(z)\) is \(\min_y f^*(-y)+g^*(y)\). Define \(A=\partial(f^*\circ(-I))\) and \(B=\partial g^*\). Douglas–Rachford splitting for \(0\in Ay+By\) uses
\[
w^{k+1}=\tfrac12\bigl(I+R_{\gamma B}R_{\gamma A}\bigr)w^k.
\]
Under the standard scaled-multiplier identification and Moreau identities for the two resolvents, this iteration yields the scaled ADMM updates
\[
x^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f}(z^k-u^k),\quad z^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}(x^{k+1}+u^k),\quad u^{k+1}=u^k+x^{k+1}-z^{k+1}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Consensus ADMM is Douglas–Rachford splitting applied to the Fenchel-dual subdifferential inclusion, after identifying the scaled multiplier and using Moreau identities.
knowledge_statements.title: ADMM–Resolvent Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ADMM–Douglas–Rachford equivalence is convention-sensitive: operator order, penalty scaling, and the identification between w^k and (z^k,u^k) must be supported by a specific source. None is supplied.

children.title: Projection Method Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Set-valued specializations using projections and reflectors.

children.title: Projection Scheduling Family
children.top_down_role: Sequential and parallel projection families.

children.title: Alternating Projections
children.top_down_role: Sequential cyclic projection families.

assumptions_latex: \(C,D\) are nonempty closed convex subsets of a real Hilbert space and \(C\cap D\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sequence \((x^k)\) converges weakly to a point of \(C\cap D\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical von Neumann–Bregman alternating projections for closed convex sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility version for two closed convex sets with nonempty intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x^0\) in the ambient Hilbert space, generate
\[
y^k=P_Dx^k,\qquad x^{k+1}=P_Cy^k,
\]
for \(k=0,1,\ldots\). Equivalently, \(x^{k+1}=Tx^k\) with \(T=P_CP_D\). Stop when a prescribed feasibility or fixed-point residual tolerance is met and return the latest \(x^{k+1}\). If \(C\cap D\ne\varnothing\), the iterates converge weakly to a fixed point of \(P_CP_D\) lying in \(C\cap D\); in finite-dimensional spaces the convergence is in norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Project successively onto two closed convex sets. When their intersection is nonempty, the resulting iterates converge weakly to a feasible point.
knowledge_statements.title: Alternating Projections

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm and weak-convergence claim are standard for two consistent closed convex sets, but no inspectable citation with a section, theorem, or page locator is supplied.

children.title: Averaged Projections
children.top_down_role: Projection families based on averaging component images.

knowledge_statements.title: Averaged Projections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted convex averaging of projections under consistent convex feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the averaged-projection mapping
\[
T x=\sum_{i=1}^m w_iP_{C_i}x.
\]
Each metric projection is firmly nonexpansive, so \(T\) is firmly nonexpansive. Under the nonempty-intersection and positive-weight assumptions,
\[
\operatorname{Fix}T=\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i.
\]
Consequently, for any initial point \(x^0\), the iteration \(x^{k+1}=Tx^k\) converges weakly to an element of the common intersection; in finite-dimensional spaces the convergence is in norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive weighted average of projections is firmly nonexpansive, has the common intersection as its fixed-point set, and yields weakly convergent iterates.
assumptions_latex: \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\) are nonempty closed convex subsets of a real Hilbert space with nonempty intersection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\), and every orbit \(x^{k+1}=Tx^k\) converges weakly to a common point.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: fixed-point characterization of convex combinations of metric projections

children.title: Simultaneous Projections
children.top_down_role: Parallel projection families using concurrent component access.

assumptions_latex: \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\) are nonempty closed convex subsets of a real Hilbert space with nonempty intersection.
The aggregation weights satisfy \(w_i>0\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^m w_i=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: All projections can be evaluated concurrently, and the aggregated iteration converges weakly to a point in \(\bigcap_i C_i\).

notation.meaning: parallel projection of the current iterate onto the ith set

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: simultaneous projection method implemented by parallel projections and convex aggregation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parallel implementation of weighted projection aggregation for consistent convex feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose an arbitrary initial point \(x^0\). At iteration \(k\), compute concurrently
\[
p_i^k=P_{C_i}x^k,	 i=1,	\ldots,	m,
\]
and then aggregate
\[
x^{k+1}=\sum_{i=1}^m w_i p_i^k.
\]
Stop when \(\lVert x^{k+1}-x^k\rVert\) or a prescribed feasibility residual is below tolerance, and return \(x^{k+1}\). Under the stated consistency and weighting assumptions, the generated sequence converges weakly to a common point of all the sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute every set projection from the same iterate in parallel, then combine them with positive weights to obtain the next iterate.
knowledge_statements.title: Simultaneous Projections

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The simultaneous weighted-projection algorithm and convergence claim are mathematically standard under the stated assumptions, but no inspectable source is supplied.

children.title: Correction-Reflection Projection Family
children.top_down_role: Best-approximation and reflected projection families.

children.title: Dykstra Methods
children.top_down_role: Correction-based projection families for best approximation.

assumptions_latex: \(C,D\) are nonempty closed convex subsets of a real Hilbert space with \(C\cap D\ne\varnothing\).
A point \(s\) is given whose projection onto \(C\cap D\) is sought.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The primal iterates converge strongly to \(P_{C\cap D}s\).

notation.meaning: correction associated with the projection onto the first set
correction associated with the projection onto the second set
metric projection onto a closed convex set

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical two-set Dykstra projection algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-set Dykstra algorithm for the best approximation from a nonempty convex intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(x^0=s\) and \(p^0=q^0=0\). For \(k=0,1,\ldots\), perform
\[
y^k=P_C(x^k+p^k),\qquad p^{k+1}=x^k+p^k-y^k,
\]
\[
x^{k+1}=P_D(y^k+q^k),\qquad q^{k+1}=y^k+q^k-x^{k+1}.
\]
Stop when the change in the primal iterate and the feasibility residual meet prescribed tolerances. The correction variables retain the displacement discarded by each projection, and the primal sequence converges in norm to the best approximation \(P_{C\cap D}s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dykstra alternates two projections while retaining correction vectors; unlike plain alternating projections, it computes the projection of the starting point onto the intersection.
knowledge_statements.title: Dykstra Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The recurrence matches a standard two-set Dykstra sign convention, but the strong best-approximation convergence claim requires a cited theorem or textbook locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong convergence of cyclic Dykstra iterates to the best approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded algorithm and convergence theorem for a finite family of closed convex sets in a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $m\geq1$, $I=\{1,\ldots,m\}$, and let $(C_i)_{i\in I}$ be closed convex subsets of a Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ such that $C=\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i\neq\varnothing$. Given $x_0\in\mathcal H$, define $\mathrm i(n)=1+\operatorname{rem}(n-1,m)$, cyclically set $C_n=C_{\mathrm i(n)}$ and $P_n=P_{C_n}$, and initialize $q_{-(m-1)}=\cdots=q_{-1}=q_0=0$. For $n\geq1$, set
\[
x_n=P_n(x_{n-1}+q_{n-m}),\qquad q_n=x_{n-1}+q_{n-m}-x_n.
\]
Then
\[
x_n\to P_Cx_0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For finitely many closed convex subsets of a Hilbert space with nonempty intersection, the cyclic Dykstra iteration with the stated correction initialization converges in norm to the metric projection of the initial point onto their intersection.
assumptions_latex: (\forall i\in I)\;C_i\subseteq\mathcal H\text{ is closed and convex}

source_evidence.locator: Best Approximation Algorithms / 30.2. Dykstra's Algorithm / Theorem 30.7

source_refs.locator: Best Approximation Algorithms / 30.2. Dykstra's Algorithm / Theorem 30.7

knowledge_statements.title: Strong convergence of cyclic Dykstra iterates to the best approximation

source_witnesses.locator: Best Approximation Algorithms / 30.2. Dykstra's Algorithm / Theorem 30.7

directory_assessment.rationale: The supplied A08 node matches the general Dykstra method, but campaign policy assigns general first-order and projection-algorithm theory to A05. The A10 Dykstra node is a legitimate conic-feasibility specialization and should remain a cross-indexed specialization rather than a second primary home. No A05 parent is supplied, so reparenting remains a structural candidate requiring broader confirmation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vanishing liminf for finite-window increments of cumulative square-summable sequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded auxiliary sequence lemma used in the convergence analysis of cyclic Dykstra iterations; the lagged expression is considered for sufficiently large indices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $(\rho_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\in\ell_+^2(\mathbb N)$, let $m\in\mathbb N$, and define $\sigma_n=\sum_{k=0}^n\rho_k$. Then
\[
\liminf_{n\to\infty}\sigma_n\bigl(\sigma_n-\sigma_{n-m-1}\bigr)=0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonnegative square-summable sequence and any fixed natural number m, the liminf of its cumulative sum multiplied by the increment over the most recent m+1 terms is zero.

source_evidence.locator: Best Approximation Algorithms / 30.2. Dykstra's Algorithm / Lemma 30.6

children.title: Reflector-Based Methods
children.top_down_role: Projection-derived families organized around reflector compositions.

assumptions_latex: \(C,D\) are nonempty closed convex subsets of a real Hilbert space and \(C\cap D\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Douglas–Rachford iterates converge weakly to a fixed point, and their projection shadows converge weakly to a point of \(C\cap D\).

notation.meaning: reflector across a closed convex set

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical Douglas–Rachford method for two-set convex feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Averaged composition of two convex-set reflectors, with feasibility recovered from projection shadows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(R_C=2P_C-I\), \(R_D=2P_D-I\), and
\[
T=\tfrac12(I+R_DR_C).
\]
Starting from any \(x^0\), generate \(x^{k+1}=Tx^k\), equivalently
\[
x^{k+1}=x^k+P_D(2P_Cx^k-x^k)-P_Cx^k.
\]
Stop when \(\lVert x^{k+1}-x^k\rVert\) is below tolerance and return the shadow \(P_Cx^{k+1}\). Under the stated convex consistency assumptions, \((x^k)\) converges weakly to a fixed point of \(T\), while \((P_Cx^k)\) converges weakly to a point in \(C\cap D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Douglas–Rachford averages the identity with a composition of two reflectors; projected shadows of its fixed-point iterates recover a feasible point.
knowledge_statements.title: Reflector-Based Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Douglas–Rachford iteration is correctly presented, but its weak convergence and shadow-convergence assertions require an authoritative source with a precise locator.

children.title: Correction–Reflection Boundary
children.top_down_role: Structural distinctions between correction variables and reflected iterates.

assumptions_latex: \(C\) and \(D\) are distinct one-dimensional subspaces of \(\mathbb R^2\) meeting at angle \(\theta\in(0,\pi/2)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The raw reflector iteration generally fails to converge to \(C\cap D=\{0\}\), whereas averaging or correction mechanisms change the iteration fundamentally.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary two-line counterexample separating raw reflections from averaged-reflector and correction methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete boundary showing why raw reflections cannot replace Dykstra corrections or Douglas–Rachford averaging.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For two lines through the origin, the composition \(R_DR_C\) is rotation through angle \(2\theta\). Hence the raw iteration
\[
x^{k+1}=R_DR_Cx^k
\]
preserves \(\lVert x^k\rVert=\lVert x^0\rVert\). Unless the rotation and initial point are exceptional, the sequence does not converge, although \(C\cap D=\{0\}\). Thus replacing Dykstra's additive correction variables by reflections, or deleting the averaging in the Douglas–Rachford operator \(\tfrac12(I+R_DR_C)\), destroys the corresponding best-approximation or convergence mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two intersecting lines, composing raw reflections produces a norm-preserving rotation and usually does not converge, exposing the boundary between corrections, reflections, and averaged reflections.
knowledge_statements.title: Correction–Reflection Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two-line rotation counterexample is valid, but no source is supplied. The final assertion about replacing Dykstra corrections by reflections is informal and broader than the demonstrated raw-reflector failure.
