children.title: Proximal Fixed-Point Residual Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Certificates derived from proximal displacement and fixed-point displacement.

children.title: Proximal Residuals
children.top_down_role: Certificates derived from proximal displacement.

assumptions_latex: \(A:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) is maximally monotone on a real Hilbert space and \(\gamma>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_\gamma(x)\in A(J_{\gamma A}x)\), and \(r_\gamma(x)=0\) exactly when \(0\in Ax\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resolvent-based inclusion residual for a maximally monotone operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in\mathcal H\), define
\[
r_\gamma(x)=\gamma^{-1}\bigl(x-J_{\gamma A}x\bigr).
\]
The resolvent identity gives
\[
r_\gamma(x)\in A\bigl(J_{\gamma A}x\bigr).
\]
Therefore \(r_\gamma(x)\) is a directly verifiable inclusion residual at the proximal point \(J_{\gamma A}x\), and
\[
r_\gamma(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=J_{\gamma A}x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0\in Ax.
\]
Its norm consequently certifies exactness at zero and quantifies a specific graph violation away from zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The scaled displacement from a point to its resolvent image belongs to the operator at that image and vanishes exactly at an inclusion solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Residuals

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The residual identities are correct for a maximally monotone operator, but the cited convex-optimization section does not clearly support the stated general maximally monotone-operator scope. A monotone-operator source or a source-confirmed restriction is required.

children.title: Fixed-Point Residuals
children.top_down_role: Certificates derived from fixed-point displacement.

assumptions_latex: \(T:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) is a mapping on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute fixed-point residual; normalized or relative stopping rules are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in\mathcal H\), define the fixed-point residual
\[
R_T(x)=x-Tx.
\]
Then
\[
R_T(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=Tx\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in\operatorname{Fix}T.
\]
Thus \(R_T(x)\) is an exactly computable certificate whenever \(Tx\) can be evaluated. A stopping test of the form \(\lVert R_T(x)\rVert\leq\varepsilon\) certifies an \(\varepsilon\)-approximate fixed point in the absolute-residual convention, without by itself asserting distance to \(\operatorname{Fix}T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The fixed-point residual is the displacement from a point to its image. It vanishes exactly at fixed points and supports an absolute-residual stopping test.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Point Residuals

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-point residual identity and the caution about distance to the fixed-point set are precise, but the record has no citation with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Residual Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Comparisons between proximal and fixed-point residual representations.

assumptions_latex: \(A:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) is maximally monotone and \(\gamma>0\).
The fixed-point mapping is the resolvent \(T=J_{\gamma A}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_\gamma=\gamma^{-1}R_T\), so proximal and fixed-point residual tolerances differ only by the factor \(\gamma\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact scaling correspondence when the fixed-point operator is a monotone resolvent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Since \(T=J_{\gamma A}\), for every \(x\in\mathcal H\) one has the exact identity
\[
r_\gamma(x)=\gamma^{-1}\bigl(x-J_{\gamma A}x\bigr)=\gamma^{-1}(x-Tx)=\gamma^{-1}R_T(x).
\]
Consequently,
\[
\lVert r_\gamma(x)\rVert\leq\varepsilon
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\lVert R_T(x)\rVert\leq\gamma\varepsilon,
\]
and both residuals vanish on precisely the same solution set:
\[
0\in Ax\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=Tx.
\]
The correspondence is an equality, not merely an asymptotic comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a resolvent fixed-point map, the proximal residual is exactly the fixed-point residual divided by the stepsize, so their stopping tolerances translate directly.
knowledge_statements.title: Residual Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scaling correspondence is algebraically correct, but the cited proximal-point section does not clearly support the full maximally monotone resolvent setting used by the record.

children.title: Gradient-Mapping Residuals
children.top_down_role: Composite and constrained first-order residual families.

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Mapping Residuals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composite convex gradient mapping with a fixed positive stepsize.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(f:H\to\mathbb R\) be convex and Fréchet differentiable, let \(g:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex, and fix \(\gamma>0\). The proximal-gradient mapping is
\[
G_\gamma(x):=\gamma^{-1}\bigl(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}(x-\gamma\nabla f(x))\bigr).
\]
It is a stationarity residual: \(G_\gamma(x)=0\) if and only if \(0\in\nabla f(x)+\partial g(x)\). When \(g=\delta_C\) for a nonempty closed convex set \(C\), this becomes the projected-gradient residual \(\gamma^{-1}(x-P_C(x-\gamma\nabla f(x)))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The scaled displacement of one proximal-gradient step is zero exactly at composite stationary points; constraints arise by taking the nonsmooth term to be an indicator.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and Fréchet differentiable on \(H\).

notation.meaning: proximal mapping of gamma times g

children.title: Natural-Normal Map Residual Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Projection-based certificates for variational and constrained inclusions.

children.title: Natural-Map Residuals
children.top_down_role: Projection-based certificates expressed through natural maps.

knowledge_statements.title: Natural-Map Residuals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward–backward natural residual for a monotone inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximal monotone, let \(B:H\to H\) be single-valued, and fix \(\gamma>0\). With \(J_{\gamma A}:=(I+\gamma A)^{-1}\), define the natural-map residual
\[
R_\gamma(x):=\gamma^{-1}\bigl(x-J_{\gamma A}(x-\gamma Bx)\bigr).
\]
The resolvent identity gives \(R_\gamma(x)=0\) if and only if \(0\in Ax+Bx\). Thus \(\lVert R_\gamma(x)\rVert\) is a computable residual whenever evaluations of \(B\) and \(J_{\gamma A}\) are available.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The natural residual is the scaled displacement of a forward–backward step and vanishes exactly at solutions of the inclusion.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: resolvent identity for the standard forward–backward natural map
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically standard, internally consistent, and appropriately classified as a definition, but no inspectable source with a specific locator is supplied. A source is required for the natural-map terminology and residual formulation.

children.title: Normal-Map Residuals
children.top_down_role: Projection-based certificates expressed through normal maps.

knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Map Residuals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal-map residual in the resolvent-coordinate variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximal monotone, let \(B:H\to H\) be single-valued, and fix \(\gamma>0\). For \(z\in H\), set \(p:=J_{\gamma A}z\) and define
\[
N_\gamma(z):=Bp+\gamma^{-1}(z-p).
\]
Because \(\gamma^{-1}(z-p)\in Ap\), the equality \(N_\gamma(z)=0\) implies \(0\in Ap+Bp\). Conversely, every solution \(p\) of this inclusion admits \(z=p-\gamma Bp\) with \(J_{\gamma A}z=p\) and \(N_\gamma(z)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normal map expresses the inclusion in resolvent coordinates; its zeros correspond exactly to primal solutions, with an explicit coordinate transformation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_\gamma(z)=0\Rightarrow 0\in A(J_{\gamma A}z)+B(J_{\gamma A}z)\), and every solution is represented by such a zero.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard resolvent-coordinate normal map for a monotone inclusion
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The resolvent-coordinate normal map and its zero-to-solution correspondence are mathematically coherent, and definition is the correct content kind. No source or locator is supplied for this convention, so the record requires authoritative support.

children.title: Natural-to-Normal Map Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural conversion between natural-map and normal-map certificates.

knowledge_statements.title: Natural-to-Normal Map Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact residual identity under the natural-to-normal coordinate change.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the natural- and normal-map definitions above, fix \(x\in H\), set \(z:=x-\gamma Bx\), and let \(p:=J_{\gamma A}z\). Then \(p=x-\gamma R_\gamma(x)\) and
\[
N_\gamma(z)=R_\gamma(x)+Bp-Bx.
\]
If \(B\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, then
\[
\lVert N_\gamma(z)\rVert\le (1+\gamma L)\lVert R_\gamma(x)\rVert.
\]
If additionally \(\gamma L<1\), then
\[
(1-\gamma L)\lVert R_\gamma(x)\rVert\le\lVert N_\gamma(z)\rVert,
\]
so the two residuals are quantitatively equivalent under this coordinate change.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A forward coordinate change links natural and normal residuals exactly; Lipschitz continuity makes their norms equivalent when the stepsize is sufficiently small.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_\gamma(z)=R_\gamma(x)+Bp-Bx\), with two-sided norm control when \(\gamma L<1\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct algebraic correspondence between standard natural and normal maps
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact identity and both Lipschitz norm bounds are correct under the stated coordinate change, and representation is the appropriate content kind for this correspondence leaf. No inspectable source is supplied for the identity or quantitative equivalence.

children.title: Primal–Dual Residuals
children.top_down_role: Coupled feasibility, stationarity, and consistency certificates.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Residuals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: KKT residual certificate for linearly composed convex objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, let \(K:X\to Y\) be linear, and let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(g:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex. For \((x,y)\in X\times Y\), define
\[
r_{\mathrm p}(x,y):=\operatorname{dist}(-K^*y,\partial f(x)),\qquad r_{\mathrm d}(x,y):=\operatorname{dist}(Kx,\partial g^*(y)).
\]
The combined residual \(r_{\mathrm{pd}}(x,y):=(r_{\mathrm p}(x,y)^2+r_{\mathrm d}(x,y)^2)^{1/2}\) is zero exactly when \((x,y)\) satisfies the primal–dual KKT inclusion for minimizing \(f(x)+g(Kx)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The combined distances to the two KKT inclusions certify simultaneous primal–dual stationarity and consistency, vanishing exactly at a KKT pair.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces and \(K:X\to Y\) is linear.
\(f\) and \(g\) are proper, closed, and convex.

source_refs.locator: 3.1.9 Basic Elements of Primal-Dual Methods p. 191

source_witnesses.locator: 3.1.9 Basic Elements of Primal-Dual Methods p. 191

children.title: Residual-to-Error Principles
children.top_down_role: Regularity mechanisms converting residual control into distance, value, or stability control.

children.title: Strong-Monotonicity Error Control
children.top_down_role: Residual control in strongly monotone regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Monotonicity Error Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global residual-to-distance bound for strongly monotone inclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(T:H\rightrightarrows H\) be \(\mu\)-strongly monotone for some \(\mu>0\), meaning that
\[
\langle u-v,x-y\rangle\ge \mu\lVert x-y\rVert^2
\]
whenever \(u\in Tx\) and \(v\in Ty\). If \(0\in Tx^*\), then \(x^*\) is the unique zero of \(T\), and for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}T\) and every \(u\in Tx\),
\[
\lVert x-x^*\rVert\le \mu^{-1}\lVert u\rVert.
\]
Consequently, \(\operatorname{dist}(x,T^{-1}(0))\le\mu^{-1}\operatorname{dist}(0,Tx)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong monotonicity makes the norm of any inclusion residual control distance to the unique solution with constant one over the monotonicity modulus.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: immediate standard error bound for a strongly monotone operator
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem and constant are correct: strong monotonicity yields uniqueness and the stated global residual-to-distance estimate. The theorem content kind fits the error-control leaf, but no source with a specific locator is provided.

children.title: Metric Regularity Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Local residual-to-solution-set control for set-valued mappings.

children.title: Metric Regularity
children.top_down_role: Residual-to-solution control associated with full metric regularity.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local two-variable metric regularity of a set-valued mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be metric spaces, let \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), and let \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\). The mapping \(F\) is metrically regular at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar y\) if there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\), and a constant \(\kappa\ge0\), such that
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,F^{-1}(y))\le \kappa\operatorname{dist}(y,F(x))
\]
for every \((x,y)\in U\times V\), using distance \(+\infty\) to the empty set. The least admissible \(\kappa\) is the local regularity modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric regularity uniformly bounds distance to nearby inverse images by the corresponding residual for both the point and right-hand side varying locally.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical variational-analysis definition of metric regularity
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed local two-variable inequality is the standard metric-regularity definition, and definition is the correct content kind. An authoritative source is absent. The source should also clarify the modulus convention: it is normally defined as the infimum of admissible constants over suitable neighborhoods, not necessarily an attained least constant.

children.title: Metric Subregularity
children.top_down_role: Localized residual-to-solution control associated with metric subregularity.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric Subregularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-right-hand-side local metric subregularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be metric spaces, let \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), and let \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\). The mapping \(F\) is metrically subregular at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar y\) if there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and a constant \(\kappa\ge0\) such that
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,F^{-1}(\bar y))\le \kappa\operatorname{dist}(\bar y,F(x))
\]
for every \(x\in U\). Unlike metric regularity, the target value remains fixed at \(\bar y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric subregularity gives a local residual-to-solution error bound for one fixed target value, without requiring uniform control over nearby targets.

notation.meaning: inverse image of the fixed target value

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical variational-analysis definition of metric subregularity
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-target inequality correctly distinguishes metric subregularity from metric regularity, and definition is the correct content kind. No authoritative citation with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Regularity-Strength Boundary
children.top_down_role: Distinctions in scope and strength between the two regularity regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Regularity-Strength Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict separation between metric regularity and subregularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Metric regularity of \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar y\) implies metric subregularity there by fixing \(y=\bar y\), but the converse fails. For example, let \(X=Y=\mathbb R\) and \(F(x):=\{0\}\) for every \(x\). At \((0,0)\), subregularity holds with any \(\kappa\ge0\), because \(F^{-1}(0)=\mathbb R\) and both sides of the subregularity inequality are zero. Metric regularity fails because for every nearby \(y\ne0\), \(F^{-1}(y)=\varnothing\) while \(\operatorname{dist}(y,F(x))=|y|<+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regularity always implies subregularity, while a constant zero mapping is subregular at zero but cannot be regular because nearby nonzero targets have empty inverse images.
assumptions_latex: Distance to the empty set is \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Metric regularity implies metric subregularity, but metric subregularity does not imply metric regularity.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: implication follows by fixing the target; the displayed constant-map counterexample is directly checkable
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The implication and constant-zero-map counterexample are correct, and failure_boundary is the exact mathematical role of this leaf. The record nevertheless has no inspectable source or locator supporting the strict separation.

children.title: Growth-Polyhedral Error-Bound Family
children.top_down_role: Function-growth and polyhedral regimes supporting strengthened certification.

children.title: Growth-Based Error Bounds
children.top_down_role: Error control supported by objective-growth geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Growth-Based Error Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subgradient error control derived from local quadratic growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex, and let \(S:=\operatorname*{argmin}f\ne\varnothing\). Suppose that on a neighborhood \(U\) of \(S\),
\[
f(x)\ge \inf f+\frac{\mu}{2}\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^2
\]
for some \(\mu>0\). Then every \(x\in U\) and \(v\in\partial f(x)\) satisfy
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le \frac{2}{\mu}\lVert v\rVert.
\]
Hence \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le(2/\mu)\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\) whenever the subdifferential value is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local quadratic objective growth converts a subgradient norm into a local distance-to-solution bound with constant two over the growth modulus.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, closed, and convex with \(S=\operatorname*{argmin}f\ne\varnothing\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard convex subgradient inequality combined with quadratic growth
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The local quadratic-growth hypothesis yields the stated convex subgradient error bound with constant 2/mu, and theorem is the appropriate content kind. No source with a specific theorem, section, or page locator is supplied.

children.title: Polyhedral Error Bounds
children.top_down_role: Error control supported by polyhedral structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Error Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hoffman error bound for a nonempty polyhedral system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
S:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b,\ Cx=d\}
\]
be nonempty. There exists a constant \(H\ge0\), depending only on the matrices \(A\) and \(C\) and on the chosen norms, such that every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfies
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le H\left\lVert
\begin{pmatrix}
(Ax-b)_+\\
Cx-d
\end{pmatrix}
\right\rVert.
\]
Thus the readily evaluated inequality violations and equality residuals provide a global certificate of distance to the feasible polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any consistent finite linear system, the combined constraint violation globally controls distance to its feasible polyhedron through a matrix-dependent Hoffman constant.
assumptions_latex: The residual and distance use fixed finite-dimensional norms.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical finite-dimensional Hoffman error bound
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is recognizably the classical Hoffman error-bound theorem and theorem is the correct content kind, but it lacks a source. The dimensions and domains of A, b, C, and d are also not explicitly introduced; these must be specified when a sourced replacement is prepared.

children.title: Growth–Polyhedral Overlap
children.top_down_role: Settings where growth geometry and polyhedral structure provide parallel certification.

knowledge_statements.title: Growth–Polyhedral Overlap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concurrent growth and subregularity mechanisms for convex piecewise linear-quadratic objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(q:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, convex, and piecewise linear-quadratic, and suppose \(S:=\operatorname*{argmin}q\ne\varnothing\). For every \(\bar x\in S\), there are a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and constants \(\alpha,\kappa>0\) such that
\[
q(x)\ge\inf q+\frac{\alpha}{2}\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^2,
\qquad
\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial q(x))
\]
for all applicable \(x\in U\). Thus this class supports both a growth-based explanation and a polyhedral-multifunction explanation of the same local residual-to-error control.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex piecewise linear-quadratic objectives locally exhibit both quadratic growth and a polyhedral subdifferential error bound, so the two certificate mechanisms overlap.
assumptions_latex: \(q\) is proper, closed, convex, and piecewise linear-quadratic on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local quadratic growth and local subgradient error bounds both hold around every \(\bar x\in S\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: convex piecewise linear-quadratic functions have piecewise-polyhedral subdifferentials and local quadratic growth at minimizers
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Property is a suitable content kind for an overlap statement, but the joint quadratic-growth and subdifferential-error-bound claim for every proper closed convex piecewise linear-quadratic function needs an authoritative theorem-level source. The phrase 'all applicable x' must also be replaced by an explicit domain convention, particularly when the extended-valued function has an empty subdifferential.

children.title: Approximate Optimality Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Relationships among residual, objective, feasibility, and solution-distance accuracy.

children.title: Accuracy-Measure Conversion System
children.top_down_role: Alternative accuracy measures and their regularity-dependent conversions.

children.title: Residual Accuracy
children.top_down_role: Approximation quality measured through residual certificates.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Accuracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual accuracy for a monotone inclusion in a finite-dimensional Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, let \(T:H\rightrightarrows H\), and let \(\rho\ge 0\). A point \(x\in\operatorname{dom}T\) has residual accuracy \(\rho\) for \(0\in T(x)\) when
\[
r_T(x):=\operatorname{dist}(0,T(x))=\inf_{v\in T(x)}\|v\|\le \rho.
\]
Equivalently, because \(T(x)\) is closed, there exists \(v\in T(x)\) with \(\|v\|\le\rho\). Residual accuracy zero is precisely the inclusion \(0\in T(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual accuracy bounds the norm of the smallest inclusion vector at the candidate point; zero residual is exact stationarity.

notation.meaning: distance from zero to the value set T(x)

children.title: Objective Accuracy
children.top_down_role: Approximation quality measured through objective gaps.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute primal objective accuracy for convex minimization with an attained finite optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space. Let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex, and suppose \(f^*:=\min_{y\in H}f(y)\) is finite and attained. For \(\varepsilon\ge0\), a point \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) has objective accuracy \(\varepsilon\) when
\[
0\le f(x)-f^*\le\varepsilon.
\]
Thus objective accuracy measures primal suboptimality rather than stationarity or distance to the solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A candidate has objective accuracy epsilon when its objective value exceeds the attained optimum by at most epsilon.
knowledge_statements.title: Objective Accuracy

children.title: Distance Accuracy
children.top_down_role: Approximation quality measured through distance to a solution set.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space.

notation.meaning: distance from x to the solution set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance-to-solution accuracy for an inclusion with a nonempty closed solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space, let \(T:H\rightrightarrows H\), and let its solution set be \(S:=\{x\in H:0\in T(x)\}\). Assume \(S\) is nonempty and closed. For \(\delta\ge0\), a point \(x\in H\) has distance accuracy \(\delta\) when
\[
d_S(x):=\operatorname{dist}(x,S)=\inf_{x^*\in S}\|x-x^*\|\le\delta.
\]
In finite dimensions the infimum is attained, so this is equivalent to the existence of \(x^*\in S\) satisfying \(\|x-x^*\|\le\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance accuracy bounds how far the candidate lies from the inclusion's solution set.
knowledge_statements.title: Distance Accuracy

children.title: Accuracy-Measure Conversions
children.top_down_role: Regularity-dependent relationships among the three accuracy measures.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversions for differentiable objectives that are strongly convex and smooth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space. Let \(f:H\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable, \(\mu\)-strongly convex, and have \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, where \(0<\mu\le L\). Let \(x^*\) be its unique minimizer, and define \(r=\|\nabla f(x)\|\), \(e=f(x)-f(x^*)\), and \(d=\|x-x^*\|\) for \(x\in H\). Then
\[
\frac{\mu}{2}d^2\le e\le\frac{r^2}{2\mu},\qquad
\mu d\le r\le Ld,
\]
and
\[
r\le\sqrt{2Le},\qquad d\le\sqrt{\frac{2e}{\mu}}.
\]
Consequently, any certified bound on one measure yields the corresponding displayed bounds on the others.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a differentiable, strongly convex, smooth objective on a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space, gradient residual, objective gap, and distance to the minimizer satisfy the displayed conversion inequalities.
knowledge_statements.title: Accuracy-Measure Conversions

children.title: Pointwise-Ergodic Certificate Pair
children.top_down_role: Certificate distinctions used by inclusion-solving analyses.

children.title: Pointwise Certificates
children.top_down_role: Certificates attached to individual iterates.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A current-iterate certificate for approximate solution of a monotone inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(T:H\rightrightarrows H\), and let \(\rho\ge0\). A pointwise \(\rho\)-certificate is a pair \((x,v)\in H\times H\) satisfying
\[
v\in T(x),\qquad \|v\|\le\rho.
\]
The pair directly certifies \(\operatorname{dist}(0,T(x))\le\rho\). It is verifiable whenever membership in the graph of \(T\) and the norm of \(v\) can be checked. For \(\rho=0\), the certified point is an exact solution of \(0\in T(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph pair with a small inclusion vector certifies that its own point has small residual.
knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise Certificates

children.title: Ergodic Certificates
children.top_down_role: Certificates attached to averaged iterate aggregates.

knowledge_statements.title: Ergodic Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An averaged certificate expressed through the enlargement of a monotone operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a monotone operator \(T:H\rightrightarrows H\), define
\[
T^{[\varepsilon]}(x):=\{v:\langle x-y,v-w\rangle\ge-\varepsilon\ \text{for every }(y,w)\in\operatorname{gra}T\}.
\]
An ergodic \((\rho,\varepsilon)\)-certificate is a pair \((\bar x,\bar v)\) satisfying
\[
\bar v\in T^{[\varepsilon]}(\bar x),\qquad \|\bar v\|\le\rho,
\]
where \(\rho,\varepsilon\ge0\). It certifies approximate stationarity in the enlarged inclusion; when \(\varepsilon=0\), it reduces to a pointwise residual certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ergodic certificate gives a small averaged vector belonging to an epsilon-enlargement of the operator at the averaged point.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source or inspectable locator is supplied for the enlargement definition. Moreover, for a merely monotone operator, \(T^{[0]}\) need not equal \(T\); the asserted reduction to a pointwise graph certificate generally requires maximal monotonicity. The space \(H\) and the domain of the variable in the enlargement are also undeclared. Source-supported correction of the hypotheses is required.

children.title: Pointwise-to-Ergodic Comparison
children.top_down_role: Comparative scope of individual-iterate and averaged certificates.

knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise-to-Ergodic Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted graph pairs always produce an enlargement certificate, but generally not a graph pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T:H\rightrightarrows H\) be monotone, let \((x_i,v_i)\in\operatorname{gra}T\), and let \(\alpha_i\ge0\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i=1\). Define
\[
\bar x=\sum_i\alpha_i x_i,\qquad \bar v=\sum_i\alpha_i v_i,
\]
and
\[
\bar\varepsilon=\sum_i\alpha_i\langle x_i-\bar x,v_i-\bar v\rangle.
\]
Then \(\bar\varepsilon\ge0\) and \(\bar v\in T^{[\bar\varepsilon]}(\bar x)\). Hence averaging pointwise certificates yields an ergodic certificate, although generally \(\bar v\notin T(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted average of graph pairs satisfies an enlarged inclusion, while it need not remain on the operator’s graph.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The transportation formula and enlarged-inclusion conclusion are standard and mathematically plausible, and property fits the comparison leaf, but no authoritative source or locator is supplied. The statement also uses \(H\), its inner product, and the enlargement notation without introducing them locally. A source-supported complete formulation is required.

children.title: Proximal Oracle Complexity Interface
children.top_down_role: Complexity interfaces indexed by evaluation cost and proximal accuracy.

children.title: Oracle-Algebra Cost Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Primitive-oracle and explicit linear-algebra cost regimes.

children.title: Unit-Cost Oracle Models
children.top_down_role: Complexity accounting that treats proximal evaluations as primitive calls.

knowledge_statements.title: Unit-Cost Oracle Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact proximal-oracle complexity with free local arithmetic and one unit per query.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix an operator class \(\mathcal T\). In the exact unit-cost proximal-oracle model, an algorithm may query \((T,z,\lambda)\), where \(T\in\mathcal T\), \(z\in H\), and \(\lambda>0\), and receive
\[
J_{\lambda T}(z):=(I+\lambda T)^{-1}(z).
\]
Each oracle query costs one unit; scalar arithmetic, vector combinations, comparisons, and storage are uncharged. The oracle complexity of an algorithm is the worst-case number of such queries required to return its prescribed accuracy certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The model counts each exact resolvent evaluation as one operation and ignores internal algebra and storage costs.
assumptions_latex: \(J_{\lambda T}(z)\) is single-valued for admissible queries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\mathrm{oracle}}\) equals the worst-case number of resolvent queries before certification.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition is an appropriate content kind for this model leaf, but the exact query interface, free-operation convention, and worst-case accounting rule are model choices requiring a source. No citation is supplied, and \(H\) and the identity map \(I\) are not introduced. The assumptions also need a sourced admissible operator class ensuring single-valued resolvent responses.

children.title: Structured-Algebra Cost Models
children.top_down_role: Complexity accounting based on explicit structured linear-algebra work.

knowledge_statements.title: Structured-Algebra Cost Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Implementation-aware accounting for the primitive operations used by proximal oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let oracle call \(k\) be implemented by a finite sequence of primitive algebraic operations from a declared set \(\mathcal P\), with nonnegative operation weights \(w_p\). If \(n_{k,p}\) operations of type \(p\) are used, define
\[
c_k:=\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}w_p n_{k,p}.
\]
For \(N\) oracle calls and outer-method overhead \(c_{\mathrm{out}}\), the structured-algebra cost is
\[
C_{\mathrm{alg}}:=c_{\mathrm{out}}+\sum_{k=1}^N c_k.
\]
The primitive set, weights, dimensions, sparsity assumptions, and factorization reuse must be fixed before comparing algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Structured cost totals weighted primitive operations inside every oracle call together with outer-algorithm overhead.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P\) and its weights are fixed.
Every oracle implementation has a finite primitive-operation count.

notation.meaning: algebraic cost of oracle call k

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted primitive-operation accounting is coherent and definition fits the model leaf, but it is a declared cost convention rather than a source-independent mathematical fact. No citation or locator supports the primitive set, charging convention, or treatment of reuse and overhead.

children.title: Oracle-to-Algebra Cost Translation
children.top_down_role: Comparisons between primitive-call counts and structured computational costs.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle-to-Algebra Cost Translation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translation of an oracle-call bound under uniform implementation and overhead bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose an algorithm returns the required certificate after at most \(N(\eta)\) oracle calls at target accuracy \(\eta\). If every call costs at most \(c_{\mathrm{orc}}\) primitive-operation units and the outer work per call costs at most \(c_{\mathrm{out}}\), with fixed setup cost \(c_0\), then
\[
C_{\mathrm{alg}}(\eta)\le c_0+N(\eta)\bigl(c_{\mathrm{orc}}+c_{\mathrm{out}}\bigr).
\]
Thus a unit-cost oracle bound becomes an algebraic bound only after the oracle implementation, dimensions, precision, and reusable setup have been accounted for.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiply the oracle-call bound by a valid per-call implementation cost, then add outer work and one-time setup.
assumptions_latex: \(N(\eta)\) bounds the number of oracle calls.
Per-call oracle and outer costs are uniformly bounded.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed bound follows from the stated uniform per-call and setup bounds, and complexity_bound fits the translation leaf. However, no source supports the accounting assumptions or the precise oracle-to-algebra translation convention, so an authoritative locator is required before candidate review.

children.title: Nested-Solve Cost Models
children.top_down_role: Nested evaluations, caching, and warm-start cost regimes.

children.title: Iterative Inner-Solve Models
children.top_down_role: Nested cost models for iterative proximal subproblem evaluation.

knowledge_statements.title: Iterative Inner-Solve Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nested complexity accounting when each proximal oracle call is computed iteratively.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose outer iteration \(k\) requests a proximal point \(y_k^*=J_{\lambda_kT_k}(z_k)\) and an inner method returns \(y_k\) satisfying \(\|y_k-y_k^*\|\le\delta_k\) after \(q_k(\delta_k)\) inner iterations. If one inner iteration costs \(c_k\) primitive-operation units, then after \(N\) outer iterations the inner-solve cost obeys
\[
C_{\mathrm{inner}}\le\sum_{k=1}^N c_k q_k(\delta_k).
\]
Any outer accuracy claim is conditional on an explicit error rule for \((\delta_k)_{k=1}^N\), such as a summability or weighted-budget condition required by that outer method.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nested cost sums the iterations used by every inexact proximal solve; the tolerances must also satisfy the outer method’s error rule.
assumptions_latex: Each requested resolvent value exists uniquely.
The outer convergence theorem specifies an admissible error rule.

notation.meaning: inner-solve accuracy at outer iteration k

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nested-cost idea fits the leaf, but no source is supplied for either the inner-solve model or the method-dependent outer error condition. The phrase that one inner iteration costs \(c_k\) does not clarify whether this is an exact cost or an upper bound, which is necessary for the displayed upper bound. A source-supported formulation must specify the outer method's admissible error rule and the cost inequality.

children.title: Amortized Inner-Solve Models
children.top_down_role: Sequence-level cost models incorporating reuse across evaluations.

knowledge_statements.title: Amortized Inner-Solve Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Average inner-solve cost across a sequence of related proximal subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(N\) outer iterations, let \(C_k\ge0\) be the realized primitive-operation cost of the \(k\)-th inner solve, including any update of reusable state. An amortized inner-solve bound consists of constants \(C_0\ge0\) and \(\bar C\ge0\) such that
\[
\sum_{k=1}^N C_k\le C_0+N\bar C
\]
for every admissible run. Consequently,
\[
\frac1N\sum_{k=1}^N C_k\le\bar C+\frac{C_0}{N}.
\]
The bound is valid only when setup, failed inner iterations, and maintenance of cached state are included in the charged costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An amortized model bounds total inner work by one setup charge plus a uniform average charge per outer iteration.
assumptions_latex: \(C_k\) includes all realized inner and state-maintenance work.
The inequality holds for every admissible run.

notation.meaning: realized cost of inner solve k

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement primarily defines what qualifies as an amortized inner-solve model rather than deriving a method-specific complexity bound, so definition would better fit its mathematical role. No source or locator supports the charging convention or the universal admissible-run quantifier. Source-supported revision, including correction of the content kind, is required.

children.title: Warm-Start Cost Regimes
children.top_down_role: Amortized regimes driven by initialization reuse across inner solves.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone.
At outer step \(k\), an inner method computes an approximation to \(J_{\lambda_k A}(x_k)\), initialized from state \(w_{k-1}\).
\(N(d,\varepsilon)\) bounds the inner iterations needed when the initial state is within distance \(d\) of the current inner solution set.

notation.meaning: Resolvent of the maximally monotone operator at parameter lambda
Solution set of the kth inner proximal subproblem
Total number of inner iterations through K outer steps

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Warm-start cost is conventionally parameterized by initial distance to each changing inner solution set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract iteration accounting for sequentially warm-started proximal subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each outer index \(k\), let \(S_k\) be the solution set of the inner problem defining \(J_{\lambda_kA}(x_k)\), and initialize its solver at the preceding state \(w_{k-1}\). If the inner solver reaches tolerance \(\varepsilon_k\) in at most \(N(d_k,\varepsilon_k)\) iterations whenever \(d_k=\operatorname{dist}(w_{k-1},S_k)\), then the cumulative inner work through \(K\) outer steps satisfies \[T_K^{\mathrm{warm}}\leq\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}N(d_k,\varepsilon_k).\] A warm-start regime is one in which these distances are explicitly charged and are smaller than the corresponding cold-start distances used by the reference cost model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Warm-start complexity sums inner iteration bounds evaluated at the distance from each reused solver state to the next proximal subproblem's solution set.
knowledge_statements.title: Warm-Start Cost Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The accounting bound and complexity-bound kind fit the leaf, but no inspectable source supports this particular warm-start distance model or its comparison with cold starts.

children.title: Cached-Structure Cost Regimes
children.top_down_role: Amortized regimes driven by reusable algebraic structure.

assumptions_latex: A family of proximal subproblems shares invariant data \(D\).
Preprocessing \(D\) costs \(P(D)\), and the cached representation supports the \(k\)-th solve at cost \(C_k(D,\varepsilon_k)\).

notation.meaning: Invariant structural data shared by the nested proximal problems
Cached per-solve cost at requested tolerance

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Reusable preprocessing is charged once in standard amortized computational cost models.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost accounting for reusable factorizations, preconditioners, or symbolic structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the first \(K\) inner proximal subproblems share invariant data \(D\), such as a linear operator, sparsity pattern, or fixed metric. If constructing a valid cached representation costs \(P(D)\) operations and, after construction, the \(k\)-th solve to tolerance \(\varepsilon_k\) costs at most \(C_k(D,\varepsilon_k)\), then the cached-structure cost is bounded by \[T_K^{\mathrm{cache}}\leq P(D)+\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}C_k(D,\varepsilon_k).\] The cache is admissible only while the data on which its correctness depends remain unchanged; otherwise preprocessing must be charged again.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When proximal subproblems share valid invariant structure, preprocessing is charged once and only the cached per-solve costs accumulate.
knowledge_statements.title: Cached-Structure Cost Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cost accounting is coherent and fits the cached-structure leaf, but no cited source establishes its use for nested proximal solves or specifies when cached preprocessing remains valid.

children.title: Inexact Oracle Error Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Principal models for approximate proximal and resolvent evaluations.

children.title: Absolute Error Models
children.top_down_role: Approximate proximal evaluations controlled by absolute error levels.

knowledge_statements.title: Absolute Error Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-norm definition of an absolute-error proximal oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x\in H\), \(\lambda>0\), and \(\delta\geq0\), an oracle output \((y,v)\) is an absolute-error approximation to the resolvent inclusion for \(A\) if \[v\in A(y)\quad\text{and}\quad \|x-y-\lambda v\|\leq\delta.\] Equivalently, with \(r=x-y-\lambda v\), one has \(\|r\|\leq\delta\) and \(x-r\in y+\lambda A(y)\). The tolerance \(\delta\) is prescribed independently of the step displacement and operator value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An absolute-error oracle returns a graph point whose resolvent residual has norm at most a prescribed, scale-independent tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\), \(x\in H\), and \(\lambda>0\).
An inexact oracle returns \((y,v)\in H\times H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair is absolutely \(\delta\)-accurate when \(v\in A(y)\) and \(\|x-y-\lambda v\|\leq\delta\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Absolute inexactness bounds the norm of the resolvent residual by a prescribed scale-independent tolerance.

children.title: Relative Error Models
children.top_down_role: Approximate proximal evaluations controlled relative to problem-dependent scales.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\), \(x\in H\), and \(\lambda>0\).
An inexact oracle returns \((y,v)\) with \(v\in A(y)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Relative accuracy holds when \(\|x-y-\lambda v\|\leq\sigma\sqrt{\|x-y\|^2+\|\lambda v\|^2}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Relative proximal criteria compare the residual with a homogeneous scale formed from the computed step and operator value.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogeneous residual criterion scaled by the computed proximal step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0\leq\sigma<1\), an oracle output \((y,v)\) is a relative-error approximation to the resolvent inclusion for \(A\) at \((x,\lambda)\) if \[v\in A(y)\quad\text{and}\quad \|x-y-\lambda v\|\leq\sigma\bigl(\|x-y\|^2+\|\lambda v\|^2\bigr)^{1/2}.\] Both sides scale identically under a common rescaling of \(x-y\) and \(\lambda v\). In particular, if the scale on the right vanishes, the criterion forces the residual to vanish and hence yields an exact resolvent evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relative-error oracle bounds the resolvent residual by a dimensionless fraction of the combined step and scaled operator-value norm.
knowledge_statements.title: Relative Error Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally precise and fits the relative-error leaf, but this normalization is one particular relative proximal criterion and has no inspectable supporting citation.

children.title: Enlargement-Based Error Models
children.top_down_role: Approximate resolvent evaluations represented through operator enlargements.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is monotone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An enlargement-based proximal output satisfies \(v\in A^{[\varepsilon]}(y)\) together with a stated residual bound for \(x-y-\lambda v\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The displayed inequality is the standard epsilon-enlargement definition for a monotone operator.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Brøndsted-Rockafellar enlargement model with a separate resolvent residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\varepsilon\geq0\), define the enlargement of a monotone operator \(A\) by \[A^{[\varepsilon]}(y)=\{v\in H:\langle y-z,v-w\rangle\geq-\varepsilon\ \text{for every}\ (z,w)\in\operatorname{gra}A\}.\] An enlargement-based inexact proximal output at \((x,\lambda)\) is a triple \((y,v,\varepsilon)\) satisfying \(v\in A^{[\varepsilon]}(y)\), together with an explicitly imposed bound on the residual \(r=x-y-\lambda v\). The model separates graph inexactness, measured by \(\varepsilon\), from algebraic inexactness, measured through \(r\); when both vanish, the exact resolvent inclusion holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enlargement-based inexactness permits a quantified violation of graph membership while separately controlling the resolvent residual.
knowledge_statements.title: Enlargement-Based Error Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The enlargement formula is standard, but the proposed proximal error model leaves the accompanying residual bound unspecified and supplies no authoritative source selecting the intended variant.

children.title: Error-Model Comparability
children.top_down_role: Structural relationships among the principal inexactness models.

knowledge_statements.title: Error-Model Comparability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion between absolute and relative residual criteria under scale bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r=x-y-\lambda v\) and \(s=(\|x-y\|^2+\|\lambda v\|^2)^{1/2}\). If \(s\geq m>0\), then \(\|r\|\leq\delta\) implies \(\|r\|\leq\sigma s\) with \(\sigma=\delta/m\); under the convention \(0\leq\sigma<1\), this conversion requires \(0\leq\delta<m\). Conversely, if \(s\leq M<\infty\), then \(\|r\|\leq\sigma s\) implies \(\|r\|\leq\delta\) with \(\delta=\sigma M\). Thus neither model uniformly dominates the other without a corresponding scale bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Absolute and relative residual criteria convert under lower or upper bounds on the normalization scale; conversion to a relative tolerance below one additionally requires the absolute tolerance to be smaller than the lower scale bound.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(x,y,v\in H\), \(\lambda>0\), and \(r=x-y-\lambda v\).
Absolute and relative tolerances satisfy \(\delta\geq0\) and \(0\leq\sigma<1\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(s\geq m>0\) and \(\delta<m\), absolute error \(\delta\) implies relative error \(\sigma=\delta/m<1\); if \(s\leq M<\infty\), relative error \(\sigma\) implies absolute error \(\delta=\sigma M\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Comparability follows by upper or lower bounding the normalization scale.

children.title: Long-Run Error-Control Regimes
children.top_down_role: Long-run error-control families used in convergence theory.

children.title: Summable Error Regimes
children.top_down_role: Long-run inexactness controlled through cumulative error budgets.

assumptions_latex: The inexact proximal iteration is perturbed by vectors \(e_k\in H\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Absolute summability is the classical long-run perturbation condition for inexact fixed-point and proximal iterations.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute summability of additive proximal-step perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an inexact proximal iteration of the form \[x_{k+1}=J_{\lambda_kA}(x_k)+e_k,\] the additive errors are in a summable-error regime when \[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\|e_k\|<\infty.\] Equivalently, the tails \(E_n=\sum_{k=n}^{\infty}\|e_k\|\) are finite and satisfy \(E_n\to0\). This condition controls cumulative perturbation, not merely individual accuracy: it implies \(e_k\to0\), whereas pointwise decay alone does not imply summability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proximal iteration has summable errors when the series of additive error norms is finite, so every tail error budget vanishes.
knowledge_statements.title: Summable Error Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The summability condition is precise, and condition is the correct knowledge kind, but no inspectable source connects it to the stated inexact proximal iteration.

children.title: Decaying Error Regimes
children.top_down_role: Long-run inexactness controlled through diminishing error levels.

assumptions_latex: The inexact proximal iteration uses error magnitudes \(a_k\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A profile-controlled decaying regime satisfies \(a_k\leq C\rho_k\) eventually for some \(C<\infty\), and therefore \(a_k\to0\).

notation.meaning: Magnitude of the kth oracle or step error

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Big-O control by a vanishing positive profile is a standard precise formulation of a decay regime.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise error decay relative to a prescribed vanishing profile.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a_k\geq0\) measure the error of the \(k\)-th inexact proximal-oracle call, and let \(\rho_k>0\) satisfy \(\rho_k\to0\). The errors obey the decay profile \(\rho_k\) if there exist \(C<\infty\) and \(k_0\) such that \[a_k\leq C\rho_k\quad\text{for every }k\geq k_0.\] This condition implies \(a_k\to0\). It imposes no finite cumulative error budget unless the chosen profile is itself summable, that is, unless \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\rho_k<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Errors follow a decaying regime when they are eventually bounded by a constant times a prescribed profile tending to zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Decaying Error Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The profile-controlled decay condition and its distinction from summability are mathematically correct, but no source supports this selected taxonomy for proximal-oracle errors.

children.title: Summability–Decay Boundary
children.top_down_role: Distinctions between cumulative control and pointwise decay requirements.

assumptions_latex: The nonnegative error sequence has polynomial form \(a_k=(k+1)^{-p}\) with \(p>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: One has \(a_k\to0\) for every \(p>0\), but \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_k<\infty\) exactly when \(p>1\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The p-series criterion gives the exact boundary between polynomial decay and absolute summability.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp polynomial boundary separating mere decay from summability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the polynomial error family \[a_k=(k+1)^{-p},\qquad p>0,\] one has \(a_k\to0\) for every \(p>0\). However, the cumulative error is finite precisely when \[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_k<\infty\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p>1.\] Hence \(p=1\) is the sharp summability boundary: errors with \(0<p\leq1\) decay to zero but are not summable. This family demonstrates that pointwise decay, even with an explicit polynomial rate, cannot replace summability in convergence results that require finite accumulated perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial errors always decay for positive exponent, but they are summable only above the sharp exponent-one boundary.
knowledge_statements.title: Summability–Decay Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exponent-one boundary is correct and failure_boundary fits the leaf, but the record has no specific textbook section, theorem, or page locator.

children.title: Rate Interfaces by Operator Geometry
children.top_down_role: Qualitative rate families organized by mapping geometry and certificate type.

children.title: Baseline Convergence-Rate Regimes
children.top_down_role: Baseline convergence and residual-rate families.

children.title: Asymptotic Convergence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Baseline qualitative convergence behavior for proximal and inclusion methods.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone with \(A^{-1}(0)\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iterates converge weakly to some \(x_\star\in A^{-1}(0)\), and \(\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|\to0\).

notation.meaning: Resolvent of A with parameter lambda

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: This is the classical weak-convergence form of the proximal point theorem in Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact proximal point method in a Hilbert space; qualitative weak convergence only.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximally monotone with nonempty zero set, and let \(\lambda_k\geq\underline{\lambda}>0\). Starting from any \(x_0\in H\), define \[x_{k+1}=J_{\lambda_kA}(x_k).\] Then there exists \(x_\star\in A^{-1}(0)\) such that \(x_k\rightharpoonup x_\star\). Moreover, for every \(z\in A^{-1}(0)\), the sequence \(\|x_k-z\|\) is nonincreasing, and the fixed-point residual vanishes: \[\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|\to0.\] No nonasymptotic rate for the last iterate follows from maximal monotonicity alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a nonempty zero set and steps bounded away from zero, exact proximal-point iterates converge weakly and their successive differences vanish.
knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Convergence Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The qualitative proximal-point theorem is correctly scoped to exact iterations in a Hilbert space, but an authoritative theorem locator is required for its hypotheses and conclusions.

children.title: Sublinear Rate Regimes
children.top_down_role: Quantitative rate families below geometric convergence.

knowledge_statements.title: Sublinear Rate Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ergodic generated-value rate for the exact fixed-step proximal point method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximally monotone, choose \(z\in A^{-1}(0)\), and fix \(\lambda>0\). Generate \(x_{k+1}=J_{\lambda A}(x_k)\), define \(v_{k+1}=(x_k-x_{k+1})/\lambda\in A(x_{k+1})\), and set \(\bar v_K=K^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}v_{k+1}\) for \(K\geq1\). Then \[\bar v_K=\frac{x_0-x_K}{\lambda K},\qquad \|\bar v_K\|\leq\frac{2\|x_0-z\|}{\lambda K}.\] Hence \(K\geq 2\|x_0-z\|/(\lambda\varepsilon)\) guarantees \(\|\bar v_K\|\leq\varepsilon\). This is an ergodic norm bound and does not assert graph membership for an averaged primal point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For fixed-step exact proximal-point iterations, the average generated operator value has norm at most twice the initial distance to a zero divided by lambda times the iteration count.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone, and \(z\in A^{-1}(0)\).
The iteration is \(x_{k+1}=J_{\lambda A}(x_k)\) with fixed \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\bar v_K\|\leq2\|x_0-z\|/(\lambda K)\), giving an \(O(K^{-1})\) ergodic residual bound.

notation.meaning: Resolvent of A with parameter lambda
Operator value generated by the kth proximal step
Average of the first K generated operator values
Initial distance to a selected zero

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Telescoping gives the averaged value, while Fejer monotonicity and the triangle inequality give the factor-two bound.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inverse-Square Complexity from a Square-Root Sublinear Rate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A method-independent conversion from a residual-rate bound to an iteration threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let (r_k)_{k\ge 1} be nonnegative and suppose that r_k\le c/\sqrt{k} for every k\ge 1, where c>0. Then, for every \epsilon>0, r_k\le\epsilon for every integer k\ge(c/\epsilon)^2.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a nonnegative residual is at most c divided by the square root of the iteration count, every iteration at or beyond (c/epsilon)^2 has residual at most epsilon.

source_evidence.locator: Nonlinear Optimization / Local Methods in Unconstrained Minimization / Newton’s Method / Proposition 1.7.4

source_refs.locator: Nonlinear Optimization / Local Methods in Unconstrained Minimization / Newton’s Method / Proposition 1.7.4

knowledge_statements.title: Inverse-Square Complexity from a Square-Root Sublinear Rate

source_witnesses.locator: Nonlinear Optimization / Local Methods in Unconstrained Minimization / Newton’s Method / Proposition 1.7.4

directory_assessment.rationale: The result is method-independent, whereas the supplied sublinear-rate node is restricted to proximal performance. A general rate-to-complexity container should be considered in A05; the A08 node should remain a specialization rather than a second primary home.

children.title: Asymptotic-to-Rate Transition
children.top_down_role: Structural conditions separating qualitative convergence from explicit sublinear rates.

assumptions_latex: A nonnegative merit sequence \(q_k\) satisfies \(q_{k+1}\leq q_k-cq_k^{1+\theta}\) for some \(c>0\) and \(\theta>0\).
The iterates remain in the region where this recurrence is valid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q_k\leq(q_0^{-\theta}+c\theta k)^{-1/\theta}\), so a qualitative limit is upgraded to the rate \(q_k=O(k^{-1/\theta})\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: A quantitative descent recurrence is a standard interface converting asymptotic convergence into a polynomial rate.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rate extraction from a quantitative scalar descent recurrence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a nonnegative proximal merit sequence satisfies \[q_{k+1}\leq q_k-cq_k^{1+\theta}\] for every \(k\geq0\), with \(c>0\) and \(\theta>0\), and with the right-hand side nonnegative along the sequence. Then \[q_k\leq\bigl(q_0^{-\theta}+c\theta k\bigr)^{-1/\theta}\] whenever \(q_0>0\); if \(q_0=0\), all subsequent terms vanish. Consequently, the additional quantitative descent relation strengthens the qualitative conclusion \(q_k\to0\) to \(q_k=O(k^{-1/\theta})\). Establishing such a recurrence requires operator geometry beyond maximal monotonicity alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quantitative descent recurrence upgrades asymptotic vanishing of a proximal merit measure to an explicit polynomial rate determined by its geometry exponent.
knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic-to-Rate Transition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scalar recurrence and polynomial estimate are coherent, and property fits the transition leaf, but no source links this recurrence to a specified proximal merit measure or operator geometry.

children.title: Linear Local-Acceleration Regimes
children.top_down_role: Rate families induced by contraction, strong monotonicity, or error bounds.

children.title: Linear Convergence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Geometric rate families supported by contraction or regularity.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally \(\mu\)-strongly monotone with \(\mu>0\).
\(\lambda>0\), \(x^{k+1}=J_{\lambda A}x^k\), and \(x^\star\) is the unique zero of \(A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact global contraction regime for the proximal point iteration under strong monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Strong monotonicity makes the resolvent a contraction: for all \(x,y\in H\), \[\|J_{\lambda A}x-J_{\lambda A}y\|\le \frac{1}{1+\lambda\mu}\|x-y\|.\] Consequently, the proximal point sequence is globally linearly convergent to the unique zero \(x^\star\), with \[\|x^k-x^\star\|\le \left(\frac{1}{1+\lambda\mu}\right)^k\|x^0-x^\star\|.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strongly monotone inclusion has a contractive resolvent, so the proximal point iterates converge globally at an explicit geometric rate.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear Convergence Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem is mathematically plausible and fits the Linear Convergence Regimes container, but it provides no citation supporting the resolvent contraction factor, existence and uniqueness assertion, and resulting global rate. An authoritative monotone-operator source with a specific proposition, theorem, section, or page locator is required.

children.title: Local Acceleration Regimes
children.top_down_role: Enhanced local rate behavior near solution sets.

assumptions_latex: \(T:H\to H\) has a fixed point \(x^\star\) and is Fréchet differentiable at \(x^\star\).
The iteration \(x^{k+1}=T(x^k)\) converges to \(x^\star\), and its reference local linear factor is \(q\in(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local acceleration occurs when \(\rho(DT(x^\star))<q\); it is superlinear when \(DT(x^\star)=0\).

notation.meaning: Derivative of the local fixed-point map

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Derivative-based local criterion relative to an established linear baseline.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The iteration is locally accelerated relative to factor \(q\) when \[\rho(DT(x^\star))<q.\] In finite dimensions, this implies that for every \(r\) satisfying \(\rho(DT(x^\star))<r<q\), all sufficiently late iterates obey \(\|x^{k+1}-x^\star\|\le r\|x^k-x^\star\|\) after passage to an equivalent norm. If \(DT(x^\star)=0\), differentiability yields \[\frac{\|x^{k+1}-x^\star\|}{\|x^k-x^\star\|}\longrightarrow 0,\] which is local superlinear convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Acceleration begins when the derivative of the identified local iteration has spectral radius below the reference linear factor; a zero derivative gives superlinear convergence.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Acceleration Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the Local Acceleration Regimes container, but the derivative-based spectral-radius criterion, equivalent-norm qualification, and superlinear conclusion are unsupported. A precise finite-dimensional fixed-point convergence source is needed to establish the hypotheses under which these claims hold.

children.title: Linear-to-Accelerated Transition
children.top_down_role: Local geometric conditions associated with rate enhancement.

assumptions_latex: \(T_\theta:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) is differentiable at a fixed point \(x_\theta^\star\) for parameters \(\theta\) near \(\bar\theta\).

The linear-to-accelerated transition is classified by comparing the local spectral factor with the certified baseline: \[r(\theta)\begin{cases}>q(\theta),&\text{no improvement over the baseline is certified},\\=q(\theta),&\text{transition boundary},\\<q(\theta),&\text{local acceleration}.
\end{cases}\] The limiting case \(r(\theta)=0\) permits superlinear convergence when the differentiability remainder is \(o(\|x-x_\theta^\star\|)\). Thus the transition concerns local operator geometry, not merely a change in the global iteration count.

children.title: Fixed Metrics
children.top_down_role: Proximal constructions using a stationary Hilbertian metric.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(U:H\to H\) is bounded, self-adjoint, and satisfies \(mI\preceq U\preceq MI\) for some \(0<m\le M<\infty\).
\(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A fixed-metric proximal step uses the same operator \(U\) at every iteration.

notation.meaning: Norm induced by the positive-definite metric

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic proximal geometry whose positive-definite metric is constant across iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The fixed-metric proximity operator is \[\operatorname{prox}^{U}_{f}(x)=\underset{y\in H}{\operatorname{argmin}}\left\{f(y)+\frac12\|y-x\|_U^2\right\}.\] Equivalently, \(p=\operatorname{prox}^{U}_{f}(x)\) exactly when \(0\in\partial f(p)+U(p-x)\), or \(p=(I+U^{-1}\partial f)^{-1}x\). A proximal iteration is in the fixed-metric regime when one such operator \(U\) is selected once and used in every update.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-metric proximal method minimizes the objective plus the same positive-definite quadratic displacement penalty at every iteration.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed Metrics

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally consistent and fits Fixed Metrics, including the metric proximal minimization and resolvent representation. It nevertheless has no cited source; a specific textbook definition, section, or page covering variable-metric proximity is required.

children.title: Iteration-Dependent Metrics
children.top_down_role: Proximal constructions using metrics that vary across iterations.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and each \(U_k:H\to H\) is bounded and self-adjoint.
There exist \(0<m\le M<\infty\) such that \(mI\preceq U_k\preceq MI\) for every \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Iteration-dependent proximity replaces the single metric by the sequence \((U_k)_{k\ge0}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniformly coercive and bounded quadratic metrics allowed to change with the iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function \(f\), an iteration-dependent metric step is \[x^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}^{U_k}_{f}(x^k)=\underset{y\in H}{\operatorname{argmin}}\left\{f(y)+\frac12\|y-x^k\|_{U_k}^2\right\}.\] The uniform inequalities \(mI\preceq U_k\preceq MI\) make every metric norm equivalent to the ambient norm with constants independent of \(k\). Additional control of the changes \(U_{k+1}-U_k\) is separate from this definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An iteration-dependent proximal method changes its positive-definite quadratic metric with the iteration while retaining uniform coercivity and boundedness.
knowledge_statements.title: Iteration-Dependent Metrics

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition appropriately distinguishes iteration-dependent metrics from fixed metrics and states uniform coercivity and boundedness clearly. No citation is supplied for this standard variable-metric formulation, so an authoritative source with an inspectable locator is required.

children.title: Metric-Variation Boundary
children.top_down_role: Stability distinctions between stationary and changing metric regimes.

assumptions_latex: \((U_k)_{k\ge0}\) is a sequence of bounded self-adjoint operators satisfying \(mI\preceq U_k\preceq MI\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Summable relative variation, \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\eta_k<\infty\), bounds cumulative metric drift.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Summable Loewner variation as the standard boundary for controlling accumulated metric drift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The summable metric-variation regime is defined by \[U_{k+1}\preceq(1+\eta_k)U_k,\qquad \eta_k\ge0,\qquad \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\eta_k<\infty.\] It yields \[U_j\preceq\left(\prod_{k=i}^{j-1}(1+\eta_k)\right)U_i\preceq \exp\left(\sum_{k=i}^{j-1}\eta_k\right)U_i\quad(j>i).\] Hence cumulative relative growth remains finite. Uniform spectral bounds alone do not supply this inter-iteration comparison and therefore lie outside this metric-drift certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Summable relative Loewner changes keep cumulative metric growth finite; uniform eigenvalue bounds alone do not control drift between successive metrics.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Variation Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The one-sided summable Loewner-variation condition and its product bound are mathematically coherent and fit the Metric-Variation Boundary container. Because this is one particular variation regime rather than a uniquely canonical boundary, a specific source supporting this formulation and interpretation is required.

children.title: Separability-Coupling Metric Boundary
children.top_down_role: Metrics distinguished by whether they preserve separability.

children.title: Block-Diagonal Metrics
children.top_down_role: Metric geometries preserving blockwise separability.

assumptions_latex: \(H=H_1\oplus\cdots\oplus H_m\) is a finite Hilbert product.
Each \(U_i:H_i\to H_i\) is bounded, self-adjoint, and strongly positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The metric \(U=\operatorname{diag}(U_1,\ldots,U_m)\) contains no cross-block quadratic terms.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product-space quadratic metrics with independent diagonal blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A metric \(U:H\to H\) is block diagonal relative to \(H=\bigoplus_{i=1}^m H_i\) when \[U(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=(U_1x_1,\ldots,U_mx_m).\] Its quadratic form decomposes as \[\|x\|_U^2=\sum_{i=1}^m\|x_i\|_{U_i}^2.\] Consequently, if \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x_i)\), then \(\operatorname{prox}^{U}_{f}(x)\) is obtained blockwise as \(\bigl(\operatorname{prox}^{U_i}_{f_i}(x_i)\bigr)_{i=1}^m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block-diagonal metric has independent positive-definite blocks, so the metric norm and proximal map of a separable function decompose blockwise.
knowledge_statements.title: Block-Diagonal Metrics

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and blockwise decomposition are appropriate for Block-Diagonal Metrics, with the separability hypothesis explicitly stated for the proximal-map conclusion. A specific source locator is still required because the record contains no citation.

children.title: Coupled Metrics
children.top_down_role: Metric geometries introducing cross-block interactions.

assumptions_latex: \(H=H_1\oplus\cdots\oplus H_m\) is a finite Hilbert product.
\(U:H\to H\) is bounded, self-adjoint, and strongly positive, with block operators \(U_{ij}:H_j\to H_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The metric is coupled exactly when \(U_{ij}\ne0\) for some \(i\ne j\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-definite product-space metrics containing at least one cross-block interaction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A metric is coupled relative to the product decomposition when at least one off-diagonal block is nonzero. Its quadratic form is \[\|x\|_U^2=\sum_{i=1}^m\langle U_{ii}x_i,x_i\rangle+2\sum_{1\le i<j\le m}\langle U_{ij}x_j,x_i\rangle.\] The cross terms make the optimality system for \(\operatorname{prox}^{U}_{f}\) jointly dependent on multiple blocks, even when \(f(x)=\sum_i f_i(x_i)\); blockwise evaluation therefore requires additional structure or a transformation that removes the coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coupled metric has nonzero off-diagonal blocks, producing cross terms that generally link the block optimality conditions of an otherwise separable objective.
knowledge_statements.title: Coupled Metrics

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record fits Coupled Metrics and correctly identifies off-diagonal blocks as cross-block quadratic interactions in the real product-space setting. The general claim about joint proximal optimality and the required additional structure is uncited; an authoritative product-space or preconditioned-proximity source is required.

children.title: Separability–Coupling Boundary
children.top_down_role: Computational distinctions caused by cross-block metric structure.

assumptions_latex: \(H=H_1\oplus\cdots\oplus H_m\) is a finite Hilbert product.
\(U:H\to H\) is bounded, self-adjoint, and strongly positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Metric additivity across blocks holds if and only if \(U\) is block diagonal.

notation.meaning: Canonical injection of block i into the product space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact algebraic boundary between additive and cross-block quadratic proximal geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The following conditions are equivalent: \(U\) is block diagonal; \(E_i^*UE_j=0\) for every \(i\ne j\); and there exist quadratic forms \(Q_i\) on \(H_i\) such that \[Q_U(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=\sum_{i=1}^m Q_i(x_i)\quad\text{for every }x\in H.\] Thus a nonzero off-diagonal block is exactly the boundary at which metric energy ceases to be separable. For every block-separable proper convex function, unconditional blockwise proximal decomposition is guaranteed on the block-diagonal side.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic metric is separable exactly when all off-diagonal blocks vanish; any nonzero cross block moves the geometry into the coupled regime.
knowledge_statements.title: Separability–Coupling Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits the Separability–Coupling Boundary container and states the expected equivalence between block diagonality and additive quadratic energy. No evidence is supplied for the equivalence or the universal blockwise proximal-decomposition consequence, so a precise source locator is required.
