children.title: Conjugate Lookup Failures
children.top_down_role: Catalog mismatches involving conjugacy, scaling, or domain structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Conjugate Lookup Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exhibits failure caused by omitting the scaling in Moreau's identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(t)=\tfrac12t^2\) on \(\mathbb R\), let \(\lambda=2\), and let \(x\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\). Since \(f^*=f\) and \(\operatorname{prox}_{2f}(x)=x/3\), the unscaled expression satisfies \(\operatorname{prox}_{2f}(x)+\operatorname{prox}_{2f^*}(x)=2x/3\neq x\). The correctly scaled identity is \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)+\lambda\operatorname{prox}_{f^*/\lambda}(x/\lambda)=x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every nonzero scalar input, a self-conjugate quadratic disproves the unscaled conjugate lookup, while the parameter-scaled Moreau identity remains valid.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct quadratic check of Moreau-scaling failure

children.title: Spectral Lookup Failures
children.top_down_role: Catalog mismatches involving spectral invariance or matrix structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Lookup Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes singular-value proximal calculus from entrywise scalar lookup.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H=\mathbb R^{2\times2}\) with the Frobenius inner product, let \(f(Z)=\|Z\|_*\), use the unit proximal parameter, and set \(X=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\). The singular values of \(X\) are \(2\) and \(0\), so singular-value soft thresholding gives \(\operatorname{prox}_{f}(X)=\tfrac12X\). Entrywise scalar soft thresholding at level \(1\) instead gives the zero matrix. Thus the spectral proximal rule cannot be replaced by entrywise lookup.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the Frobenius matrix space, nuclear-norm proximity thresholds singular values rather than entries; on the all-ones rank-one matrix the spectral result is one half of the matrix, whereas entrywise thresholding gives zero.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal H=\mathbb R^{2\times2}\text{ with the Frobenius inner product}

notation.meaning: unit-parameter proximal mapping in the Frobenius metric
entrywise scalar soft thresholding at level one

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: singular-value thresholding on an explicit rank-one matrix

children.title: Catalog Recognition Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits of recognizing proximal forms under transformations.

knowledge_statements.title: Catalog Recognition Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary for combining proximal catalog entries without verifying domain compatibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a Hilbert space and let \(f,g\in\Gamma_0(H)\). Separate catalog formulas for \(\operatorname{prox}_f\) and \(\operatorname{prox}_g\) do not by themselves produce a formula for \(\operatorname{prox}_{f+g}\): the sum must first be proper and the proposed calculus rule must satisfy its stated qualification conditions. For distinct points \(a,b\in H\), take \(f=\iota_{\{a\}}\) and \(g=\iota_{\{b\}}\). Then \(\operatorname{prox}_f(x)=a\) and \(\operatorname{prox}_g(x)=b\) for every \(x\in H\), but \(f+g\equiv +\infty\), so \(\operatorname{prox}_{f+g}\) is not defined as a proximal mapping of a proper convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recognizing both summands in a proximal catalog is insufficient: their sum may be improper, so no proximal formula exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{prox}_f\) and \(\operatorname{prox}_g\) exist everywhere, whereas \(\operatorname{prox}_{f+g}\) is unavailable because \(f+g\notin\Gamma_0(H)\).

children.title: Monotone Inclusion Failures
children.top_down_role: Failures involving zeros, maximality, operator sums, and solution sets.

children.title: Inclusion Nonsolvability Family
children.top_down_role: Models with no inclusion solution or feasible equilibrium.

children.title: Empty Zero Sets
children.top_down_role: Operator models whose zero sets contain no solution.

knowledge_statements.title: Empty Zero Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A maximal monotone operator need not possess a zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(A:\mathbb R\rightrightarrows\mathbb R\) by \(A(x)=\{e^x\}\). Equivalently, \(A=\partial f\) for the proper lower-semicontinuous convex function \(f(x)=e^x\). Hence \(A\) is maximally monotone. Nevertheless, \(e^x>0\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R\), and therefore its zero set is empty: \[\operatorname{zer}A=\{x\in\mathbb R:0\in A(x)\}=\varnothing.\] Thus maximal monotonicity alone supplies resolvent well-posedness, not existence of a solution to the associated inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdifferential of the exponential function is maximally monotone but has no zero because the exponential is always positive.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exponential-subdifferential counterexample is precise and fits the leaf, but no source with a specific locator is supplied for the nontrivial maximal-monotonicity claim. An authoritative subdifferential maximality theorem locator is required.

children.title: Inconsistent Inclusions
children.top_down_role: Inclusion formulations with incompatible equilibrium requirements.

knowledge_statements.title: Inconsistent Inclusions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A monotone inclusion can be inconsistent even when its operator is maximally monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a nonzero real Hilbert space, choose \(b\in H\setminus\{0\}\), and define \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) by \(A(x)=\{b\}\) for every \(x\in H\). This constant, full-domain operator is maximally monotone. The inclusion \[0\in A(x)\] is inconsistent, since it is equivalent to \(0=b\). Equivalently, taking the zero operator \(M\) and the constant operator \(B(x)=\{b\}\), the structured inclusion \(0\in Mx+Bx\) has no solution although both summands are maximally monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero constant maximal monotone operator yields the impossible inclusion zero equals a nonzero vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is maximally monotone and \(\{x\in H:0\in A(x)\}=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: constant set-valued operator with singleton value \(b\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The constant-operator example correctly expresses an inconsistent inclusion and fits the counterexample container, but the assertion that the full-domain constant operator is maximally monotone lacks an inspectable authoritative citation.

children.title: Nonsolvability Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Connections between zero-set emptiness and inclusion inconsistency.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsolvability Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resolvent fixed points correspond exactly to zeros of a maximal monotone operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximally monotone on a real Hilbert space and let \(\lambda>0\). Its resolvent \(J_{\lambda A}=(\operatorname{Id}+\lambda A)^{-1}\) is everywhere defined and single-valued. For every \(x\in H\), \[x=J_{\lambda A}x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in x+\lambda A(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0\in A(x).\] Consequently, \(\operatorname{Fix}J_{\lambda A}=\operatorname{zer}A\), and the monotone inclusion is nonsolvable exactly when the resolvent has no fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximal monotone inclusion has no solution exactly when its resolvent has no fixed point.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-point/zero-set equivalence is mathematically standard and matches the leaf title, but it has no source locator. In addition, this is an equivalence property or correspondence, not a duality; the content kind should be corrected when a sourced replacement is prepared.

children.title: Operator-Sum Maximality Failures
children.top_down_role: Incomplete graphs and unqualified operator sums.

children.title: Operator Nonmaximality
children.top_down_role: Monotone operators whose graphs lack maximality.

knowledge_statements.title: Operator Nonmaximality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonicity does not imply maximal monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a nonzero real Hilbert space \(H\), define \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) by \(A(0)=\{0\}\) and \(A(x)=\varnothing\) for \(x\ne0\). Its graph \(\{(0,0)\}\) is monotone. It is not maximally monotone, because it is properly contained in the graph of the zero operator \(Z(x)=\{0\}\) for every \(x\in H\), and \(Z\) is monotone. Thus an operator can satisfy the monotonicity inequality while admitting a proper monotone graph extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The singleton graph containing only the origin is monotone but not maximal because the zero operator properly extends it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is monotone but not maximally monotone.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The singleton-graph operator is a valid counterexample to monotonicity implying maximal monotonicity and fits the terminal container. No authoritative definition or theorem locator is provided, however.

children.title: Sum-Maximality Failure
children.top_down_role: Operator sums that fail maximality under missing qualification.

knowledge_statements.title: Sum-Maximality Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite-dimensional sums of maximal monotone operators may lose maximality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space containing closed vector subspaces \(U,V\) such that \(U^\perp+V^\perp\) is not closed. Set \(A=N_U\) and \(B=N_V\). Both normal-cone operators are maximally monotone, while \(A+B\) is monotone with domain \(U\cap V\) and values \[(A+B)(x)=U^\perp+V^\perp\qquad(x\in U\cap V).\] Its graph is not closed because its constant value is not closed; consequently, \(A+B\) is not maximally monotone. Individual maximality therefore does not ensure sum maximality without a qualification condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normal cones to two closed subspaces can each be maximal while their sum is nonmaximal when the summed orthogonal complements are nonclosed.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is an infinite-dimensional real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_U\) and \(N_V\) are maximally monotone, but \(N_U+N_V\) is not maximally monotone.

notation.meaning: normal-cone operator of a closed convex set \(C\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional closed-subspace construction is coherent and has the correct counterexample role. Its substantive claims about maximal normal cones and failure of sum maximality require an authoritative infinite-dimensional example or theorem locator.

children.title: Individual-to-Sum Maximality Boundary
children.top_down_role: Distinctions between maximality of components and maximality of their sum.

knowledge_statements.title: Individual-to-Sum Maximality Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional interior qualification separating guaranteed and unguaranteed sum maximality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A,B:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\) be maximally monotone. If \[\operatorname{dom}A\cap\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}B)\ne\varnothing,\] or symmetrically with \(A\) and \(B\) interchanged, then the pointwise sum \(A+B\) is maximally monotone. The implication from individual maximality to maximality of the sum is not valid without an appropriate domain qualification in general; in infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, normal cones to closed subspaces with a nonclosed sum of orthogonal complements furnish a failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An interior-domain qualification guarantees maximality of a finite-dimensional operator sum; individual maximality alone does not guarantee it generally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A+B\) is maximally monotone under the qualification; removing such qualifications invalidates the general implication.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-dimensional interior-domain qualification and the stated infinite-dimensional failure boundary are plausible and appropriately scoped, but neither the sum theorem nor the counterexample is supported by a citation with a specific locator.

children.title: Range-Solution Geometry Failures
children.top_down_role: Approximate solvability, nonattainment, and nonunique solution geometry.

children.title: Nonclosed Operator Ranges
children.top_down_role: Range geometry permitting approximate solvability without exact attainment.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Operator Ranges
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A bounded maximal monotone linear operator may have nonclosed range.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(H=\ell^2\), define the bounded linear operator \(T\) by \((Tx)_n=x_n/n\). The operator is self-adjoint, positive, and maximally monotone. Its range is not closed: for \(y=(1/n)_{n\ge1}\in\ell^2\), the finite truncations \(y^{(k)}\) belong to \(\operatorname{ran}T\) and converge to \(y\), but \(y\notin\operatorname{ran}T\), since \(Tx=y\) would require \(x=(1,1,\ldots)\notin\ell^2\). Hence \(y\in\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}\setminus\operatorname{ran}T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The diagonal operator dividing the nth coordinate by n is maximal monotone and has a dense-limit point missing from its range.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is maximally monotone and \(\operatorname{ran}T\) is not closed.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The diagonal operator and nonclosed-range calculation are correct and fit the counterexample leaf. The nontrivial assertion of maximal monotonicity has no authoritative source locator.

children.title: Nonisolated Solutions
children.top_down_role: Solution sets lacking local isolation.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonisolated Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximal monotonicity does not imply that zeros are isolated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(A:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2\) by \(A(x_1,x_2)=(x_1,0)\). This continuous linear operator is monotone, has full domain, and is maximally monotone. Its zero set is \[\operatorname{zer}A=\{(0,t):t\in\mathbb R\}.\] Every solution is therefore a limit point of other solutions. In particular, neither maximal monotonicity nor single-valued linearity ensures local uniqueness or isolation of a solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coordinate projection is maximal monotone, yet its zero set is an entire line and contains no isolated point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is maximally monotone and every point of \(\operatorname{zer}A=\{0\}\times\mathbb R\) is nonisolated.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coordinate-projection example correctly has a line of nonisolated zeros and fits the leaf. A specific authoritative source is still required for the maximal-monotonicity assertion.

children.title: Approximate-Solvability Boundary
children.top_down_role: Separation between near-range behavior and attained solution geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate-Solvability Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure of the range characterizes arbitrarily small residuals, not exact solvability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any operator \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\), arbitrarily accurate residual solutions exist precisely when \[\inf_{x\in H}\operatorname{dist}(0,A(x))=0,\] equivalently \(0\in\overline{\operatorname{ran}A}\). Exact solvability requires the stronger condition \(0\in\operatorname{ran}A\). To separate them, let \((Tx)_n=x_n/n\) on \(\ell^2\), take \(y=(1/n)_{n\ge1}\), and define \(A(x)=Tx-y\). Then \(0\in\overline{\operatorname{ran}A}\setminus\operatorname{ran}A\): residuals can converge to zero although \(0\in A(x)\) has no solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vanishing residuals mean zero lies in the range closure; an exact solution exists only when zero lies in the range itself.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_x\operatorname{dist}(0,A(x))=0\iff0\in\overline{\operatorname{ran}A}\), while exact solvability is equivalent to \(0\in\operatorname{ran}A\).

notation.meaning: distance from zero to the value set \(A(x)\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distinction between membership in the range and its closure is mathematically coherent and matches the failure-boundary container. No inspectable source supports the general residual equivalence or the shifted diagonal example.

children.title: Fixed-Point Certificate Failure System
children.top_down_role: Limits of fixed-point existence, convergence interpretation, and residual certification.

children.title: Fixed-Point Existence-Contraction Boundary
children.top_down_role: Well-defined mappings without fixed points, uniqueness, or contractive behavior.

children.title: Empty Fixed Sets
children.top_down_role: Mappings that are well defined but possess no fixed points.

knowledge_statements.title: Empty Fixed Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonexpansiveness alone does not guarantee a fixed point on an unbounded domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(H=\mathbb R\), define \(T(x)=x+1\). For all \(x,y\in\mathbb R\), \[|T(x)-T(y)|=|x-y|,\] so \(T\) is nonexpansive, with Lipschitz constant one. However, \(T(x)=x\) would imply \(1=0\), and hence \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\varnothing\). Thus a nonexpansive self-map of a complete Hilbert space need not have a fixed point when no compactness, bounded invariant set, coercivity, or strict contraction hypothesis is imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Translation by one is a nonexpansive self-map of the real line with no fixed point.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Translation by one is a valid, precisely stated counterexample showing that nonexpansiveness alone does not ensure a fixed point. The record nevertheless lacks the required authoritative citation and locator.

children.title: Noncontractive Geometry
children.top_down_role: Fixed-point geometry lacking contractive control or uniqueness.

knowledge_statements.title: Noncontractive Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Firm nonexpansiveness permits Lipschitz factor one and nonunique fixed points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\mathbb R\times\{0\}\subset\mathbb R^2\) and let \(P_C(x_1,x_2)=(x_1,0)\) be the metric projection. The mapping \(P_C\) is firmly nonexpansive, but its optimal Lipschitz constant is one because distances between distinct points of \(C\) are preserved. Moreover, \[\operatorname{Fix}P_C=C,\] so its fixed points are nonunique. Therefore firm nonexpansiveness, although stronger than nonexpansiveness, does not provide the strict contraction factor required for Banach's contraction principle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto a line is firmly nonexpansive but not a strict contraction, and every point on the line is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_C\) is firmly nonexpansive with Lipschitz constant one and \(\operatorname{Fix}P_C=C\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Projection onto a line correctly demonstrates firm nonexpansiveness without strict contraction or fixed-point uniqueness, and the failure-boundary kind fits the leaf. The projection facts require an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: Existence–Contraction Boundary
children.top_down_role: Distinctions between fixed-point existence and contractive behavior.

assumptions_latex: \((D,d)\) is a nonempty complete metric space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q<1\) guarantees a unique fixed point, whereas \(q=1\) alone guarantees neither existence nor uniqueness.

notation.meaning: Lipschitz constant of the fixed-point map

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Banach contraction boundary for a self-map of a complete metric space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(d(Tx,Ty)\le qd(x,y)\) for every \(x,y\in D\) and some \(q\in[0,1)\), then \(\operatorname{Fix}T\) consists of exactly one point. This conclusion fails at the nonexpansive boundary \(q=1\): on \(D=\mathbb R\), the translation \(T(x)=x+1\) satisfies \(|T(x)-T(y)|=|x-y|\) but has \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\varnothing\). Thus nonexpansiveness cannot replace both an independent fixed-point existence hypothesis and strict contraction when uniqueness or linear distance control is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict contraction gives a unique fixed point. At the nonexpansive boundary, even existence can fail, as shown by translation on the real line.
knowledge_statements.title: Existence–Contraction Boundary

children.title: Small Residual Without Error Control
children.top_down_role: Residual decay that does not certify solution distance without regularity.

assumptions_latex: \(T:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is the displayed fixed-point map.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of a global residual error bound without metric subregularity or comparable regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(T(x)=x-x/(1+x^2)\) on \(\mathbb R\). Its fixed-point set is \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\{0\}\). For \(x_n=n\), the residual satisfies \(r(x_n)=|x_n-Tx_n|=n/(1+n^2)\to0\), but \(\operatorname{dist}(x_n,\operatorname{Fix}T)=n\to\infty\). Consequently, no finite constant \(\kappa\) can satisfy the global error bound \(\operatorname{dist}(x,\operatorname{Fix}T)\le\kappa\|x-Tx\|\) for all \(x\in\mathbb R\). Residual decay alone therefore does not certify proximity to a solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-point residual may vanish along points whose distance from every fixed point diverges, so an error-bound regularity assumption is essential.
knowledge_statements.title: Small Residual Without Error Control

children.title: Shadow-Recovery Convergence Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Distinctions between fixed variables, recovered solutions, and convergence modes.

children.title: Shadow-Solution Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on interpreting shadow variables as recovered inclusion solutions.

assumptions_latex: \(A,B:H\rightrightarrows H\) are maximally monotone on a real Hilbert space.

notation.meaning: resolvent of a maximally monotone operator

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-stepsize Douglas–Rachford recovery boundary for a two-operator monotone inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x=J_Az\). From \(z\in\operatorname{Fix}T\) one obtains \(J_B(2x-z)=x\). The resolvent relations give \(z-x\in Ax\) and \(x-z\in Bx\), hence \(0\in Ax+Bx\). Therefore the shadow \(x\) solves the inclusion \(0\in(A+B)x\). The fixed variable \(z\), however, is only a certificate from which a solution is recovered; it need not itself solve the inclusion. Any convergence claim about solutions must consequently identify and analyze the shadow sequence rather than silently identifying it with the fixed-point sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Douglas–Rachford fixed point certifies a solution through its resolvent shadow; the fixed variable itself need not be a solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Shadow-Solution Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The unit-stepsize Douglas–Rachford recovery statement and normalization are mathematically plausible and internally consistent, but no source is supplied for this specialized fixed-point/shadow correspondence.

children.title: Weak-Convergence Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits associated with weak rather than strong convergence.

notation.meaning: weak convergence in the Hilbert space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite-dimensional boundary separating weak convergence from norm and distance convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(y=(y_j)_{j\ge1}\in\ell^2\), one has \(\langle e_n,y\rangle=y_n\to0\), so \(e_n\rightharpoonup0\). Nevertheless, \(\|e_n-0\|=1\) for all \(n\). Hence weak convergence of fixed or shadow variables in an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space does not imply strong convergence, vanishing solution distance, or convergence of arbitrary norm-continuous merit quantities. Such conclusions require additional structure, for example finite dimensionality, compactness, uniform monotonicity, or an independent error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In infinite dimensions, weakly convergent iterates can remain a fixed positive norm from their limit, so weak convergence alone gives no norm convergence.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak-Convergence Boundaries

children.title: Fixed-Variable Recovery Gap
children.top_down_role: Distinctions between convergence of fixed variables and recovery of target solutions.

assumptions_latex: \(U,V\) are closed vector subspaces of a real Hilbert space \(H\).

notation.meaning: orthogonal projector onto a closed subspace
Douglas–Rachford operator for the two subspaces

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact fixed-variable versus shadow decomposition for Douglas–Rachford splitting on two closed subspaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Douglas–Rachford fixed-point set decomposes as \(\operatorname{Fix}T=(U\cap V)\oplus(U^\perp\cap V^\perp)\). Thus a fixed variable has the form \(z=x+w\), where \(x\in U\cap V\) is feasible and \(w\in U^\perp\cap V^\perp\) is an invisible displacement. Its shadow satisfies \(P_Uz=x\in U\cap V\). Whenever \(U^\perp\cap V^\perp\ne\{0\}\), fixed points exist that are not feasible points, demonstrating that convergence of the fixed variable cannot be reported as convergence to a primal solution without applying the recovery map.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two subspaces, a Douglas–Rachford fixed point may contain an orthogonal displacement; projection removes it and recovers the feasible shadow.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Variable Recovery Gap

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated Douglas–Rachford fixed-set decomposition is specialized and has no citation. A targeted source is required before accepting the exact formula and recovery claim.

children.title: Metric-Computational Failure Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Breakdowns caused by invalid metrics, costly proximal subproblems, and unstable evaluation.

children.title: Metric Validity Failure Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Loss of coercivity, resolvent geometry, or metric stability.

children.title: Indefinite Metrics
children.top_down_role: Geometric failures caused by negative-curvature directions in the chosen metric.

knowledge_statements.title: Indefinite Metrics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of metric proximal minimization when positive semidefiniteness is lost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(M:H\to H\) be bounded and self-adjoint. Suppose that some \(v\in H\setminus\{0\}\) satisfies \(\langle Mv,v\rangle<0\). For \(f:H\to\mathbb R\) given by \(f\equiv0\) and proximal center \(x=0\), the nominal metric proximal objective along \(y=tv\) is \(f(tv)+\tfrac12\langle M(tv),tv\rangle=\tfrac12t^2\langle Mv,v\rangle\), which tends to \(-\infty\) as \(|t|\to\infty\). Hence the proximal subproblem is unbounded below and has no minimizer. Thus an indefinite operator does not define a squared norm or provide the coercive convex regularization required by standard metric proximal theory.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a real Hilbert space, a negative direction of a bounded self-adjoint metric candidate makes the quadratic proximal objective unbounded below, so even the proximal map of the zero function is undefined.
assumptions_latex: \(M:H\to H\) is bounded and self-adjoint, and some \(v\ne0\) satisfies \(\langle Mv,v\rangle<0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{y\in H}\tfrac12\langle My,y\rangle=-\infty\), so the metric proximal point is undefined.

notation.meaning: quadratic form induced by the metric candidate

children.title: Degenerate Metrics
children.top_down_role: Loss of coercive control caused by singular or nearly singular metric structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonuniqueness boundary for a positive-semidefinite but singular proximal metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(y=(y_1,y_2)\), the metric proximal objective is \(\tfrac12\|y-x\|_M^2=\tfrac12(y_1-x_1)^2\), independently of \(y_2\). Every point \((x_1,t)\) is therefore a minimizer. Thus positive semidefiniteness without positive definiteness supplies only a seminorm and need not make a proximal subproblem strongly convex or its proximal mapping single-valued. Uniqueness requires curvature from the objective along \(\ker M\) or a metric bounded below by \(mI\) for some \(m>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singular metric ignores its null directions, allowing an entire affine set of proximal minimizers unless the objective supplies the missing curvature.
knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Metrics

children.title: Uncontrolled Metric Variation
children.top_down_role: Instability arising when metric changes lack sufficient uniform control.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without summable relative variation, descent measured in \(M_k\) need not yield a common quasi-Fejér Lyapunov inequality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lyapunov boundary for variable-metric proximal and splitting analyses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Changing the metric introduces the exact energy increment \(\|u\|_{M_{k+1}}^2-\|u\|_{M_k}^2=\langle(M_{k+1}-M_k)u,u\rangle\), whose positive part is not controlled by a descent inequality written only in the current metric. A standard sufficient variation budget is \(M_{k+1}\preccurlyeq(1+\eta_k)M_k\) with \(\eta_k\ge0\) and \(\sum_k\eta_k<\infty\), together with uniform positive-definiteness. Without comparable control, successive Lyapunov functions may increase arbitrarily at metric changes, so the usual variable-metric quasi-Fejér convergence inference is unavailable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Per-iteration descent can be erased by arbitrary metric changes; summable relative variation and uniform definiteness restore a comparable Lyapunov scale.
knowledge_statements.title: Uncontrolled Metric Variation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited general-convergence section is not a targeted source for the specialized variable-metric quasi-Fejér condition. Support is needed for the summable relative-variation criterion and the claimed convergence boundary.

children.title: Proximal Cost-Conditioning Tradeoff
children.top_down_role: Formal proximability that fails to yield an effective computation.

children.title: Expensive Proximal Solves
children.top_down_role: Proximal subproblems whose resource cost defeats their formal tractability.

knowledge_statements.title: Expensive Proximal Solves
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle accounting for proximal steps implemented by nested iterative optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose that after \(j\) inner oracle calls at outer iteration \(k\), an inner solver guarantees \(E_{k,j}\le C_k\rho_k^j\), where \(C_k>0\) and \(0<\rho_k<1\). If \(C_k>\delta_k>0\), choosing \(N_k\ge\left\lceil\log(C_k/\delta_k)/(-\log\rho_k)\right\rceil\) is sufficient for this bound to certify \(E_{k,N_k}\le\delta_k\); if \(C_k\le\delta_k\), the bound already certifies the target at \(N_k=0\). When \(K\) outer proximal iterations use \(N_k\) inner calls, their total inner-oracle cost is exactly \(\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}N_k\). Treating each generic proximal evaluation as unit cost can therefore conceal the dominant computational expense.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A geometric inner-error guarantee gives a sufficient logarithmic inner-iteration budget for each requested tolerance, and total nested work is the sum of those inner iterations rather than merely the number of outer steps.
assumptions_latex: At outer iteration \(k\in\{0,\ldots,K-1\}\), the inner solver satisfies \(E_{k,j}\le C_k\rho_k^j\) after \(j\) oracle calls, with \(C_k>0\) and \(0<\rho_k<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The certified choice is \(N_k\ge\left\lceil\log(C_k/\delta_k)/(-\log\rho_k)\right\rceil\) when \(C_k>\delta_k\), and the total inner-oracle cost is \(\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}N_k\).

notation.meaning: inner oracle calls at outer iteration k
certified inner error after j calls at outer iteration k

children.title: Ill-Conditioned Proximal Solves
children.top_down_role: Proximal subproblems with severe sensitivity or unstable numerical behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Ill-Conditioned Proximal Solves
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean smooth proximal subproblem with scalar positive-definite metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable and suppose \(0\le\mu\le L\) and \(\mu I\preccurlyeq\nabla^2f(y)\preccurlyeq LI\) for every \(y\in\mathbb R^d\). For \(m>0\), \(\lambda>0\), and \(x\in\mathbb R^d\), define \(\phi_x(y)=f(y)+\tfrac{m}{2\lambda}\|y-x\|^2\). Then \((\mu+m/\lambda)I\preccurlyeq\nabla^2\phi_x(y)\preccurlyeq(L+m/\lambda)I\), so its Hessian condition number is at most \((L+m/\lambda)/(\mu+m/\lambda)\). Equality is possible for a quadratic whose Hessian has eigenvalues \(\mu\) and \(L\). In particular, when \(\mu=0\), the bound is \(1+\lambda L/m\), which becomes large as the proximal stepsize grows relative to the metric scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a smooth convex objective on Euclidean space, the proximal quadratic shifts the Hessian spectrum by m/lambda. The resulting condition-number bound can still become large when the original objective is not strongly convex and the proximal stepsize is large.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is twice continuously differentiable.
\(0\le\mu\le L\) and \(\mu I\preccurlyeq\nabla^2f(y)\preccurlyeq LI\) for every \(y\in\mathbb R^d\).
The proximal metric is \(M=mI\) with \(m>0\), and \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The proximal subproblem has Hessian condition number at most \((L+m/\lambda)/(\mu+m/\lambda)\), with equality possible for quadratic \(f\).

children.title: Cost–Conditioning Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Regimes where attempts to reduce solve cost worsen numerical sensitivity.

knowledge_statements.title: Cost–Conditioning Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar-metric tradeoff between conditioning of the proximal subproblem and contraction of the exact outer map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable and satisfy \(\mu I\preccurlyeq\nabla^2f(y)\preccurlyeq LI\) for every \(y\in\mathbb R^d\), where \(0<\mu\le L\). For \(m>0\) and \(\lambda>0\), consider \(x^+=\operatorname{prox}_{(\lambda/m)f}(x)\). The inner proximal objective has condition bound \(\kappa(m)=(L+m/\lambda)/(\mu+m/\lambda)\), while the exact proximal map is Lipschitz with factor at most \(q(m)=1/(1+\lambda\mu/m)=m/(m+\lambda\mu)\). As \(m\) increases, \(\kappa(m)\) decreases toward \(1\), but \(q(m)\) increases toward \(1\). Thus improving inner conditioning by increasing the scalar metric weakens the guaranteed outer contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Increasing the scalar proximal metric improves the condition bound for the inner problem but shortens the effective proximal step and weakens the outer contraction guarantee.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is twice continuously differentiable.
\(\mu I\preccurlyeq\nabla^2f(y)\preccurlyeq LI\) for every \(y\in\mathbb R^d\), with \(0<\mu\le L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Increasing \(m\) decreases \(\kappa(m)=(L+m/\lambda)/(\mu+m/\lambda)\) toward \(1\) but increases \(q(m)=m/(m+\lambda\mu)\) toward \(1\).

notation.meaning: upper bound on the outer contraction factor

children.title: Nested-Accuracy Recognition Failures
children.top_down_role: Incompatible inner accuracy or incorrect closed-form catalog matches.

children.title: Inner Accuracy Budgets
children.top_down_role: Permissible inexactness within proximal subproblem evaluations.

assumptions_latex: \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone on a real Hilbert space with \(\operatorname{zer}A\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accumulated inner perturbation is finite, and \((x_k)\) converges weakly to a point of \(\operatorname{zer}A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute summable-error budget for an inexact proximal-point iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An admissible absolute inner-accuracy budget chooses nonnegative tolerances \((\varepsilon_k)\) satisfying \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\varepsilon_k<\infty\) and enforces \(\|e_k\|\le\varepsilon_k\) in every proximal computation. Under the stated maximal-monotonicity, solvability, and stepsize assumptions, the resulting inexact proximal-point sequence converges weakly to some \(x_\star\in\operatorname{zer}A\). Merely requiring \(\varepsilon_k\to0\) is weaker than this budget and does not provide the same finite accumulated-perturbation control.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A standard inner budget makes proximal errors absolutely summable; under maximal monotonicity and positive stepsizes, this preserves weak convergence to a zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Inner Accuracy Budgets

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The absolute summable-error condition is a standard inexact proximal-point budget and the kind fits the leaf, but the supplied locators do not specifically support the maximal-monotone weak-convergence theorem. A targeted inexact-PPA theorem or section is required.

children.title: Outer Progress Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Dependence of outer-level progress on the quality of inner solves.

knowledge_statements.title: Outer Progress Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-error sensitivity of one proximal step for a maximally monotone inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p=J_{\lambda A}x\) and let \(q\) satisfy \(e\in q-x+\lambda A q\) for some \(e\in H\) with \(\|e\|\leq\eta\). Then \(q=J_{\lambda A}(x+e)\), \(\|q-p\|\leq\eta\), \(\|(x-q)-(x-p)\|\leq\eta\), and \(\|x-q\|\geq\max\{0,\|x-p\|-\eta\}\). If \(\eta\geq\|x-p\|\), these residual bounds alone provide no positive lower bound on the computed outer displacement \(\|x-q\|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inner residual bounded by eta perturbs the exact proximal point and its displacement by at most eta. If eta is at least the exact displacement, these residual bounds alone give no positive lower bound on the computed outer displacement.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone, \(x\in H\), \(\lambda>0\), and \(\eta\geq0\).
\(p=J_{\lambda A}x\), while \(q\in H\) satisfies \(e\in q-x+\lambda A q\) for some \(e\in H\) with \(\|e\|\leq\eta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|(x-q)-(x-p)\|\leq\eta\) and \(\|x-q\|\geq\max\{0,\|x-p\|-\eta\}\); when \(\eta\geq\|x-p\|\), the latter bound cannot certify positive outer displacement.

children.title: Inner–Outer Accuracy Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Failure regimes caused by incompatible inner precision relative to outer requirements.

knowledge_statements.title: Inner–Outer Accuracy Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility condition between an inner inclusion residual and an outer proximal-gap test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p=J_{\lambda A}x\) and let \(q\) satisfy \(e\in q-x+\lambda A q\) for some \(e\in H\) with \(\|e\|\leq\eta\). Then \(\|x-p\|/\lambda\leq\|x-q\|/\lambda+\eta/\lambda\). Therefore, acceptance under \(\|x-q\|/\lambda\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{stop}}\) guarantees \(\|x-p\|/\lambda\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}\) whenever \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{stop}}+\eta/\lambda\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}\). If this budget condition is violated, the computed acceptance test and residual bound alone need not guarantee the requested true accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The stopping threshold plus the scaled inner residual tolerance must not exceed the desired outer accuracy for this sufficient guarantee. If that budget condition is violated, computed acceptance and the residual bound alone need not ensure the true proximal-gap target.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone, \(x\in H\), and \(\lambda>0\).
\(p=J_{\lambda A}x\), and \(q\in H\) satisfies \(e\in q-x+\lambda A q\) for some \(e\in H\) with \(\|e\|\leq\eta\), where \(\eta\geq0\).
\(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{stop}}\geq0\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}\geq0\), and the outer test accepts when \(\|x-q\|/\lambda\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{stop}}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{stop}}+\eta/\lambda\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}\) is sufficient for computed acceptance to imply \(\|x-p\|/\lambda\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}\).

children.title: False Proximal Recognition
children.top_down_role: Incorrect matches to closed-form proximal catalogs or familiar operator patterns.

knowledge_statements.title: False Proximal Recognition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A scalar quadratic example where loose inner tolerance produces a false zero-step signal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(t)=t^2/2\), let \(A=\partial f=I\). For any \(x\neq0\), choose the computed point \(q=x\) and residual \(e=\lambda x\). Then \(e\in q-x+\lambda A q\), so the residual test \(|e|\leq\eta\) is satisfied whenever \(\eta\geq\lambda|x|\). Nevertheless, \(|x-q|=0\), whereas \(0\notin A(x)\) and \(|x-J_{\lambda A}x|=\lambda|x|/(1+\lambda)>0\). Thus the loose residual test recognizes a nonstationary point as proximal-stationary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a scalar quadratic, returning the current nonzero point produces a zero computed step and passes the residual test when eta is at least lambda times the magnitude of the point, even though the exact proximal displacement is positive and the point is not stationary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q\) passes the residual test and has \(|x-q|=0\), although \(0\notin A(x)\) and \(|x-J_{\lambda A}x|=\lambda|x|/(1+\lambda)>0\).
